Title: IGE: Enhancing Diversity by Changing Institutional Culture and Scaffolding Student Success
Program(s): Project & Program Evaluation, NSF Research Traineeship (NRT)
Organization: Board of Regents, NSHE, obo University of Nevada, Reno
Abstract:
Racial, ethnic and gender diversity enhances creativity and is essential for sustained innovation, entrepreneurial activity and global competitiveness. However, diversification at the graduate level remains a major challenge for many universities. What is needed is a comprehensive, scalable and cost-effective approach that can address: low ethnic/racial diversity; low doctoral degree completion rates, and inadequate preparation to succeed in graduate school and pursue academic, private sector and professional careers in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM). This National Science Foundation Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) award to the University of Nevada, Reno will test a novel recruitment, retention and career preparedness approach for increasing the representation of first-generation college students and students from historically underrepresented groups in STEM graduate education.  Students will be engaged in two 3-week summer boot camps as well as additional professional development, mentoring, and social network support activities during the first 1.5 years of graduate school.  Unique elements of this project include (1) intentional development of a recruitment/retention positive feedback loop, (2) family/community involvement to enhance support groups, and (3) training in marketable skills (e.g. communication via virtual reality platforms). Outcomes from this project will generate new knowledge concerning best practices for recruitment and retention of historically underrepresented populations.  

While this project is broadly focused on recruitment, retention and career preparedness for historically underrepresented groups of graduate students, there are five major areas being addressed.  Specifically, the project will test interventions and compare results across control and test groups to examine potential changes in: (1) academic performance and research quality, (2) non-financial family support, (3) ease of navigation toward degree completion and career placement, (4) recruitment and retention, and (5) student research and communication skills. Interventions include quantitative disciplinary and transferrable skills modules, social support networks and enhanced mentoring and mentor training.  Formative/summative assessment and hypothesis testing procedures will include surveys, academic performance comparisons, course evaluations, focus groups, one-on-one interviews, social network interviews, FIG (Family Involvement in Graduate School) assessment of students/family members and National Resource Mentoring Network surveys of faculty members. Interventions will be evaluated individually and collectively to determine whether student and faculty participation enhanced graduate education outcomes, improved mentor/mentee relationships and enhanced recruitment of historically underrepresented groups and first-generation students through positive feedback loops.  

The Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) program is focused on research in graduate education. The goals of IGE are to pilot, test and validate innovative approaches to graduate education and to generate the knowledge required to move these approaches into the broader community.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.
Outcome Report:
Despite the efforts of universities, government, and instruction, diverse groups with doctoral degrees in STEM remain underrepresented. However, our project has made strides in addressing this issue. The NSF-IGE-funded Graduate Acceleration through Innovation and Networking (GAIN) Scholars program, a two-year doctoral retention program, has been instrumental in generating enthusiasm for STEM, building community among participants and families, and providing critical skills germane to STEM careers. It incorporated two three-week-long boot camps implemented by an interdisciplinary team of faculty members from diverse fields such as biology, civil and environmental engineering, computer science and engineering, human development and family science, mathematics and statistics, diversity and equity, journalism, and public health. In synergy with an existing recruitment program, the GAIN program has not only addressed the need for a globally competitive, diverse academic and private sector workforce but has also made a tangible impact on diversity in STEM education.
  The GAIN Scholars program has been a platform for personal and professional growth. It provided faculty mentor training and summer intensive training modules for GAIN Scholars. At the end of these modules, GAIN Scholars reported substantial improvements in skill assessment and individual development plans, smartphone app development, R-based statistical analysis, computational tools for big data, virtual/augmented reality, and family support and content within family life education. The overall outcome data is a testament to the program's effectiveness, significantly enhancing participants' competencies in these domains. 
  One of the key pillars of the GAIN Scholars program was its inclusive approach, extending support not just to the scholars but also to their families. Family members were invited to the opening ceremony, a day of programming, and online activities, fostering a sense of community and shared responsibility. We learned from the GAIN Scholars and their families that families play supportive and connective roles and that challenges to family roles and support are in areas of communication, doctoral student stress, and having different worldviews and approaches to life. GAIN Scholars and their family members spoke highly of the program, and families appreciated the program's support opportunities, further reinforcing the program's inclusive nature. We developed and validated a Family Involvement in Graduate School measure, an instrument to measure family involvement in graduate students’ education.     
  Due to limited sample sizes, the researchers looked at trends in data and effect sizes due to concerns of being underpowered for statistical analyses. Results indicated a favorable response to the program with 86% of participants in the GAIN Scholars program reporting being somewhat or very somewhat satisfied with the program. Scholars in the GAIN program reported a higher number of presentations at regional or state conferences (3.0) compared to the control group students at 2.36. For research presentations given on campus, the average was 1.12 presentations for the GAIN Scholars, and 1.1 for the comparison group. GAIN Scholars had 1.1 research papers in review, while comparison students had 0.36; similarly, GAIN Scholars had 2.2 papers in progress, while comparison students had 1.2 papers. GAIN Scholars also received more scholarships and other funding. Findings from this project also indicated that GAIN Scholars were more likely to complete individualized development plans and there was some evidence to suggest that GAIN Scholars had greater interpersonal skills and support networks.

Title: IGE: Graduate Opportunities to Learn Data Science (GOLD): Empowering female and underrepresented graduate students through inclusive data science training
Program(s): NSF Research Traineeship (NRT), Project & Program Evaluation
Abstract:
The amount of data generated by modern scientific research is unprecedented. While this leads to technological advances and scientific discoveries, it also creates a dire need for a workforce with data science skills. In addition, society needs a more diverse science workforce, as creative and robust scientific and technological advances result from more diverse scientific teams. With the right approach, we can train diverse basic science graduate students in data science to fill these workforce needs. This National Science Foundation Innovations of Graduate Education (IGE) award to San Francisco State University will evaluate a novel, modular approach for inclusive graduate education to advance data science skills in the basic sciences. The Graduate Opportunities to Learn Data science (GOLD) strategy will support basic science Masters students, focusing on women and students from historically underrepresented groups, to (1) learn computational and statistical skills, (2) apply those skills to their research projects, and (3) form strong learning and networking communities. This new approach will create inclusive environments that prepare diverse students to obtain the interdisciplinary skills necessary to boost their career development. The GOLD program is modular, so successful components can easily be adopted at other universities, creating the potential for a significant impact on graduate education. 

The Graduate Opportunities to Learn Data science (GOLD) strategy will be implemented through a 12-unit interdisciplinary certificate program. The program includes a 9-unit series of courses that will teach programming and data science, using assignments and examples drawn from biology and chemistry research. A 1-unit class taken twice will help students to apply these skills to their own thesis research supported by peer-mentors. A 1-unit professional development class will connect students with local computational biologists and chemists working in academia and industry, helping the students network and contextualize their training. To ensure an inclusive environment, GOLD will (1) use validated methods to mitigate well-known barriers that alienate many women and underrepresented students entering high-tech fields and (2) provide faculty professional development on inclusive teaching strategies, active learning, and mentoring. The success of the GOLD strategy will be assessed based on five student outcomes using a mixed methods approach: acquisition of computational skills, application of computational skills, career goals, perception of inclusive learning environments, and scientific identity. Outcomes will contribute to the current state of pedagogy in graduate education and enable successful implementation of similar programs. 

The Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) program is focused on research in graduate education. The goals of IGE are to pilot, test and validate innovative approaches to graduate education and to generate the knowledge required to move these approaches into the broader community.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.
Outcome Report:
How the GOLD certificate program started
Around 2018, undergraduate students in our departments (Biology and Chemistry) had the option to participate in the PINC computing minor, and it wasn’t long before graduate students began asking for similar opportunities. At the time, several of us computational scientists were already collaborating on initiatives like a computational summer program, united by our shared passion for data science, teaching, and promoting equity and diversity. During one of our classes with graduate students, we decided to conduct an informal survey: Who would be interested in a certificate program in data science? Many hands shot up. Encouraged by the enthusiasm, we decided to pursue NSF funding to make it happen.
What could go wrong? 
We wanted to offer data science skills to our master’s students, but from the beginning were aware of all the things that could go wrong. A. We were worried that only students with prior coding experience would join the program. B. We were worried that students would not sign up if they thought the program was too daunting (e.g., too many units). C. We were worried that the program would not be attractive to certain demographics, especially women of color. D. We were worried that offering the program would turn out to be too much work for our departments. 
How did we design the program? 
We tried to balance usefulness and doability. We ended up with a program that included 4 classes: In semester 1, students would take a 3-unit computing in Python class. In semester 2, students would take a 4-unit data science in R class. In semester 3, students would take a 1-unit class on careers in data science and a 1-unit coding support class. Finally, to make this a 12-unit certificate we included a semester of research in the requirements, but since all our master students need to take several semesters of research anyways, this doesn’t increase their workload. 
Does it work? 
Yes. We designed the program including three new data science classes. Since 2020, we have had between 30 and 40 students in the program each year, which is around half of the master students in Biology and Chemistry/Biochemistry. The program is also doable for the departments. The first class (the Python class) is offered by Computer Science. The other classes are offered by Biology or Chemistry/Biochemistry. There is enough interest amongst our faculty to teach the classes. In fact, this year (2024), none of the original people who designed the program are teaching in it. 
How did the pandemic affect our efforts? 
The launch date for GOLD was fall 2020. Obviously, the pandemic changed many things. We couldn’t do all the activities we had planned, especially professional development we had planned for faculty. However, for the students, the pandemic sped up the rolling out of the GOLD program. We had originally planned to only enroll a pilot cohort of 10 students in 2020, but because our campus was closed and many students couldn’t do the experimental work they had planned, there was a lot of interest in the GOLD program and we enrolled almost 40 students that first year. 
Issues and pitfalls
The GOLD program has changed our graduate programs. We estimate that about half of our master students enroll in the program. But that doesn’t mean that there are no issues. A) The 1-unit classes are good for the students, but hard to staff because most of our classes are 3 units and 1 unit doesn’t count enough. B) We are always worried that with the four-class schedule, the students are not exposed to enough topics and skills. For example, they don’t take machine learning, statistics or sequence analysis. C) The success of the GOLD program classes has led to reduced enrollment in “real” biology classes which worries some faculty. D) Because we only offer GOLD classes only once a year, students need to sign up for the Python class in their first semester. If they miss that opportunity it is much harder for them to do the program. 
Conclusion
Thanks to our previous experience, high student interest, support from our departments and an NSF grant, we were able to design a certificate program that allows a large fraction of our graduate students to learn coding and data science skills.

Title: IGE: Building practical, evidence-based teaching capacity in tomorrow's doctorates
Program(s): NSF Research Traineeship (NRT), Project & Program Evaluation
Abstract:
Future faculty can expect that they will instruct students from many diverse populations. While access to college science education has democratized, the methods used to teach these diverse cohorts of students are not always aligned with evidence-based best practices.  This project implements and evaluates a training approach for future faculty that leverages best practices in inclusive science teaching within a multi-stage practical experience. This National Science Foundation Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) award to the University of Washington will make use of the best features of top professional development models to innovatively prepare future professors for the unique challenges of teaching college STEM courses. The undergraduate students that the participating graduate students will teach will join the workforce having more than basic memorized knowledge: they will also understand scientific practice, know how to apply scientific thinking and generate scientific questions, and be prepared to partake in a more diverse and effective scientific community. 

This project balances cutting-edge teacher development within the constraints of modern graduate work to develop dual expertise in science and teaching. Practice of active teaching skills will help trainees develop classroom tools and teaching approaches that put engaging work in the hands of their students.  Rapid feedback from expert instructors, outside consultants, test classrooms, and their own video analysis will further their development as teachers capable of effectively employing methods far beyond simple passive lecturing. While developing a syllabus around their own cutting-edge research, trainees will be guided through challenges in a teaching course centered on diversity and equity for all students. When ready, trainees will teach their own mentored courses to college seniors as a starting point for careers that include ambitious and equitable teaching of science. These courses will introduce undergraduates directly to current research in their field of study as taught by the scientists actively doing the work. Success of the training for each graduate instructor will be investigated and communicated through interviews with students, student project work, and professional evaluation by expert instructors in the field.  Collectively, these results will inform the overall evaluation of the training approach.        

The Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) program is focused on research in graduate education. The goals of IGE are to pilot, test and validate innovative approaches to graduate education and to generate the knowledge required to move these approaches into the broader community.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.
Outcome Report:
Outcomes for IGE #1855841:
Building practical, evidence-based teaching capacity in tomorrow's doctorates
  College STEM professors instruct many thousands of students, but their training in active and inclusive teaching is often marginal or gained only in the midst of complex research and teaching careers. It is in this learning context that talented STEM students must navigate their foundational coursework, and this contributes to inequities that we see in STEM success and lack of skill building for STEM careers. To maximize the success of future generations of scientists, our students in STEM need professors who teach with great equity, great skill-development, and without the need to learn their teaching craft through teaching many courses. Grant #1855841 provided the support to develop, run, and research the training of excellent college science instructors within the constraints of their science PhDs.
  The Science Teaching Experience Program for Upcoming PhDs (STEP-UP) was based at the University of Washington. Advanced graduate students in a broad range of STEM fields were taught through a multi-step program in which they learned the fundamentals of education philosophy, practiced large-scale and micro-skills in teaching with expert guidance, and developed courses within their areas of active research. Under the mentorship of experienced professional developers, the trainees in STEP-UP taught new courses to STEM students.
  Independent research on the teaching of these trainees and the experiences of their students found the teaching and learning in these courses to be excellent. Students were driven to engage in high-level scientific skill development and perceived these STEM courses to be demanding, emotionally supportive, and more inclusive than other courses taught by much more experienced instructors. The direct observation of STEP-UP-trained instructors compared favorably in their depth of active learning techniques when measured against a national sample of experienced professors. These benefits were achieved without slowing the progress of their PhD graduations, and alumni found the experience to be central to their career progress and earning new faculty positions. These findings were published in two peer-reviewed manuscripts.
  Throughout STEP-UP, thirty-one graduating STEM PhDs developed critical teaching skills and direct experience that show them to be successful STEM instructors already. This program, and others that might draw on design elements identified by this funded research, have the potential to overhaul instructional techniques and STEM equity throughout academia. In particular, STEP-UP focused on practice-based skill development and authentic practice opportunities for those skills. These aspects, which are described in research manuscripts now, will stand as a model for institutions to successfully and efficiently broaden the skills of their graduate scientist instructors.

Title: IGE: Building A Multi-University Consortium
Program(s): Project & Program Evaluation, NSF Research Traineeship (NRT)
Full Address: 601 S KNOLES DR RM 220, FLAGSTAFF, AZ, ="86011"
Abstract:
This National Science Foundation Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) award to Northern Arizona University will implement and test a new consortium model for building a multi-institution, multi-disciplinary, high-quality graduate curricula. This collaborative effort ? WindU, for graduate training in wind energy - between Northern Arizona University, Texas Tech University, Penn State University, and the University of Massachusetts Amherst will offer expanded graduate educational opportunities beyond what each institution can provide. The project team will pilot and test a new, replicable model for creating an expandable consortium in STEM graduate education, designed to increase the breadth and frequency of course offerings and educational opportunities available to a diverse group of students. The new model, Rapid, proposes an innovative delineation of the elements required to successfully set up a consortium, covering a range of activities from curriculum planning to financial agreements, consortium management and governance, student support systems and course delivery, and including future consortium expansion and sustainability. Also innovative is its goal to create a consortium that is readily able to add new members, and the inclusion of webinars shared among consortium members and international partner organizations for swift diffusion of new knowledge. As universities respond to society's demand for educational programs in rapidly evolving technical fields, models for multi-university, multi-disciplinary consortiums such as Rapid provide critical pathways for success. 

The main objective of the project is to pilot and test the Rapid model, and to add to the knowledge base in how to effectively establish a consortium. The Rapid model is a new facilitation model developed from evidence-based models described in the literature and implemented in practice. The goal of the project is to study the pilot-test of the Rapid model as applied to a consortium in wind energy graduate education (WindU). Questions guiding this research study are: 1) How was the Rapid model used for developing a consortium in STEM graduate education? and, 2) In what ways was the Rapid model effective for consortium development? The project team will use a design and development research process described in the Common Guidelines for Education Research and Development to provide real-time evidence for model pilot-testing during consortium development and, ultimately, for identifying the final model for dissemination. Design-based research supports the development and continuous improvement of education innovations in complex systems, such as the WindU consortium, by engaging the program team in iterative cycles of design, implementation, analysis and redesign.

Outcome Report:
Project Outcomes Report
IGE: WindU - A Multi-University Consortium in Wind Energy Graduate Education - Meeting a National Need
WindU was a collaborative effort between Northern Arizona University, Texas Tech University, Penn State University, and the University of Massachusetts Amherst to jointly plan and offer expanded graduate educational opportunities in wind energy. Building upon published literature, the project team piloted and tested a new, replicable model for rapidly creating an expandable, multi-university, multi-disciplinary consortium in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) graduate education, designed to increase the breadth and frequency of course offerings and educational opportunities available to a diverse group of students. The new model, Rapid, describes a comprehensive set of activities to successfully set up a consortium in one year, including curriculum planning, financial agreements, consortium management and governance, student support systems and course delivery, and consortium sustainability. Wind energy graduate education is the STEM discipline in which the model was tested.
The purpose in creating a multi-university consortium is to leverage the academic talent and programs of several universities together in a common vision to create a robust STEM graduate academic program, available online, with the breadth of courses required to meet the needs of students, business, research, and society. STEM education is rapidly evolving as technology evolves and as educational practices and tools advance. For example, since the turn of the century in 2000, wind energy transformed from a nascent technology with potential into what is now one of the lowest cost forms of electric power generation available. As a technology, the engineering and development of wind systems spans the topics of atmospheric science, environmental science and policy, mechanical and materials engineering, design, fluid mechanics, electrical engineering, control systems, civil engineering, power systems, social sciences, optimization, computing, economics, and more. For any single university, it would be difficult to have expertise in all these fields, let alone faculty with experience in applying that expertise in any one specialization such as wind energy. Similarly, since 2000, the ability to deliver high-quality university programs has expanded from primarily in-person, on-campus classes to online programs available both synchronously and asynchronously. Successful, effective, online educational consortiums that rely on multiple universities are now more possible than ever.
The Rapid model tested a suite of coordinated activities involving defined teams of university staff and faculty both within and across universities to set up a consortium of graduate education courses. Several "functional teams" were convened to address planning activities including courses and curriculum, financial agreements, consortium management and governance, student support systems and course delivery, and future consortium expansion and sustainability. The model was successfully applied, and the "WindU" consortium was created and sharing courses within a year. The financial model required sharing $500 per semester credit hour (an amount less than the lowest per-credit-hour cost at any of the partner universities), with this amount being split 70% to the teaching institution, 20% for management of the consortium, and 10% remaining with the home institution of each student to support its participation in the consortium. After establishment, the consortium shared nine courses over the final two-years of the grant, with 92 students participating. Data was collected on the effectiveness of the model via interviews with a broad group of participants responsible for setting-up and implementing the consortium. The interviews supported several aspects of the model, in particular its use of functional teams and the need for campus champions and an objective facilitator, but also highlighted deficiencies related to the need for more communication, course approval and instructor qualifications at each university, and full involvement of the university programs with financial obligations. Challenges uncovered in setting-up the financial model included how to handle students with tuition waivers (e.g., teaching assistants), how to ensure graduate students at the universities were eligible for the courses offered at the partner universities, and ensuring the programs responsible for sending tuition to the partner institutions were aware of the costs and benefits. The experience of the project team in piloting the model combined with the interviews led to several revisions of the Rapid model, depicted in the illustration below. The intellectual merit of the project centered on the creation of the Rapid model, its investigation and revision, and dissemination of the results at national conferences such as the North American Wind Energy Academy (NAWEA) WindTech Conference, and other venues. The broader impacts include establishment of the consortium, publicly available webinars from international experts, and wind energy programs made available to online students broadening the potential to reach a diversity of communities.

Title: IGE: Creative Interdisciplinary Research in Graduate Education (CIRGE)
Program(s): Project & Program Evaluation, NSF Research Traineeship (NRT)
Abstract:
Creativity is at the heart of innovation, and yet STEM graduate courses are rarely devoted to explicitly teaching creative practices and problem-solving strategies. Instead, graduate students often struggle to develop creative thinking skills on their own. Graduate training also typically takes place within academic silos that limit students' exposure to other disciplinary approaches and cross-disciplinary problem solving.  This National Science Foundation Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) award to Drexel University will test the purposeful infusion of creative thinking and problem solving into the STEM graduate curriculum within an interdisciplinary space. The project will test whether such an approach can enhance creativity and collaborative problem-solving skills beyond the boundaries of the classroom and beyond an individual discipline. The goal is to train students in best practices for team-based research by providing a versatile skill set to address team processes and interpersonal issues and foster synergy towards arriving at creative solutions that exceed those achieved by a collection of individuals.

Two graduate courses will be developed in creativity to explicitly expose students to creative practices and problem-solving strategies within an interdisciplinary team space.  The two courses will allow students to discover recent advances in creativity research and practice. During the courses, students will apply these principles by devising team-based solutions to STEM-related societal problems and by creatively improving student thesis research. The project has an implementation component to ensure smooth integration across university disciplines and a research component that evaluates the effectiveness of the courses in enhancing creativity, problem-solving and team practices. The research component will examine student, peer, and faculty stakeholders using a mixed-methods, longitudinal approach to generate formative and summative assessments. The goal is to arrive at an evidence-based set of learning experiences for enhanced creative practices and improved problem solving. Dissemination of these results may provide a platform for other institutions to adapt.

The Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) program is focused on research in graduate education. The goals of IGE are to pilot, test and validate innovative approaches to graduate education and to generate the knowledge required to move these approaches into the broader community.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.
Outcome Report:
Intellectual Merit. CIRGE, Creative Interdisciplinary Research in Graduate Education, was designed to help graduate students become proficient in creative problem solving through interdisciplinary teamwork. A new graduate minor Interdisciplinary Team-Oriented Creativity (ITOC) was developed that facilitated students from disparate disciplines to be creative, innovative problem solvers through two core courses in creativity and two electives; at least one elective was outside the home department. The core course Creative Interdisciplinary Team Research: Principles and Practice provided fluency with the foundational principles in cognitive research that demonstrably enhance creative practice and problem-solving skills. Students learned of recent advances in creativity research and practice and also gained practice developing these skills in team-based projects that addressed societal problems. The second core course, Enhancing the Creativity of a Research Project, involved students working in interdisciplinary teams with faculty coaching, to infuse greater creativity into each student's research project.
Broader Impact. Two manuscripts were published from research into the efficacy of the ITOC program. One manuscript described the effective practices for teaching the interdisciplinary courses that were employed by a five-membered, disciplinarily diverse faculty team with expertise in chemistry, design, education, and business/psychology. The main finding was that convergence, reaching a common understanding of information through discussion, was more important, and more difficult, than conveyance, sharing new information. A second manuscript described the process of developing the two courses and the course iterations based on mixed methods data. Collectively, these two manuscripts provide a valuable resource for others interested in developing interdisciplinary courses, particularly in creativity. The impacted more than 30 students who completed one or more of the courses.

Abstract:
This National Science Foundation Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) award to North Carolina A&T State University (NCAT) will study the development of research identity in engineering graduate students. Briefly stated, research identity refers to the ways in which graduate students define themselves as researchers and is an important factor in student success. Specifically, this project will implement and test approaches to foster research identity development for graduate students in non-research-intensive institutions. It should be noted that smaller institutions/programs often face deficiencies that can impact the ability of faculty mentors to foster student research identities both individually and as part of a larger group. In engineering, a faculty advisor generally guides the graduate research experience and the advisor is the primary resource to help graduate students develop their identities as engineering researchers.  Given this apprenticeship model, the mentoring and guidance that a student receives in developing a professional identity is largely dependent on the style, resources, and graduate student group size of the faculty mentor.  This project is testing interventions that could potentially overcome these limitations, particularly for students in smaller graduate programs.

This study on engineering research identity will be conducted at a Carnegie R2 institution (NCAT), a leading producer of African-American engineers, and it will implement a three-pronged approach that is grounded in sociological and psychological theories of identity.   The project entails (1) establishing a Research Engineer Network that will help graduate students develop a research engineer identity; (2) forming Small Research Groups of faculty members with common interests who will foster students' research skills; and (3) designing and administering a survey-based Research Engineer Identity scale and assessment using a mixed-methods research design that includes focus groups, structured interviews, and web-based surveys. The design will culminate with a quasi-experimental test comparing the development of research identify among students participating in the study and a control group of matched students. The three coordinated innovations in this project will collectively build and assess an innovative infrastructure for developing research identify in graduate engineering students. It is anticipated that the project results will be applicable to universities broadly, while particularly informing practice in smaller graduate programs.

The Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) program is focused on research in graduate education. The goals of IGE are to pilot, test and validate innovative approaches to graduate education and to generate the knowledge required to move these approaches into the broader community.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.
Outcome Report:
In this National Science Foundation Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) project, a team of sociologists, engineering faculty, researchers, and administrators at North Carolina A&T State University have been building a graduate learning environment that promotes the development and assessment of students' research identity (RI). A Research Identity (RI) includes personal, role, and group-based defining oneself as someone who "solves problems by rearranging the stuff of the world to make new things." Specifically, this project has implemented and tested approaches to foster research identity development for graduate students in non-research-intensive institutions. We have fostered a mentorship model wherein; the student receives mentoring and guidance in developing a professional identity to broaden their research and professional competencies.
Intellectual Merit: The IGE project includes three coordinated initiatives. First, the Graduate Researcher Identity Development (GRID) program was developed that provides research-intensive degree-seeking students in STEM disciplines with knowledge and a skill set that will enhance their graduate researcher experience. The course introduces students to the concept of "Graduate Researcher Identity" and a set of academic, professional, and personal skills that foster the development of GRID. The course includes a series of asynchronous, self-paced modules and in-person events focused on networking, mentoring, and career preparation. Second, the IGE project supports the development of Small Research Groups (SRGs) in which two or more faculty and graduate students collaborate on a research or creative product. Finally, the IGE project engages in a Research Identity (RI) Assessment Process that involves pairing well-established social and psychological theories of identity with a mixed-method social science research design to identify the content, character, and complications associated with efforts to develop RI among graduate students.
Broader Impact: The core components of the three coordinated initiatives for developing research identify in graduate engineering students has been developed. A mentorship program is established with academic, industry and research organizations for graduate students to explore a variety of career pathways and collaborations with external partners under expert guidance. The research identity project has been adopted by other graduate disciplines at NC A&T beyond engineering, while particularly informing practice in smaller graduate programs. The GRID program is also extended to the undergraduate researchers via the NC-LSAMP program on campus. The results of this project have been disseminated via conference proceedings, presentations, panel discussions, manuscripts, and a web-portal. This project has validated interventions to graduate education and generated the knowledge required to move these approaches into the broader community.

Title: IGE: STEM Graduate training in Data Science: solution-oriented, student-led, team-based, computationally-enriched (SOLSTICE) training
Program(s): Project & Program Evaluation, NSF Research Traineeship (NRT)
Abstract:
There has been a rapid increase in both the amount and type of data collected in many fields of science, technology and engineering; this requires new approaches to train graduate students to meet these needs.  The new data revolution calls for a new data-savvy workforce capable of using data effectively to answer important scientific and practical questions and to communicate the results to a broad audience. These data scientists should have strong technical and leadership skills and the ability to work in teams comprising different and complementary expertise. To meet this training need, the National Science Foundation Innovations of Graduate Education (IGE) award to Tufts University will test an innovative approach to project-based learning, teaching graduate students in data-intensive fields using real datasets to solve real-world problems. This solution-oriented, student-led, team-based, computationally-enriched (SOLSTICE) training environment will offer multidisciplinary team role-play and experience in data analytics and scientific communication. This project will evaluate the effectiveness of the SOLSTICE approach in providing an adaptable method for instructors in a range of fields that use large datasets at diverse institution types. As the SOLSTICE approach is refined, it will pave the way for students to enter the workforce with strong technical skills in data analytics and be effective members of research teams. 

The project will answer two overarching research questions: (1) To what extent does the SOLSTICE approach provide opportunities for students to achieve 21st-century data intensive knowledge, skills, and attitudes? and (2) Are there variations in students' achievement over time, across different courses that use the SOLSTICE approach, and across different STEM disciplines? The approach consists of three components: (1) 3D Role Play, in which each student plays the role of Team Lead, Collaborator, and Reviewer in three different interdisciplinary teams aiming to develop, execute and communicate a research project based on authentic secondary data analyses; (2) Feedback on Feedback, which provides students with experience in giving and receiving effective critiques to their peers to strengthen inter-team communication; and (3) Data Analysis Roadmap, which offers knowledge-building guides and examples of key elements for efficient data analysis plans and other documents needed for effective communication of results. The approach will be tested and evaluated in six data-intensive courses in the Friedman School of Nutrition and in the School of Engineering, with approximately 270 participants monitored before, during, and for at least six months after participation in a SOLSTICE-based course. Educational resources will be developed based on successful components to guide replications of the training process, to train faculty in the SOLSTICE approach, and to disseminate it to other STEM fields. 

The Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) program is focused on research in graduate education. The goals of IGE are to pilot, test and validate innovative approaches to graduate education and to generate the knowledge required to move these approaches into the broader community.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.
Outcome Report:
Innovative approaches for STEM education that address the rapidly changing demands of data-intensive fields are critical to prepare graduate students for the modern workforce. We conducted an NSF-funded study aimed at implementing, evaluating, and disseminating a transformative learning approach to offer students SOLution-oriented, STudent-Initiated, Computationally-Enriched (SOLSTICE) training. The SOLSTICE approach emphasizes the incorporation of three components in the course curricula: 3D Role Play to facilitate team-based problem solving; Feedback-on-Feedback to enhance collaborative work; and an Analytic Roadmap to support the navigation and management of a semester-long project.
In SOLSTICE-based courses, each student was designated the Principal Investigator (PI) of their own research project, a collaborating PI (Co-PI) of one partner's project, and a Reviewer of a second partner's project. Thus, mimicking team-based research environments, 3D Role allowed each student to lead their own project, collaborate with a peer's project, and evaluate or review another peer's research. Each week, groups have designated instruction time for in-class discussions, peer feedback, and feedback on the quality and focus area of each other's feedback (e.g., Feedback-on-Feedback). To facilitate collaboration, course instructors developed online discussion forums where homework assignment responses were posted and commented on prior to in-class discussion. For courses rich in the instruction of visualization software, student websites were created using WordPress to create a research portfolio for storing images. These websites aimed to communicate research to diverse audiences and were designed to demonstrate the effects before and after addressing peer feedback comments and recommendations. Peer feedback and Feedback-on-Feedback was also integrated into midterm and end-of-term project rubrics to encourage collaborative discussion of research hypotheses, statistical methodology, and anticipated research challenges. Finally, to hone project and time management skills, we required students to complete data management and analysis plans (DMAPs) to serve as a roadmap for midterm and final project submissions. These plans were completed incrementally throughout the semester; each weekly assignment incorporated questions from the final DMAP that, when combined, ensured its completion by the conclusion of the semester. This scaffolded incremental approach also allowed for students to iteratively reflect on and revise research project components, including data quality inspections, study aims, research hypotheses, analytical methods, visuals, and results tables/figures, throughout the semester.   
As part of the human subjects IRB approval process (approved in January 2020), we received written approval to enroll courses across 6 schools of Tufts University. These schools reside on 3 campuses and offer a wide range of data-intensive courses in engineering, social, medical, and veterinary sciences. For each participating school, we reviewed all available courses prior to each academic semester to identify those suitable for participation. Of all available courses, we created an inventory of 30 courses whose syllabi met the following criteria: a) most enrolled students had graduate level standing; and b) course objectives emphasized skills to form research hypotheses and require students to examine, analyze, and/or visualize data (biostatistics, statistics, geographic information systems, remote sensing, data visualization, statistical programming, epidemiology, informatics, etc.); and c) courses with midterm and end of term projects or project-based learning opportunities prioritized student research projects. Instructors for these courses were invited to participate in the study and offered clarifications on the study design, consent process, and pre/post-assessment surveys via remote information sessions.
Over the 3-year study, we collected pre/post assessments from 249 consented students enrolled in 26 data-intensive courses to explore how well the proposed approach provided opportunities to achieve the desired knowledge, skills, and attitudes. The 95-question surveys were constructed to reflect the proficiency in introductory, intermediate, and advanced tasks typically performed in data-intensive courses. The questions were asked on a student's years of active experience with specific software packages and programming languages and their preferred software to perform data management and analysis tasks; students' experiences providing and receiving peer feedback and critical evaluation; familiarity with common tools to complete data-oriented tasks, and students' opinions regarding the importance of those tools. Students' responces were collected using an electronic survey hosted on the Qualtrics platform at the beginning (entry survey) and end (exit survey) of each academic semester. We created knowledge, skills, and attitudes scores based on questions ranked in accordance with typical requirements for introductory, intermediate, and advanced courses for students studying public health, nutrition, and biological/environmental sciences.
We compared the change in knowledge, skills, and attitudes scores among 158 students whose courses fully or partially implemented the SOLSTICE approach (treatment group) and compared this group to the 91 students whose courses did not implement the SOLSTICE approach (control group) using linear regression models adjusted for baseline score levels and key demographic factors. While significant improvements were observed in all participating courses, students exposed to the SOLSTICE training approach demonstrated significantly higher advanced knowledge as compared to controls. Furthermore, students taking SOLSTICE-based courses were often engaged in research activities, participated in scientific conferences, and publishing their work in peer-reviewed journals.

Title: IGE: Enhancing imaginative and collaborative STEM capacity through creative inquiry
Program(s): NSF Research Traineeship (NRT), Project & Program Evaluation
Organization: University of Georgia Research Foundation Inc
Full Address: 310 E CAMPUS RD RM 409, ATHENS, GA, ="306021589"
Abstract:
Advanced scientific and technical training is insufficient to position the leaders of tomorrow to solve the complex problems we face. They must also be able to think creatively, to collaborate across disciplines, and to work with people with different perspectives, knowledge, and values. There is compelling evidence that creativity training can stimulate both scientific creativity and interdisciplinary collaboration, but to date, little attention has been given to creativity training in STEM graduate education. This National Science Foundation Innovations of Graduate Education (IGE) award to the University of Georgia will bring a diverse group of graduate students together from STEM and arts disciplines to address issues in the local watershed using creativity-based training methods from the arts. This project will investigate the impact of targeted creativity training on the ability of STEM students to frame problems in new ways and help diverse teams solve complex problems. If successful, widespread adoption of these methods will contribute to equipping STEM graduates across the country with communication and collaboration skills and ultimately increase creative and innovative solutions to complex global environmental challenges.

Over each of five semesters, this project will recruit a cohort of ten students in the early stages of graduate study, five from STEM disciplines who self-identify as interested in environmental science, and five from arts disciplines. Cohorts will meet for six workshops facilitated by two faculty members from STEM and arts disciplines. Workshops are designed to build core creative competencies and develop skills for collaborative interdisciplinary practice. Students will gain practical experience sharing disciplinary viewpoints, creating analogies from scientific concepts, and developing collaborative frameworks for complex problem solving. The final workshop will result in a set of proposed solutions to a local watershed problem, collaboratively identified by students and stakeholders. Complementary quantitative and qualitative methods will be used to examine students' abilities to shift thinking (increase "cognitive flexibility"), generate novel ideas, and effectively communicate and collaborate with one another. This project seeks to fundamentally enhance how STEM students are educated by engaging them in creative processes related to their research topics. Successful elements will be incorporated into a scalable training model that will be widely disseminated and available for adoption at other institutions.

The Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) program is focused on research in graduate education. The goals of IGE are to pilot, test and validate innovative approaches to graduate education and to generate the knowledge required to move these approaches into the broader community.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.
Outcome Report:
To solve today's most complex challenges, scientists need more than just technical expertise. They must also think creatively and work effectively with people from different backgrounds. Research shows that creativity training can boost scientific innovation and teamwork, yet such training is rarely included in STEM graduate education. The Creativity and Collaboration in STEM project at the University of Georgia (UGA), explored how creativity-based training from the arts can help STEM graduate students improve their problem-solving and collaboration skills. The program brought together graduate students from STEM, arts, and other disciplines for a series of workshops designed to strengthen creative thinking and interdisciplinary teamwork
Key Findings
First, participants unanimously reported that the program was engaging and valuable, for both their professional and personal development. Program evaluators reported that there were four components of the program that created effective learning conditions: 1) activities were open ended and exploratory, 2) activities were fun, but challenging, 3) the environment created by instructors was low-pressure and supportive, and 4) activities were designed to push participants beyond their comfort zones, but in a safe environment. Quantitative analyses showed a modest increase in cognitive flexibility (a measure of creativity) before and after the program. Qualitative analyses indicated that participants increasingly recognized the benefits of working with peers from different disciplines throughout the program, regularly commenting about how the outcomes of various activities that integrated multiple perspectives.
Intellectual Merit
This study provides valuable insights into how graduate education can better prepare students for interdisciplinary problem-solving. Key contributions include:
Development of curriculum materials for workshops in Creativity and Collaboration featuring arts-based, STEM-friendly activities.
Among 38 participating graduate students, all reported increased imaginative and collaborative abilities, personal observations that were also supported by quantitative and qualitative assessment.
Multiple research papers advancing our knowledge of arts-STEM training and collaboration are published or in preparation; results were presented at major conferences; and curriculum will be shared broadly via the web and through partner networks.
Broader Impacts
The curriculum has been integrated into other courses, benefiting over 300 students at UGA beyond the 38 participants in the study.
The project team is creating an online resource to share the curriculum with graduate educators nationwide.
Project leaders have been invited to share results and experiences in a variety of venues, including faculty training seminars, symposia, and spin-off workshops.
Conclusion
This project demonstrated that integrating creativity and collaboration training into STEM graduate education can help future scientists tackle real-world challenges more effectively by enhancing individual motivation and capacity to collaborate and innovate. The project team aims to expand the program's reach, publish research findings, and continue working with universities to enhance graduate education nationwide.

Title: RoL: FELS: RAISE:  Rules That Govern Seasonal Migration of Birds Through the Air
Program(s): Integrat & Collab Ed & Rsearch, Research Infra Cluster Prgrm, Cross-BIO Activities, NSF Research Traineeship (NRT)
Abstract:
Each year in the Northern Hemisphere, birds, bats, and insects fly north in spring and south in autumn. These aerial migrations have fascinated people for millennia; however, given the difficulty of tracking animals flying through the open skies, little is known about the rules that govern life in the air. Human activities have local and global impacts on these migrations by eliminating stopover habitats where migrants rest and refuel during their hazardous journeys and by altering atmospheric conditions. This project asks whether aerial migrants can keep pace with these rapid changes and what traits make some migrants more adaptable to change than others. The collaborative team of biologists and meteorologists will develop and employ advanced animal tracking methods to reveal both the precise locations of birds during migratory flights and the atmospheric conditions they fly through. This tracking will include novel microsensors placed on birds and aerial vehicles to collect heretofore-elusive data streams that reveal the environment experienced by birds in flight. The research team will combine these new observations with weather radar data from across the U.S. that already captures massive quantities of data on migrating birds, bats, and insects as they fly over the countryside. This combination of new and existing data may yield novel insights into migrant behavior within their changing atmospheric habitats. By bringing together scientists across disciplines, this research will develop and test different ways to enhance communication, collaboration, and teamwork among the next generation of students and their teachers. Finally, this project will communicate to the public how the changing environment influences the timing of migration over and through their communities.  Workshops in schools and community centers and work with local landowners will foster "citizen science" and adaptive strategies to contribute to this national effort. 

To uncover scaling rules that control phenology of life in the air, this study implements a research framework that integrates the spatiotemporal rescaling hypothesis and the metabolic theory of ecology. From this basis the study predicts that seasonal phenology of aerial migration is accelerating in response to environmental changes and that small-bodied migrants should have a greater capacity to speed up migration than larger-bodied migrants. The project studies the central flyway of North America and focuses on the impact of the central plains low-level jet on aerial migration patterns. The low-level jet is a prominent feature of the North American atmosphere to which many aerial migrants are known to be highly adapted. Recent evidence that the low-level jet is both expanding in geographic scope and intensity provides an ideal context for testing the study's predictions. The project team will leverage existing open-access and newly collected data from two coincident aerial migration systems; nocturnal bird and insect migration. Sensors for tracking location and atmospheric conditions will be placed on migratory birds that span two orders of magnitude in body size. Integrated biological and meteorological data will be used to improve our understanding of the rescaling of the low-level jet and to test predictions about how that rescaling impacts the phenology of life in the air.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.
Outcome Report:
Intellectual Merit: Although most organisms are likely to be vulnerable to climate change in some way, Animals that demonstrate seasonal behaviors are arguably among the most affected and may face the most unique challenges. This project investigated the limits to which migratory species can cope with climate warming. This warming is speeding up many biological and biophysical processes such as snow melt, evaporation and transpiration of moisture, seasonal greening of vegetation. While these changes drive behaviors, adaptation, and evolution in many organisms, the limits to these mechanisms of coping with climate warming are not well known. This project focused on whether the speed of avian migration is constrained by relationships between body size and energy demand required for migration. One primary prediction is that small-bodied migrants will having more capacity to track the speed of climate warming than large-bodied migrants. Several approaches were used to address this question. First, we assembled archived migration tracking data of over 200 individual birds representing 19 species and a wide range of body sizes. For individuals, we compiled daily decisions as to whether birds undertook a long-distance flight or remained in the same area, and we examined whether local weather conditions were correlated to each fly/no-fly decision. We also collected new, detailed geospatial migration data on 2 species of waterbirds that migrate through the central plains of North. We used these data to assess optimal migration routes that take into account weather variables across a range of relevant altitudes. Yet another approach to our research question used long-term community-science data to investigate whether body size and migration distance influence migrant birds’ ability to respond to climate change. Finally, we used NEXRAD radar network to produce the first continental scale view of the spatial and temporal distributions of day-flying insects. Taken together, these research approaches supported our prediction that smaller migrants are potentially more responsive to ongoing climate-change trends. However, body size was ultimately one of several life history variables that helped to explain migration speed and behavioral flexibility.
Broader Impacts: The project created and hosted workshops for Oklahoma High School Teachers that used mismatches in timing of seasonal events (e.g., green up of vegetation, emergence of insects, and arrival of migrant birds) as a basis for understanding the biological implications of climate warming. The workshop was based on a “Shiny app" in the R coding language through which the teachers could visualize seasonal timing data for vegetation green up, insect emergence, and migratory bird arrival dates. Teachers simulated different timing mismatches and create hypotheses about the consequences of different mismatch scenarios. These scenarios formed the basis for lesson planning exercises in which teachers created classroom activities for their students to learn about the concepts of phenology, climate change and tropic interactions. The project also trained two post-doctoral scholars and two doctoral students. Finally, the project supported substantial development of new methods for studying migratory birds. In particular, we built upon previous development of a new method of moonwatching (i.e. observing birds at night through a telescope using the moon as a backdrop) to enable new forms of data collection. By incorporating some mechanical automation and computer-aided video analysis into the moonwatching paradigm, we can now observe the body orientations of individual birds in conjunction with their flight direction to infer the influence of crosswinds. Similarly, we published a novel account of social behavior (i.e. flying as groups) in nocturnally migratory birds, which challenged the long-held assumption that they fly singly. We also employed moonwatching in three separate radar validation studies that involved a mobile weather radar, a stationary WSR-88D (NEXRAD) radar, and a BirdScan radar designed to detect flying animals. The study involving the WSR-88D radar verified that close range (i.e. <5000 m) detection of individual birds is possible using NEXRAD radars, which opens up the possibility of harvesting a new bird-migration data product from the NEXRAD radar network.

Title: ERC History Project: Phase Two
Full Address: 1818 N ST NW STE 600, WASHINGTON, DC, ="200362476"
Abstract:
Since 1984, the NSF's highly successful Engineering Research Centers (ERC) Program has led the Foundation in developing innovative new modes of support for research and education, led U.S. academic institutions to evolve the ways in which research is structured and form intellectual and financial partnerships with industry, produced thousands of engineering graduates who are highly productive leaders and innovators in industry and academe, and enabled thousands of innovative new technologies and companies that have stimulated the U.S. economy and provided a substantial return on NSF's investment.  The proposed project is the second phase of a two-part project to prepare a detailed, book-length History of the ERC Program over the program's more than 30-year span. The History will serve the national interest by providing lessons learned, best practices, and management guidance to government program managers, academic faculty and administrators, and industry leaders regarding the structure, operation, and management of such centers, not only in engineering but in any field of science and technology. 

The ERC Program History will be published as an e-book to have the maximum reach to different interested communities. The core narrative of the History will contain hundreds of links to ancillary material in various media - official documents, interview summaries, personal essays, meeting presentations, reports, graphics, videos, and captured websites. This material will be accessible to audiences ranging from engineering faculty and students to academic administrators and government officials, to industry executives and research managers, and to scholars of history and the management of technology. The online History will be marketed via email and the Web to all these audiences nationwide and worldwide. The book-length narrative and its ancillary resources will together provide a thoroughly documented understanding of how various groups involved in the ERC Program responded to the challenges inherent in the ERC construct, and how through their collective experiences it evolved through time to become one of the most recognized, respected, and productive centers programs worldwide.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.
Outcome Report:
The primary goal of this project was to produce and publish a detailed history of the National Science Foundation’s Engineering Research Centers (ERC) Program (available at https://erc-history.erc-assoc.org/). The secondary goals were to describe the evolution of ERC Program goals, key features, and management; to explore and document how the Program’s important impacts in research, education, and industrial collaboration were achieved and to educate the History’s various audiences about these achievements; to provide policy and management guidance to a range of interested audiences; and to capture the historical details for posterity, including historians and other scholars.
Intellectual Merit
The History is valuable from a management standpoint for those planning or operating government programs to support academic research centers, for those planning or operating centers, for administrators of center host institutions, and for representatives of industrial firms engaged in ongoing centers or contemplating joining centers because it contains detailed information on processes, outcomes, and lessons learned. The History also contains useful summaries of the state of the art at various points in time in emerging fields impacted by ERCs and enabled by their interdisciplinary configuration.
The History is useful to those planning or operating academic research centers in terms of strategies and lessons learned regarding:  
organizing and managing interdisciplinary teams of faculty and students to pursue research with shared goals;
staffing of the various functions in a large academic research center and the roles served by staff;
engineering and technical workforce development, including improving the diversity of the workforce and of engineering faculty;
overhead return and multi-institutional collaborations;
post-award oversight, reporting, and data collection; and
technology transfer to industry partners and center-associated startups, as well as industrial collaboration/membership in general.
Broader Impacts
The ERC Program History should have a broader impact in terms of lessons learned regarding the management and dynamics of large academic and/or research organizations, regardless of field, and their impact on student education as well as on the culture of academe locally and more broadly. There is also an impact on the education of large numbers of precollege students and teachers, resulting in a more technically literate public (as opposed to technology development as such). In addition, there is a potential impact on those studying, or preparing to form and operate, government/university/industry partnerships within the US or other governments.

Title: NRT: Enhancing conservation science and practice: An Interdisciplinary program
Program(s): NSF Research Traineeship (NRT), Project & Program Evaluation
Abstract:
Global and local changes in environmental, social, and climatic conditions increasingly stress, alter, or degrade ecosystems and human quality of life despite continued efforts to develop integrated natural and human models that help support effective decision-making. In response, organizations must focus on managing for resilient human-natural systems - those that are able to respond and adapt to the effects of rapid change. This National Science Foundation Research Traineeship (NRT) award to the University of Maine will create a new graduate education model that integrates faculty and students from the social and biophysical sciences in order to prepare the next generation of conservation leaders to address these challenges. The project anticipates training twenty-five (25) MS and PhD trainees, including twenty (20) funded trainees from forest resources, wildlife conservation, communications, and environmental sciences. An additional twenty (20) graduate students will participate in one or more of the traineeship program components. Trainees will develop interdisciplinary communication, collaboration, and professional skills to address emergent conservation issues. 
 
The project will develop an interdisciplinary curriculum based on active learning models, professional development, and collaborative research that integrates biophysical and social sciences. The program will develop new master's and doctoral concentrations that can be transferred to other settings in the U.S. and abroad, and that promote the diversification of the STEM workforce. The curriculum consists of four diverse learning experiences: (1) integrated courses that provide theoretical and research foundations in socio-ecological resilience and science communication; (2) an internship with a conservation management, policy or science organization to master STEM professional skills; (3) an interdisciplinary research project; and (4) a mentoring program to ensure trainee success. Training will include close interactions with key conservation partners from state and local agencies, the National Park Service, non-governmental organizations, and community partners. Interdisciplinary courses and research will address governance frameworks, biodiversity conservation, sustainable rural livelihoods and resource-dependent economies, stewardship values, citizen science and participation, and spatial sciences. NRT Trainees will learn to promote a systems approach to conservation through a wide range of biophysical and social science models and methods. 

The NSF Research Traineeship (NRT) Program is designed to encourage the development and implementation of bold, new potentially transformative models for STEM graduate education training. The program is dedicated to effective training of STEM graduate students in high priority interdisciplinary research areas through comprehensive traineeship models that are innovative, evidence-based, and aligned with changing workforce and research needs.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.
Outcome Report:
This project created a graduate education model that integrates faculty, students, and partners from social and biophysical sciences to prepare the next generation of conservation leaders to address challenges presented by a rapidly changing world. The project included 14 partner organizations (Federal government, Tribal Nations, state government, non-profit, and private) that supported professional development, research, teaching, and outreach strategies. A total of 48 faculty members were involved in the effort, including 13 who served as part of the leadership team.
As part of the project, the team developed and offered five courses on team science, science communication and community engagement, resilience, and internship. Over 70 graduate students benefited from the program (Figures 1); 18 undergraduate students and nine postdoctoral associates participated in professional development workshops and training sessions organized by the project team.
The collaboration among faculty, graduate students (NRT trainees), partners resulted in 128 publications, of which 63% (81) were in the form of refereed journal articles (Figure 2). NRT trainees co-authored 36% of the publications; multiple publications were led by trainees, demonstrating the strong research, collaborative, and leadership training obtained through the program. 
Furthermore, as shown on figure 3, faculty and students gave 210 presentations at international and national conferences (104), invited presentations (67), and guest lectures in courses (39). Of the total number of presentations, trainees served as co-presenters on 43% of the conference presentations, significantly demonstrating the strong training, science communication, and leadership skills gained through the program.
As trainees progressed through the program, their contributions to products increased. In the program’s final year, trainees co-authored 81% of conference presentations, and 82% of publications (Figure 4). This includes a reflective essay on transdisciplinary research authored by 5 trainee alumni.
Additionally, the collaboration led to securing over $51 million in external and internal grants (54 funded projects over the life of the grant) to support research, outreach, education, and economic development strategies. Trainees contributed to securing additional funding. Over the course of the program, there were eight grants with trainees as Co-PIs, totaling >$700k. This number includes a collaborative project co-developed by 6 trainees and Penobscot Nation partners that was awarded a Maine Outdoor Heritage Fund grant.
The project also led to significant research collaborations via a transdisciplinary approach. Teams were formed to research an array of topics related to climate change adaptation, community resilience, community engagement and participation conservation, outdoor recreation and underrepresented minorities, ecosystem health and conservation, adaptation to economic and health shocks, among others. Transdisciplinary collaborations between faculty, trainees, and partners from social, economic and biophysical sciences were created and strengthened.
Finally, the project implemented multiple strategies to attract and support trainees from diverse backgrounds. Of the 28 trainees recruited through the program (Figure 5), 96% identified with at least one underrepresented minority group: 86% identified as female or non-binary, 16% identified with an ethnic or racial minority groups, 11% reported being non-traditional students, and 32% were 1st generation college students.
