The program is dedicated to effective training of STEM graduate students in high priority interdisciplinary research areas through comprehensive traineeship models that are innovative, evidence-based, and aligned with changing workforce and research needs.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.
Outcome Report:
Interdisciplinary Training in Agricultural Biotechnology
  Agricultural biotechnologies are evolving rapidly and technical research in this area requires more and more sophisticated expertise in sub-disciplines of genetics, genomics and computational biology. This results in a tendency for biotechnology graduate training to become narrowly focused. At the same time, in other parts of campus, graduate students in the social sciences and humanities are being trained to evaluate emerging technologies such as biotechnology with little personal connection to the people who are developing and using these technologies.
Our training program was designed to bring together graduate students and faculty from diverse natural and social science disciplines to develop a broad understanding of agricultural biotechnologies and related policy options, so that the potential positive effects of the overall technology could be enhanced while minimizing risks. One thrust in this training has been productive engagement with the public and policymakers.
Students in the three successive cohorts of our program have come from PhD programs as diverse as Genetics and Genomics, Crop Science, Economics, Public Administration, and Communication. To accomplish our goals within the two-year training program, we started each cohort with a summer field experience where they spent two-weeks embedded in an agricultural community in Eastern North Carolina. The students met with a diversity of farmers, agricultural researchers, extension agents, seed producers, farm loan officers, private crop consultants and environmental groups. This experience has given students a deep appreciation for the real-world context into which new biotechnologies are integrated. It also has served to give students an introduction to each other’s disciplines and how they all can contribute to the appropriate development and use of agricultural biotechnologies. 
In their first Fall semester, all of the students took a 3-credit, Genetics and Genomics course. This is a challenging course for the social science students, but also for natural science students who don’t have a background in genetics. Over the three times that the course was offered, the instructors found better ways to make the course accessible and useful to all of the students. In each cohort, those students with the best genetics backgrounds served as peer mentors for the other students.
In their first Spring semester, students participated in a 3-credit course titled “Emerging Technologies and Society”. This course provided frameworks for understanding emerging technologies and their social, political, and cultural contexts. It presented historical and current case studies that introduce students to diverse ways of thinking about science, technology and society. It is here that our humanities and social sciences PhD students helped the natural science students understand the nuances of qualitative and quantitative social science research and the theoretical contexts in which they are imbedded. Students worked together on a class project.
The final formal course was on systems thinking and modeling. The goal of this course was to bring together all of the training to this point in a way that has the students broaden their reach in understanding the interacting components of agricultural systems and how to anticipate the complex biological and societal factors that can determine the positive, neutral and negative impacts of biotechnologies from multiple perspectives. This course leads into students working as a team on a specific issue that is at the interface of biotechnology and society. Title: IGE: Enhancing Graduate Education in Systems Thinking and Multi-Stakeholder Design through a Co-Creation Toolkit
Program(s): NSF Research Traineeship (NRT), Project & Program Evaluation
Abstract:
Major global challenges often require convergent, inclusive approaches that involve science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) professionals.  Training students to work with multiple stakeholders, such as non-profit organizations and local populations could better prepare them to address problems that involve multiple disciplines or perspectives.  For example, humanitarian organizations are engaging both STEM professionals and members of affected populations to design innovative interventions for refugee relief and response. This National Science Foundation Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) award to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) will train STEM graduate students to adopt more collaborative and inclusive approaches to problem-solving within the humanitarian response context. MIT D-Lab, which focuses on Development through Discovery, Design and Dissemination, will expand its contributions to the humanitarian relief sector through a novel approach to teaching graduate-level design and systems thinking courses.  The goal is to train future STEM leaders to incorporate a more inclusive and participatory approach to problem solving. MIT D-Lab will develop, pilot, and evaluate a multi-week module on how to effectively facilitate co-creative design sessions that include both humanitarian organizations and affected populations on the design team throughout the entire process. While the module is being developed and tested within the context of D-Lab?s humanitarian efforts, it has applications in many other settings, both in academia and in the field.

Researchers will develop and pilot elements of the design and systems thinking module in D-Lab, the Systems Design and Management program and the Urban Risk Lab at MIT; in the Humanitarian Engineering program at Oregon State University; in the Program on Forced Migration and Health at Columbia University; and in the School of Information at the University of Michigan. In parallel, students will work on a semester-long project with a partner organization (such as Oxfam, UNICEF or the Red Cross) to develop a co-creative activity between the organization and an affected population. After the class, students will have the opportunity to work with D-Lab staff and partners in the field to deliver the co-creative activity. The researchers will measure learning outcomes for the curriculum and identify changes in the students? skills, knowledge, and attitudes. In addition, researchers will determine the effectiveness of co-creation processes and will compare the activities developed as part of this project to the current process for identifying solutions and engaging users in the humanitarian sector. By comparing these processes, the team will be able to identify important hypotheses about effective ways to teach co-creation and participatory principles as well as the effects of a co-creation process on students and refugees. 

The Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) program is focused on research in graduate education. The goals of IGE are to pilot, test and validate innovative approaches to graduate education and to generate the knowledge required to move these approaches into the broader community.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.
Outcome Report:
Background
D-Lab at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology has been working in the humanitarian innovation sphere for the last 15 years, with a focus on increasing participation in humanitarian innovation. As crises multiply globally, the world faces increasing numbers of displaced and dwindling resources to support them. As of January of 2024, there were 108.4 million people displaced by conflict. The humanitarian sector looks to innovation to provide new products, paradigms and processes to maximize resources. However, humanitarian response is heavily top down, and people affected by crises are rarely consulted in the design of solutions. This leads to widespread challenges around the adoption and use of innovations in humanitarian contexts because they are often culturally and contextually inappropriate.
Although humanitarian organizations recognize the need for greater participation of those impacted by crises in the development of solutions, few professionals know how to do it. Since engineers, doctors, nutritionists, designers, architects are in high demand as humanitarian professionals, MIT D-Lab identified the need to develop new educational resources to better prepare graduate students in STEM to work collaboratively with key stakeholders in the humanitarian sector. Through this project, D-Lab aims to give future humanitarian professionals the skills needed to work in ways that increase the participation of people impacted by crisis in the co-creation of innovative solutions that are more locally relevant and have a higher chance of being adopted and used. The four key outcomes of this project are summarized below.
1. Equipping graduate students with new skills for applying co-creation in humanitarian settings
Through the D-Lab course, EC.750/EC.785 Humanitarian Innovation: Design for Relief, Recovery and Rebuilding, four cohorts of graduate students from MIT and Harvard gained skills in leading co-creation activities in a humanitarian setting. D-Lab’s team evaluated student learning at the end of each semester and found the largest gains in learning were consistently in understanding how power dynamics and mindsets could affect a co-creation process. Students also indicated that they felt more confident in their ability to develop activities that address power dynamics in a co-creation process. Students consistently reported learning the importance of recognizing and understanding the perspectives of others involved in the co-creation process. Students also reported using what they learned in many different situations including group and social interactions in other academic and work settings, and development and humanitarian fieldwork, demonstrating a broad application of what they learned.
A group of 6 students demonstrated their facility with what they had learned in class by helping D-Lab staff successfully lead a week-long co-creation workshop in the Rhino Camp refugee settlement in Uganda in August 2022. The workshop brought together refugees, host community members and NGOs to build businesses around technologies that were designed and built by refugees. Students reported being able to apply material from the Co-Creation Toolkit, and that it helped prepare them for the workshop.
2. A new educational resource for STEM graduate students going into humanitarian work
The project produced the Co-Creation Toolkit, a new curricular resource for teaching STEM students who want to become humanitarian professionals. The Co-Creation Toolkit, currently being uploaded onto a website for public access includes a set of participation tools, a suite of teaching modules that cover the key aspects of co-creation (including creating an enabling environment for successful co-creation), and a co-creation planning workbook for instructors and students that guides them through the process of preparing for and delivering co-creation activities in humanitarian settings.
3. An on-line participation resource for humanitarian workers
The D-Lab team developed a participation module as part of the Co-Creation Toolkit to help graduate students going into the humanitarian sector better understand the different dimensions of participation and how it can be integrated into humanitarian projects. One version of this module is currently on the Humanitarian Innovation Fund (HIF) website as a downloadable participation toolkit for humanitarian professionals at: https://www.elrha.org/researchdatabase/participation-for-humanitarian-innovation/  and HIF promotes its use among their grantees. The D-Lab team prioritized developing tools around participation early on, because they identified a general lack of knowledge and understanding about participation within the humanitarian sector. The participation toolkit is a unique tool that educates humanitarian workers about the different types and levels of participation, helps them assess the participation that already exists in their projects, enables them to select the type of participation appropriate for achieving their goals, and what they need to do to ensure a high quality of participation. So far, there have been 387 downloads of the participation toolkit from the website.
4. Adding to the literature and understanding around participation in humanitarian innovation
Through presentations and papers at humanitarian conferences and workshops, literature reviews and research on co-creation, the products from this project have contributed to the literature about and the understanding of participation in humanitarian innovation, and how co-creation can be used to increase it.

Title: NRT-INFEWS: The DataFEWSion Traineeship Program for Innovations at the Nexus of Food Production, Renewable Energy and Water Quality
Program(s): Project & Program Evaluation, NSF Research Traineeship (NRT)
Abstract:
Agriculture lies at the heart of interactions among food, energy and water systems. It is an increasingly energy-intensive enterprise, but it is also a growing source of energy. Agriculture places large demands on water supplies while poor practices can degrade water quality. Each of these interactions creates opportunities for modeling, driven by sensor-based and qualitative data collection, to improve the effectiveness of system operation and control in the short term as well as investments and planning for the long term. The large volume and complexity of the data collected creates challenges for decision support and stakeholder communication. This National Science Foundation Research Traineeship (NRT) award to Iowa State University will build a community of researchers that explores, develops and implements effective data-driven decision-making to efficiently produce food, transform primary energy sources into energy carriers, and enhance water quality.  The project anticipates training forty-eight (48) MS and PhD students, including twenty-four (24) funded PhD trainees, from agricultural and biosystems engineering, agronomy, industrial engineering, mechanical engineering and natural resources ecology and management. The project aims to prepare trainees for multiple career paths such as research scientists, bioeconomy entrepreneurs, agribusiness leaders, policy makers, agriculture analytics specialists, or professors. 

Sustainable provision of food, energy and clean water requires understanding the interdependencies among systems as well as the motivations and incentives of farmers and rural policy makers. Effective innovation at the nexus of these food, energy and water (FEW) systems requires data-rich system modeling with analytic capabilities for diverse types of data. The traineeship has four key components. First, trainees will complete a new graduate certificate to build competencies in fundamental understanding of interactions among food production, water quality and bioenergy; data acquisition, visualization, and analytics; complex systems modeling for decision support; and the economics, policy and sociology of the FEW nexus.  Second, they will conduct interdisciplinary research on (a) technologies and practices to increase agriculture's contributions to energy supply while reducing its negative impacts on water quality and human health; (b) data science to increase crop productivity within the constraints of sustainable intensification; or (c) decision sciences to manage tradeoffs and promote best practices among diverse stakeholders. Third, they will participate in a new graduate learning community consisting of a two-year series of workshops that focus in alternate years on the context of the Midwest agricultural FEW nexus and professional development.  Fourth, they will have small-group experiences to promote collaboration and peer review. Each trainee will create and curate a portfolio that combines artifacts from coursework and research with reflections on the broader impacts of their work. 

The NSF Research Traineeship (NRT) Program is designed to encourage the development and implementation of bold, new potentially transformative models for STEM graduate education training. The program is dedicated to effective training of STEM graduate students in high priority interdisciplinary research areas through comprehensive traineeship models that are innovative, evidence-based, and aligned with changing workforce and research needs.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.
Outcome Report:
The DataFEWSion Traineeship program aimed to build a community of researchers that explores, develops and implements effective data-driven decision-making to efficiently produce food, transform primary energy sources into energy carriers, and enhance water quality. With a focus on the impacts of agricultural practices in the Midwestern US, its goals were to foster interdisciplinary research based on data-intensive methods; educate STEM graduate students for a range of research, research-related and entrepreneurial careers employing data-driven modeling at the food, energy, and water system (FEWS) nexus; and prepare STEM graduate students to work effectively in multidisciplinary teams, communicate effectively with stakeholders, and identify economically sustainable innovations. 
The major components of the traineeship program were:
1)      The student’s thesis or dissertation research on a FEWS issue;
2)      A graduate certificate in Data-Driven Food, Energy and Water Decision Making, which consists of 2.5 credits of core courses and 9 credits of electives;
3)      A graduate learning community that included a two-year series of monthly workshops, and weekly small-group activities designed to enhance the trainees’ interdisciplinary communication and collaboration skills;
4)      An e-portfolio that contains artifacts from research or coursework that demonstrate attainment of key competencies; and
5)      An annual symposium convening trainees, faculty advisors, and the external advisory board.
Four cohorts of trainees completed the two-year program in overlapping cycles, with a new cohort being recruited each year.
One of the core courses for the certificate, Biosystems for Sustainable Development, emphasized case studies in which students collaboratively examined FEWS nexus issues.  The other was a course on Communications in Science, which was revived by the Graduate College for our program and has since grown to enroll over two dozen students each year.  Some of them are trainees in another NRT program but the majority are not.  The elective courses were drawn from three topic areas: data acquisition, visualization, and analytics; complex systems modeling for decision support; and economics, policy or sociology of FEWS.  The intent of the e-portfolio was to collect artifacts that would demonstrate proficiency in each competency area of the certificate.  The monthly workshops included techniques in data science, panel discussions on current FEWS issues, professional development topics, and seasoned researchers’ perspectives on interdisciplinary research.  Small-group sessions in the first years provided the trainees with opportunities to share skills and knowledge of relevant data sources. 
As the program progressed, trainees were increasingly involved in leadership of the program. An elective representative from each active cohort joined the leadership team in monthly meetings.  Student-faculty working groups were formed to plan the networking weekends, symposia, workshops, and learning community agendas, as well as to award travel/publication grants.  Petitions for additional elective courses beyond the initial set proposed were considered and a required course on entrepreneurship was replaced by a workshop based on trainee feedback.  Two different independent study projects were allowed to substitute for completing the FEWS core course.
At the beginning of their second year of the traineeship, the final cohort of trainees proposed an agenda for the weekly learning community meetings and an alternative way to complete their e-portfolio requirements.  The twelve members of the cohort divided into four-member teams to collaborate on projects concerned with each of the three FEWS areas.  The food team studied food systems in Iowa to assess inequality in access to nutrition.  They combined production, distribution, consumption, and nutritional data at the county level to assess causes of poor health outcomes of state residents, and developed a data visualization tool to map locations of dollar stores and food pantries across the state.  This team comprises students in agricultural and biosystems engineering, animal science, economics, and nutritional science.  The energy team, combining three engineering disciplines (agricultural and biosystems, chemical, and materials science) analyzed data collected from a microgrid that combines solar photovoltaic generation and storage to power a livestock feeding facility. They assessed the economic viability for this system considering its capacity for emergency response and the production of carbon-neutral pork.  The water team studied how climate change affects regional drought and flood conditions, with the objective to produce an online, interactive map linked to low-income communities.  These majors in civil engineering, agricultural meteorology, and environmental science combined meteorological, climate, and demographic data to identify hot spots of vulnerability to water excess or deficit. 
The DataFEWSion Traineeship program trained 31 students from 16 disciplines in engineering and agriculture.  Twenty-seven faculty members served as their major professors, many of whom were also committee members for other trainees.  At the conclusion of the program, two trainees were in tenure-track faculty positions, five were in other academic positions including postdoctoral training, two were working in industry, two in government, two in non-governmental organizations, and the remaining 18 were continuing in their graduate degree programs.

Title: Collaborative Research: IGE: Scaling Faculty Development to Broaden Participation in Graduate Education
Program(s): Project & Program Evaluation, NSF Research Traineeship (NRT)

Abstract:
This National Science Foundation Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) award to the University of Southern California and Rochester Institute of Technology will pilot a network of faculty and administrators across six major California universities that aims to improve how universities choose the scientists of the future. Currently, the demographic composition of the student body in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) doctoral programs and the scientific workforce is not only different from the composition of U.S. demographics, but it is also changing more slowly than the demographic shifts in the US. It is important to address these inequities in order to create a robust domestic scientific workforce, which may contribute to a healthy economy and promote U.S. scientific superiority. Inherited practices for recruiting, admitting, and mentoring graduate students contribute to these inequities, as does the lack of opportunity for faculty to reflect upon their practices in these areas. This award creates innovative systems by which faculty can improve those practices, and therefore holds significant promise as a strategy for broadening participation in graduate education and the scientific workforce. 

The project will form a network that provides faculty and graduate school administrators within and across the University of Southern California and University of California campuses at Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, and Santa Barbara with opportunity and incentives to critically reflect upon and change longstanding practices. Participating STEM PhD programs will receive professional development from project leaders in the form of workshops and continuous learning activities on recruiting, admitting, and mentoring graduate students from diverse backgrounds. Leaders that emerge from each program in years 1 and 2 will be selected to establish campus-level teams who will deliver similar faculty-to-faculty learning opportunities on their own campuses. The research and evaluation activities of the project involve a sequential multi-method study, including the first-ever clustered randomized experiment to test the impact of faculty development around three outcomes: the admissions practices that PhD programs use, the diversity of their admitted cohorts, and the programs' selectivity. The structure of the network allows for sustainable gains, and it works with, rather than against, the decentralized nature of graduate education and its varied institutional and disciplinary contexts.

Outcome Report:
Collaborative Research: IGE: Scaling Faculty Development to Broaden Participation in Graduate Education 
The demographic composition of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) doctoral programs and the scientific workforce is not only different from the US population, but it is also changing more slowly than demographic shifts in the US. To create a robust domestic scientific workforce, it is important to address these inequities. Inherited mindsets and methods for recruiting, admitting, and mentoring graduate students are root causes of disproportionate exclusion of Black, Latinx, Indigenous people, and women of all backgrounds, as is the lack of opportunity for faculty to reflect upon and change their practices in these areas.
A growing body of social science research holds potential to improve how we select and serve PhD students. This project scaled up research-based faculty professional development curriculum and piloted a network of faculty and administrators across six California universities. The California Consortium for Inclusive Doctoral Education (C-CIDE) brought together change-ready graduate schools, PhD programs, and leaders within them. Its guiding vision was to build capacity to equitably select and serve PhD students from historically underrepresented racial/ethnic and gender backgrounds. We scaled up existing graduate admissions and recruitment workshops designed for physics departments under former NSF awards to different disciplinary and institutional contexts. We offered 75 workshops over the course of the project as a whole and, as a means of sustainability, trained more than 25 facilitators to lead workshops in equity-minded admissions and mentoring at partner universities beyond the award period.  
External evaluation using rigorous quantitative methods showed that our partners changed their admissions and recruitment practices after participating in C-CIDE workshops, and that they significantly increased the diversity and selectivity of applicants, admitted students, and enrollees. For example, most programs eliminated GRE score requirements for admission. There was also evidence of increases in admissions committees meeting to discuss criteria before file review, revisiting their admissions practices, conducting more careful reading of transcripts, and encouraging reviewers to consider applicant potential rather than just achievements. The evaluation also found statistically significant increases in the number of applications, admitted students, and enrollees from racially minoritized groups each year from 2018 through 2021. We found some evidence of increases in applicants and admits who are women post-workshop, but these changes tended to be delayed. We did not find statistically significant changes in the number of women enrolled in participating programs in post-workshop years. 
In addition to scaling up these workshops as a space for reflection, discussion, and initiating change, an important outcome was the creation of a learning community inspired by the Networked Improvement Community model. The partner universities included the graduate schools (or equivalent) of UC San Diego, UC Berkeley, UC Davis, UC Santa Barbara, UC Irvine, and University of Southern California. The PhD program partners represented the following fields of study: engineering; natural resources; environmental science and policy/management; mathematics; physical sciences; biology; neuroscience; psychology; and computer science. We purposefully developed and advanced with this group a model of equity-minded holistic admissions that complies with California?s and other states? bans on affirmative action in admissions.
Critical to C-CIDE were specific individuals or dyads within our partner graduate schools who served as campus liaisons to the project. These individuals coordinated campus-level activities and leveraged their knowledge of local needs and resources to support positive changes in partner graduate programs and the wider universities they served. Campus liaisons met regularly as a group with project leaders, and an external assessment found that liaisons experienced these meetings and community as a site of leadership development. Title: Collaborative Research:IGE: Scaling Faculty Development to Broaden Participation in Graduate Education
Abstract:
This National Science Foundation Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) award to the University of Southern California and Rochester Institute of Technology will pilot a network of faculty and administrators across six major California universities that aims to improve how universities choose the scientists of the future. Currently, the demographic composition of the student body in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) doctoral programs and the scientific workforce is not only different from the composition of U.S. demographics, but it is also changing more slowly than the demographic shifts in the US. It is important to address these inequities in order to create a robust domestic scientific workforce, which may contribute to a healthy economy and promote U.S. scientific superiority. Inherited practices for recruiting, admitting, and mentoring graduate students contribute to these inequities, as does the lack of opportunity for faculty to reflect upon their practices in these areas. This award creates innovative systems by which faculty can improve those practices, and therefore holds significant promise as a strategy for broadening participation in graduate education and the scientific workforce. 

The project will form a network that provides faculty and graduate school administrators within and across the University of Southern California and University of California campuses at Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, and Santa Barbara with opportunity and incentives to critically reflect upon and change longstanding practices. Participating STEM PhD programs will receive professional development from project leaders in the form of workshops and continuous learning activities on recruiting, admitting, and mentoring graduate students from diverse backgrounds. Leaders that emerge from each program in years 1 and 2 will be selected to establish campus-level teams who will deliver similar faculty-to-faculty learning opportunities on their own campuses. The research and evaluation activities of the project involve a sequential multi-method study, including the first-ever clustered randomized experiment to test the impact of faculty development around three outcomes: the admissions practices that PhD programs use, the diversity of their admitted cohorts, and the programs' selectivity. The structure of the network allows for sustainable gains, and it works with, rather than against, the decentralized nature of graduate education and its varied institutional and disciplinary contexts.

Title: EDT: Montana Partnership for Enriching Mathematical Knowledge and Statistical Skills (MT PEAKS)
Program(s): NSF Research Traineeship (NRT), WORKFORCE IN THE MATHEMAT SCI, GOALI-Grnt Opp Acad Lia wIndus
Abstract:
The MT PEAKS program will broaden the training of doctoral students in the mathematical sciences so that they are equipped to pursue career paths beyond the traditional academic tract and are able to recognize opportunities to apply mathematics and statistics to solve problems in a variety of settings. The project is a collaboration between the Department of Mathematical Sciences (MathStat), the Montana multi-university Materials Science (MTSI) interdisciplinary doctoral program and business, industry and government (BIG) partners. MT PEAKS program activities consist of three main pillars: interdisciplinary research project activities involving a BIG-inspired project and MTSI lab rotations, an internship experience with a BIG partner, and preparatory coursework and professional development activities. MT PEAKS students will apply their mathematical and statistical skills in the context of a year-long research project developed through collaboration with an advisory team of MathStat and MTSI faculty and a BIG partner.  They will also participate in summer internships with BIG partners. The program will produce a broadly prepared workforce of PhD mathematicians and statisticians ready to apply their technical skills and multidisciplinary exposure to help address a myriad of regional, national and global challenges outside the traditional academic environment. This project is co-funded by the NSF Research Traineeship (NRT) Program, which is dedicated to effective training of STEM graduate students in high priority interdisciplinary research areas through comprehensive traineeship models that are innovative, evidence-based, and aligned with changing workforce and research needs.

Coordination of the lab rotations, the interdisciplinary research project, and the BIG internship is a hallmark of the MT PEAKS program. Lab rotations will expose MT PEAKS participants to a variety of sophisticated large and bench scale instrumentation, experimental protocols, lab safety practices, and team dynamics. MT PEAKS students will be trained by MTSI doctoral student mentors on the use of lab equipment needed for experimentation and data collection related to their lab projects. MTSI mentors will be chosen so that their research focus complements the MT PEAKS participant's lab project. The interdisciplinary research project will include a component that involves the collection and analysis of experimental data and technical information from a core group of MathStat and MTSI faculty and a BIG partner. BIG partners will provide students with internship experiences that foster growth in communication and teamwork skills, as well as an increase in students' recognition of the ubiquitous nature of mathematics and statistics in the modern technical workplace. Students will also participate in professional development workshops to enhance networking and other professional skill sets.  Results of graduate training aspects of MT PEAKS will be disseminated through online media and educational journals.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.
Outcome Report:
The goal of the MT PEAKS (Montana Partnership for Enriching Mathematical Knowledge and Statistical Skills) program was to broaden the graduate training of doctoral students in the Department of Mathematical Sciences at Montana State University (MSU). Their experiences would equip them to pursue career paths beyond the traditional academic tract and be able to recognize opportunities to apply mathematics and statistics to solve problems in other disciplines. The program, specifically, partnered with researchers in the Material Sciences to achieve the program goal.

During the timespan of the grant, six mathematics and six statistics doctoral students participated as MT PEAKS Fellows. Fellow partnerships received hands-on experiences in the laboratories of the material scientists at MSU as well as external business, industry, and governmental partners. Collaborative manuscript preparation for submission to professional journals was an important activity. Additionally, ten masters degree students participated as MT PEAKS affiliates with less-immersive involvement in research projects.

Several laboratory experiences of the Fellows were: 

(i) The study of biomaterials related to osteoarthritis with the long term goal of developing novel treatment strategies involving a drug delivery mechanism called chondrocyte mechanotransduction.  Studying this delivery therapy through this mechanism will provide insights into the development of novel strategies for treating joint disease.

(ii) The study of 3D printing and assessment of material properties used in the printing process.  One project focuses on the additive manufacturing (aka 3D printing) of polymeric materials. 

(iii) The implementation of space-filling experimental design to study the effect of vanadium, molybdenum, and strontium mixture ratios on the electrical and ionic conductivity of a solid fuel cell.

(iv) Adapting archetypal analysis to scientific large-scale imaging problems that crop up in scientific investigations. Applications include neuroscience imaging and exoplanet classifications, as well as some classical computer vision imaging datasets. 

(iv) The development and implementation of a statistical methodology known as censored maximum likelihood estimation.

(v) Research in biodegradable and bio-derived polymers and composites along with sustainable material and energy product lifecycles.

Several fellows who have received their PhD in mathematics and statistics have pursued career paths at national laboratories and companies in the private sector, which is the ultimate indicator of the success of the MT PEAKS program. We expect other fellows who have yet to defend their dissertations will follow in their footsteps by pursuing careers focused on problem-solving collaborations with scientists from other disciplines.

Title: IGE: Advancing and Strengthening Science Identity through Systematic Training (ASSIST)
Program(s): NSF Research Traineeship (NRT), Project & Program Evaluation
Organization: University of Texas at San Antonio
Abstract:
Developing science leaders from underrepresented minority graduate student groups such as Latinos, African Americans, and women remains a national priority. Yet the barriers to success these groups face are often not adequately addressed by traditional methods of mentoring and professionalization in science. Minority-serving institutions are uniquely poised to foster diverse science leaders, but they also require a systematic, integrated, program-wide approach geared toward nurturing and validating students' identities as scientists. This National Science Foundation Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) award to the University of Texas San Antonio cultivates science identity by integrating holistic mentoring with systematic training in science writing and public science communication. This program will test an innovative and potentially transformative model for diversifying science that engages both faculty and graduate students from the department of Environmental Science and Ecology in a community-supported, holistic, and systematic approach. The project will utilize a series of graduate courses, professional workshops, and community-based activities that seek to foster and validate underrepresented minority students' science identity. Nationally, these interventions may exist informally, but they are rarely, if ever, fully integrated into a coherent graduate STEM program. Developing diverse leaders in science professions is crucial as scientists navigate interdisciplinary knowledge demands and cultural challenges in a globalized and media-saturated world. 

The goal of this IGE project is to cultivate a science identity for underrepresented minority graduate students through the acquisition of a knowledge base (competence), the ability to perform science practices (performance), and the acknowledgement by significant others in the field (recognition). The researchers propose that fostering these identity components and making them visible in scientific disciplines and public communities can be achieved through three interrelated interventions: holistic mentoring, writing-to-learn science, and public science communication. Holistic mentoring, both in and outside the classroom environment will provide the underlying framework necessary to address the needs and challenges faced by underrepresented minority students. In addition, this project hypothesizes that holistic mentoring transforms the challenges of systematic training in research-based science writing and public science communication into opportunities to validate students' scientific competence and leadership skills. The project will use a mixed-methods assessment approach to analyze not only each intervention but also on the relationships among all three interventions. Therefore, it seeks to provide an evidence-based validation of the impact of holistic mentoring and systematic communications training on cultivating a scientific ethos for underrepresented minority graduate students. 

The Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) program is focused on research in graduate education.  The goals of IGE are to pilot, test and validate innovative approaches to graduate education and to generate the knowledge required to move these approaches into the broader community.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.
Outcome Report:
This NSF-funded project aimed to enhance science identity among environmental science graduate students through a comprehensive approach involving holistic mentoring, improved science communication and writing pedagogy, and focused training to increase comprehension of ecological and environmental science topics. Our goal was to give students the tools and support they need to grow as confident, effective scientists who can communicate complex ideas to diverse audiences and become leaders in their chosen fields.
The project contributed significant advancements in understanding how science identity develops among graduate students in environmental science, with particular attention to those from historically underrepresented backgrounds. Intellectual merit outcomes include:
Development of Holistic Mentoring Practices: We designed and implemented a mentoring framework that combined academic support, professional development, and social-emotional guidance. This approach was particularly successful in helping students see themselves as scientists by aligning mentorship with their individual needs and career goals.
Science Communication and Writing Pedagogy: We developed a curriculum focused on enhancing science communication skills, specifically tailored to environmental science topics. Through workshops, assignments, and feedback loops, students substantially improved their ability to write and speak about scientific concepts for academic and public audiences.
Enhanced Understanding of Ecological and Environmental Science Concepts: We observed students with greater confidence and increased ability to communicate their understanding of environmental science topics. Course content emphasized complex issues such as climate change, ecosystem management, and biodiversity conservation, allowing students to build a solid knowledge base that informed their research and public communication efforts.
The project's approach was grounded in evidence-based instructional methods and continuous assessment, which allowed us to refine and validate our mentoring and teaching strategies. Workshops and mentoring related to attending scientific conferences also aided in removing barriers between practicing scientists and students working to become scientists. Additionally, our findings contribute to the growing body of literature on the development of science identity and the role of mentorship in shaping future scientists.
This project had a far-reaching impact beyond the immediate student population involved, extending its influence to the broader scientific community, the general public, and underserved communities' understanding of the environment.
Strengthened Science Identity in Diverse Graduate Students: The holistic mentoring model significantly increased self-identification as scientists among participating students, with the greatest impact observed among first-generation college students and those from underrepresented groups. The project has produced a replicable mentoring model that can be adopted by other programs seeking to cultivate science identity in diverse student populations.
Improvement in Public Science Communication: The project enabled graduate students to translate their specialized knowledge into accessible language, thus bridging the gap between academic research and public understanding. Students developed communication materials, including blogs, articles, and presentations, disseminated to local communities and online platforms, engaging the public in environmental science topics.
Capacity Building for Future Environmental Leaders: Students who participated in the program reported greater confidence in their scientific skills and expressed a heightened commitment to environmental advocacy and science outreach. Many graduates have taken positions in academic, nonprofit, and governmental roles where they continue to leverage their communication and mentoring skills to further environmental causes.
Building Partnerships: This project laid the foundation for building partnerships between several minority-serving institutions and several federal agencies. Seven minority-serving institutions (UTSA, New Mexico State University, Fort Valley State University, Tuskegee University, Alabama A & M, Bethune-Cookman University, and Bowe State University) have formed a consortium and signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the US Fish and Wildlife Service. We are sharing the lessons we learned from the NSF Project with these schools and agencies to improve the retention and success of graduate students in the fields of natural resources and conservation. From what we have learned from this NSF Project, we have completed a pilot internship program with the Environmental Protection Agency, leading to several graduate students working for the Agency. We are now discussing expanding this pilot to our consortium partners listed above.
This project provided invaluable insights into the development of science identity through mentoring and pedagogy designed to strengthen communication skills and comprehension of environmental science. By holistically supporting graduate students, we have prepared them for successful careers and empowered them to engage in meaningful, effective science communication. The resources and knowledge developed have been the foundation for new initiatives to foster diversity and inclusion in the environmental sciences and beyond.
The success of this project demonstrates the potential for broader adoption of these methods across STEM disciplines and serves as a model for how NSF-funded programs can impact the next generation of scientists and the communities they serve.

Title: AAU PhD Program and Career Outcome Data Workshop
Program(s): NSF Research Traineeship (NRT), ECR-EDU Core Research
Full Address: 1200 NEW YORK AVE NW, WASHINGTON, DC, ="200056122"
Abstract:
The need to reform doctoral education in the United States has been the subject of a number of national studies over the past 25 years. One particular challenge that has been noted focuses on career pathways.  Graduate students generally are not exposed to the breadth of career pathways that are open to Ph.D. recipients, thereby hampering students from making informed decisions about their educational paths and professional preparation.  Accurate and transparent program and career outcomes data are necessary to enable students to identify and direct their studies toward their desired career goals. This National Science Foundation award to the Association of American Universities (AAU) will support a workshop that will bring together representatives from a number of institutions currently engaged in efforts to document and make publicly available data on doctoral program admission, completion, and career outcome measures; scholars conducting research on doctoral career pathways; and university administrators charged with overseeing graduate education. The goal of the workshop is to survey the existing landscape for understanding doctoral education outcomes, foster synergies among participants, and determine next directions.

The one-and-a-half-day workshop will support discussions among participants regarding methodologies used in data collection, how collected data is intended or not intended to be used, and what efforts can be undertaken to increase communication across existing efforts, standardize approaches, and improve documentation and availability of data on doctoral education and career outcomes. Representatives from a number of major efforts to collect and analyze doctoral educational outcomes data, administrative leaders at doctoral-granting institutions, and leaders of efforts on broadening career pathways for students will be invited to participate. The workshop will include panel presentations and facilitated discussions. Access to reliable, accurate, and transparent data is an essential starting point for discussions that can lead to effective decision making. The immediate goal of this workshop is to determine direct steps that can make such data standardized and available to the community and stakeholders. Ultimately, the expectation is that this will lead to work that will identify and mitigate institutional, cultural, and disciplinary barriers that may prevent doctoral students from identifying, exploring, and preparing for a wide range of career pathways.

This proposal is co-funded by the Directorate for Education and Human Resources (EHR) Core Research (ECR) program and the NSF Research Traineeship (NRT) Program.  The ECR program (NSF 15-509) focuses on fundamental research in STEM education by providing funds in critical research areas that are essential, broad and enduring.  The NRT Program (17-585/18-507) is designed to encourage the development and implementation of new, potentially transformative models or approaches for STEM graduate education training that address changing workforce and research needs.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.
Outcome Report:
The “PhD Program and Career Outcome Data Workshop” hosted by the Association of American Universities (AAU) on May 31 and June 1, 2018 in Washington, D.C. served as a forum for national representatives from institutional projects, multi-institutional projects, and projects led by disciplinary professional societies that are working to document doctoral program outcomes and PhD graduates’ career pathways.  The workshop brought together over 35 faculty members, administrative leaders, institutional data analysts, career coaches, and representatives from disciplinary societies to identify areas for collaboration, potential synergies, and greater alignment between national projects committed to documenting doctoral career outcomes.   
Participants engaged in cross-project conversations about project methodologies, and the ways in which projects are using and sharing data.  The interactive workshop used several formats to foster participant dialogue, including a panel session, a design thinking activity, small group activities, and whole group conversations.  Together, workshop participants discussed key themes and challenges in carrying out their project work, as well as critical next steps for data transparency in PhD career outcome efforts.  Two themes prevalent in workshop participants’ discussions were: (1) the power of narrative and the importance of effective messaging and communication in advancing this work; and (2) the desire to reduce the proliferation of new multi-institutional data collection projects and new data categorization taxonomies. 
Outcomes from the workshop benefitted both individual project efforts and cross-project collaborations.  At the conclusion of the workshop, participants reflected on what they learned and what specific action items they will take to advance their projects.  Common across participants’ reflections was the value they saw in making and maintaining connections with others involved in similar work in order to collaborate and advance collective efforts.  
Lessons learned from the workshop also informed the development of an initial phase of work with a pilot group of AAU member campuses to launch the AAU PhD Education Initiative.  The activities carried out by the pilot cohort campuses will directly address the culture, behavior, policies, and practices necessary to construct more student-centered educational environments for all doctoral students, which make the full range of career pathways available to PhD graduates visible, valued and viable.  The broader impacts of the Initiative will foster student diversity and inclusivity in doctoral education and support PhD student preparation for careers both within and beyond the academy.

Title: Collaborative Research: NRT-IGE: Employing Model-Based Reasoning in Environmental Science (EMBeRS)
Abstract:
NRT-IGE: Employing Model-Based Reasoning in Environmental Science (EMBeRS)

Scientific synthesis across disciplines is at the heart of addressing important challenges such as impacts of global change, trade-offs between water, food, and energy production, and the need for sustainable cities. Studies of interdisciplinary research teams indicate that team members struggle to achieve knowledge synthesis across disciplines. Issues arise due to the inability of team members to develop deep knowledge at the frontier of other disciplines and to connect that knowledge with their own expertise to provide a collaborative path forward. The ability to work collaboratively in a research team with others who may hold very different perspectives is a critical aspect of preparing today's students to meet future workforce demands. This National Science Foundation Research Traineeship (NRT) award in the Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) track is a collaborative project led by the University of Texas at El Paso involving graduate students and faculty from multiple institutions.  The project will test a new model for training graduate student teams in environmental sciences to overcome knowledge integration and synthesis challenges.

This model will draw on findings from cognitive, learning, and social sciences to develop and test training for graduate students and faculty in model-based reasoning approaches. Model-based reasoning theory posits that humans reason by constructing an internal mental model of the situations, events, and processes that they encounter, and that external representations can be used to facilitate construction of these mental models. External representations include the use of analogies, metaphor, visual models, diagrams and/or other representations for abstraction and communication of complex concepts. In a team setting, these external representations are called boundary negotiating objects.  This project will place doctoral students in multidisciplinary teams and facilitate a structured, participatory process that includes a progression of standard, individual and group model-based reasoning activities as well as instruction on the purposeful co-creation of boundary negotiating objects.  Students from multiple institutions will learn together through two-week summer experiences; students who are conducting research in conjunction with larger interdisciplinary teams will be targeted.  In addition, the project will train faculty from multiple institution in the model.  The project will examine the implementation of ten faculty members.  Survey, interview, and digital data will be collected to examine how graduate students respond to being directly exposed to theories behind the approach as well as the efficacy of the approach as faculty employ it in their graduate classes. This design will allow comparison of the outcomes from guiding students on what to do, versus teaching students why and how to do it.  

The NSF Research Traineeship (NRT) Program is designed to encourage the development and implementation of bold, new, potentially transformative, and scalable models for STEM graduate education training.  The Innovations in Graduate Education Track is dedicated solely to piloting, test, and evaluating novel, innovative, and potentially transformative approaches to graduate education.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.
Outcome Report:
Every high school student knows that in a group project, bad communication can lead directly to a bad result and a bad grade. That?s even more true for research teams working on environmental problems, especially on projects that combine experts from different fields. Projects that combine different kinds of researchers are also especially important, because the problems facing the world today are very complex. Many of them are so complex that they are called wicked problems.
To even begin to solve these problems, people with different backgrounds and different values have to understand each other and cooperate. If they can?t, they will waste time and money, and delay important discoveries and advances. The EMBeRS project was designed to study people?s interactions and then apply the findings to help people from different fields work together as a team as well as possible. It also helps people learn how to teach the collaboration method we developed. The ultimate goal is to harvest the combined ingenuity of an interdisciplinary team so there is less waste and delay.
One of the major problems in working with researchers from different fields is that they all have different mental models of their work and of the problems they?re addressing. The EMBeRS project develops ways to reveal those different models and thus learn how they?re different from person to person. That way, team members can communicate more effectively and apply their different skills and knowledge to very complex problems collectively and in agreement. 
The tool we use is called model-based reasoning. Model-based reasoning asks people to use or create models. Those models or artefacts can be interacted with and can be used as objects for discussion and negotiation. In EMBeRS they are called ?boundary negotiating objects.? Through the negotiating process, team members start to change and align their mental models, which leads to thinking about problems in unexpected ways. To create the models, team members do things like draw diagrams and build sculptures to make their ideas clearer to themselves and to others. When they do that, they communicate better and that helps them come up with new and unusual solutions.
A good example was our EMBeRS Summer School. In 2016 and 2017, we held ten-day courses for graduate students that trained them to collaborate with people from different fields on the problem of getting enough food, water, and energy to people in need around the world. That?s difficult to do because it involves a lot of different fields, like agriculture, logistics, natural resource management, politics, and economics.
The course was designed by a group of instructors with backgrounds in geological science, earth science, and environmental science, as well as experts in relationship management, science education, and the study of how people learn. The students themselves were working on degrees in fields like engineering, archaeology, agriculture, and urban management.
Together, the students and instructors helped each other learn about designing teams, communication strategies, and how to approach wicked problems. We surveyed the students afterwards and they said that they had learned to use EMBeRS lessons in their own studies and in the design of workshops and research collaboration. We also used their responses to improve our courses each year. After running the Summer Schools, we tested what we had learned in 2016 and 2017 in other settings, like teacher trainings, summer schools for students, and research groups in the US, Germany, and Norway. Those test runs were very well received. Next, we are working on offering these courses to even more people.
As we get better at teaching these collaborative skills, we will also help people spread them further. In the future, those skills will help people all over the world solve increasingly difficult environmental problems.

Title: A Distributed Learning Environment for the Mathematics of Climate and Sustainability
Full Address: CALTECH, 1200 E CALIFORNIA BLVD, PASADENA, CA, ="91125"
Abstract:
The research project focus will be on the mathematics needed for understanding our climate, its impacts and will help address the pressing issues of adaptation and sustainability in light of inevitable changes. Through this program, four cohorts of students will be trained in the mathematics underlying the all-important societal and scientific issues emanating from climate and sustainability. This will span a five year period and encompass four intensive week-long summer camps. Each cohort will consist of seven graduate and three undergraduate students. They will be trained in collaborative team-work that will prepare them well for a career in any scientific endeavor involving mathematical investigation. Each year will include online training to prepare the students for the summer camp and ongoing focus research groups during the subsequent academic year, during which time the students will work on concrete research problems.

A new approach to both graduate and undergraduate student research training in applied mathematics is envisioned. The program will be based around yearly cycles in which a new cohort of students will be drawn from a national pool of applicants each year. The students will be brought through the program and trained in critical research and professional skills needed in the modern world of collaborative and interdisciplinary research. The year-long activities will be built around an intensive summer camp that kicks off the program for each student and ongoing web-based groups through which much of the skill-building and mentoring will take place. The effort is a partnership between the Mathematics and Climate Research Network (MCRN) and the American Institute of Mathematics (AIM). MCRN has considerable experience in building a web-active community that keeps a large geographically dispersed group engaged throughout the year and it will be the host environment for this effort. AIM will provide the institutional framework as well. This award was co-funded by the NSF Research Traineeship (NRT) Program.  The NRT Program is designed to encourage the development and implementation of bold, new potentially transformative models for STEM graduate education training.
Outcome Report:
Mathematics is a key player in both understanding and addressing climate change. The Mathematics and Climate Research Network (MCRN) has empowered a new generation of mathematical scientists to develop the knowledge and skills to address this major societal challenge by applying their mathematical talent. This has been achieved through a succession of summer schools and collaborative workshops coupled with ongoing research group activity throughout the year, both through traditional research groups within institutions and collaborative groups distributed across the network.. The emphasis in the research groups has been on teamwork through which each member appreciates the complementary talents and skills of other members. Since the individuals in the network are distributed across the country, the project has leveraged and developed online platforms to great effect. The teams have included students from undergraduate through advanced graduate, and postdoctoral scholars as well as senior faculty leaders. The vertical integration of the groups has been a particularly successful part of the project.
Summer schools on climate and sustainability were held in 2018, 2019 and 2023. These led to projects, and in turn papers and presentations, on abrupt change in climate systems, resilience to disturbances, specific systems like the polar vortex and El Niño, vegetation loss, and ocean circulation. The incorporation of observational data into models has been a particular focus, especially for novel underlying computational systems. In summer 2020, in a collaboration with the American Institute of Mathematics, the members of this project developed a rapid response summer school to the COVID crisis. This fully online school, spread over two months, engaged almost fifty students in projects aimed at understanding and mitigating the spread of COVID. This school led to a number of publications ranging from a study of the effect of lockdown on atmospheric carbon to one that used a novel approach combining data and transmission models to understand disparities in COVID transmission , death rates, and testing across racial and ethnic groups.
One outcome of the project has been the design of an educational environment that is particularly successful in training students in skills needed for a range of careers. It has further been notably successful in attracting women students as well as members of underrepresented minority groups.
A new MCRN leadership has emerged of early-career mathematicians. Their plans have grown out of this project and extend some of its most successful elements, including mentoring chains and online research groups, and introduce new ones, such as safe spaces for the discussion of new ideas and publication of a collection of curriculum materials. Most of these new leaders were students trained under this award and a predecessor project that laid the foundation for MCRN. A photo is attached of the community workshop in Portland (May, 2023) that brings this to life.
The challenge to develop mathematics for climate and sustainability is daunting. Mathematics departments in academia around the US have been slow to pick up the need for dedicated training, both from a general skills and specific knowledge viewpoint. The goal of this project was to fill this gap by training students in a national network that crossed institutional boundaries. What has resulted is a model not only for efforts in climate mathematics, but for other emerging areas of pressing scientific and societal importance that fall outside the traditional purview of a mathematics department.

Title: NRT: Quantitative & Evolutionary STEM Training (QUEST): An Integrative Training Program for Versatile STEM Professionals to Solve Environmental and Global Health Problems
Program(s): Project & Program Evaluation, NSF Research Traineeship (NRT)
Organization: University of Vermont & State Agricultural College
Abstract:
Major environmental and global health problems, such as emerging infectious diseases, antibiotic and pesticide resistance, reduced crop yields, and the loss of biodiversity, can be addressed through the integration of evolutionary principles with the massive amounts of available climate, genomic, and public health data.  For example, pathogens, pests, and invasive species often quickly evolve resistance to control measures, while important crops and wild populations have limited or variable capacity to adapt to rapidly changing global conditions.  Important insights into the mechanisms of pathogen/pest resistance and resilience will require collaborative efforts that apply evolutionary principles to big data analyses and visualization. However, few opportunities exist for trainees to develop the unique combination of relevant evolutionary, quantitative, and teamwork skills. This National Science Foundation Research Traineeship (NRT) award to the University of Vermont will meet this demand with an interdisciplinary PhD training program called QUantitative & Evolutionary STEM Training (QUEST). The project anticipates training 36 PhD students as core trainees, 18 of whom will receive NRT-funded stipends, from a range of disciplines including biology, mathematics and statistics, engineering, agricultural sciences, environmental studies, and health sciences. 
 
The QUEST program is unique in its emphasis on evolutionary training, modeling for prediction, and culturally sensitive teamwork. Major research efforts will focus on three areas: (i) emerging infectious diseases and modeling for prediction, (ii) rapid evolution in response to antibiotics, pesticides, and global change conditions, and (iii) pathogen interactions that affect food security and ecosystem health. A supportive and collaborative training environment will be cultivated by cohort building via a shared, physical space, a set of core courses in which trainees work in teams to solve real-world problems, and a seminar that includes invited speakers and professional development activities. In addition, QUEST trainees will complete an applied internship, selected from government, non-profit, industry, and international partners. Through cultural sensitivity and inclusion training for faculty, staff and trainees, and innovative recruitment efforts, the traineeship aims to increase underrepresented groups in STEM. Project outcomes will be (1) trainees that are experts in the application of deep evolutionary and quantitative knowledge to develop solutions for resilience in environmental and global health systems, (2) trainees that can work creatively and collaboratively to translate their skills to practical solutions in non-academic sectors, and (3) a scalable, transferable graduate training program that increases diversity in STEM fields.  

The NSF Research Traineeship (NRT) Program is designed to encourage the development and implementation of bold, new potentially transformative models for STEM graduate education training. The Traineeship Track is dedicated to effective training of STEM graduate students in high priority interdisciplinary research areas, through comprehensive traineeship models that are innovative, evidence-based, and aligned with changing workforce and research needs.
Outcome Report:
The Quantitative and Evolutionary STEM Training (QuEST) program is a National Science Foundation Research Traineeship (NRT) that provided doctoral students at the University of Vermont with funding and training to enhance their skills, knowledge, and competencies needed to better understand and solve environmental and global health challenges. QuEST has funded 36 trainees over the course of the five-year award who have carried out 31 meaningful, applied internships between 2019-2023 with non-academic partners across the U.S. and world and published >75 professional publications. Of the internships, about 33% were with government/public sector partners, 63% were nonprofit partners, and one was in the private sector. Internships spanned government labs, conservation NGOs, museums, biotech centers, and think tanks. Trainees built their disciplinary and interdisciplinary content knowledge and teamwork skills through three QuEST courses that have been institutionalized, Foundations of Quant. Reasoning, QuEST seminar, and Data Lab, and through elective courses. Students report having gained a true sense of belonging in a supportive academic community through the cohort model and interdisciplinary approach of the program. The sense of community was achieved through annual retreats that included Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion training for all trainees and participating faculty and through co-curricular activities in the weekly QuEST seminar. For example, in their first year, trainees participate in the Cajita project and gallery walk, making and sharing a “little box” with images or mementos symbolic of important people, places, and events for them to become the scientist that they are today. Trainees would also form Interest Group Networks (IGNs), self-directed collaborative working groups that would share ideas and professional research interests, offer peer support, and create opportunities for their professional growth and development, such as hosting external speakers. With the growth of the program and advancement of the trainees, the focus shifted to professional development activities such as project management, improv for science communication, curating your internet presence, building collaborative teams, submitting grants, publishing, cultivating mentor/mentee relationships, finding the next job/postdoc. The QuEST program will continue with institutional support and become the Biological Data Science (BilDS) program and Certificate of Graduate Study.
