Title: NRT-DESE: Data Intensive Research Enabling Clean Technologies (DIRECT)
Program(s): Project & Program Evaluation, IUSE, NSF Research Traineeship (NRT)
Abstract:
Discovering new materials that will generate and store renewable energy in a low cost, environmentally benign, and scalable fashion is perhaps the most important technological challenge facing society today. All phases of this scientific process (design, synthesis, and characterization) are routinely stymied by the same challenge: researchers are not equipped to handle the deluge of data coming from our labs and high performance computers. This National Science Foundation Research Traineeship (NRT) award to the University of Washington will create, test and evaluate a new training model for graduate students in the area of data intensive research in materials for clean energy. The University of Washington program, DIRECT: Data Intensive Research Enabling Clean Technologies, addresses these challenges by training a new generation of energy researchers who are equipped to handle the massive data sets arising from all stages of materials discovery. This project anticipates 72 trainees (18 MS and 54 PhD students), including 16 funded trainees, from Chemical Engineering, Chemistry, Materials Science & Engineering, Molecular Engineering and Human Centered Design & Engineering. 

DIRECT creates a new training modality comprised of three phases: 1) new graduate coursework at the nexus of data science and advanced materials for energy, 2) a project-based learning scheme to apply new skills and work on challenging real world problems in a team-based setting, and 3) capstone experiences that leverage broad networks spanning industry, national labs and several international partners. The thematic focus of the research is next-generation materials for batteries and photovoltaics. We will use an ethnographic approach rooted in the social sciences to understand why some methods are successfully deployed while others are not, and learn how to apply data science tools in a contextualized manner to materials science to maximize usability. The project-based learning component of the traineeship will provide graduate students the chance to teach and practice leadership and management skills, a unique opportunity most trainees would not otherwise receive. DIRECT trainees will be equipped for many new career options that require data science training and will be prepared with the skills needed to thrive in the economy of the 21st century. The project will also provide unique information about the effectiveness of project-based learning in the acquisition of advanced technical skills and disciplinary knowledge in graduate education.

The NSF Research Traineeship (NRT) Program is designed to encourage the development and implementation of bold, new potentially transformative models for STEM graduate education training. The Traineeship Track is dedicated to effective training of STEM graduate students in high priority interdisciplinary research areas, through the comprehensive traineeship model that is innovative, evidence-based, and aligned with changing workforce and research needs.
Outcome Report:
Project outcomes report: NRT DIRECT [Data Intensive Research Enabling Clean Technology]
This project supported a new, interdisciplinary research traineeship at the intersection of data science, chemical science and engineering, and clean energy technologies. Original participating academic departments included chemical engineering, chemistry, materials science engineering and molecular engineering. The central feature of the NRT was a three course sequence that included a one course capstone project where students gained real world experience applying new skills to data driven problems, working with external partners from companies, nonprofits and government national labs. 
The program and progress toward objectives were assessed annually by an external evaluator. Findings suggest that the curriculum was very effective at providing students with a comprehensive base of knowledge about statistics, machine learning and data science while simultaneously giving a range of practical skills implementing these methods in Python. Faculty mentors of our trainees reported many positive benefits of the program, especially the dissemination of new research methods within their own teams. The program was also designed to be lean, enabling participation of students from across the UW College of Engineering. More than 50 students took the theory/practice courses each year, and around 25 students completed the capstone project each year for the duration of the project. Throughout the course of the project, we expanded to other application areas beyond clean energy including biotechnology, molecular engineering and others.
Given the success of the program and high demand for spots in the courses, we developed multiple ways to sustain the curriculum beyond the duration of the NRT project period.

Title: NRT-IGE: Promoting Creativity in Engineering and Technology Graduate Education through Integration of Arts, Design and Experiential Learning in the Curriculum
Abstract:
Engineering graduate education in the U.S. is considered to be among the best in the world; however, studies demonstrate that American education has been losing competitiveness when compared with that of emerging economies and other developed nations. Members of the U.S. Congress have expressed concern about the health and competitiveness of the nation's colleges and universities.  Furthermore, employers often indicate that new university graduates lack creativity and problem solving skills, even when they have advanced degrees in specialized fields. Because creativity and innovation are the driving forces for economic growth, it is critical to infuse innovative thinking and hands-on experience into the engineering and technology graduate curricula. This National Science Foundation Research Traineeship (NRT) award in the Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) Track to Indiana University-Purdue University Indianapolis (IUPUI) will pilot a new cross-disciplinary education model to achieve these ends. This project will promote creativity and innovation by integrating arts and experiential learning components, such as intense studio training, into engineering and technology graduate curricula. 

Faculty members in engineering and technology will work with their counterparts in the fine arts to integrate Engineering, Technology, and Arts (ETA) and develop an experimental Design Track in the existing Mechanical Engineering master's program at IUPUI. Students in the proposed ETA Design Track will acquire real-world problem solving skills through short-term programs with industry and national laboratories. This project involves the development of three interdisciplinary courses: (i) Irregular, free-form, and origami inspired structures, (ii) Optimal design of mechatronic systems: toys, robots and interactive structures, and (iii) Environmental pollution and emission control. The courses will be team-developed and taught by faculty from programs in interior design, video art and interactive installations, mechanical engineering, and electrical engineering technology. These three courses will constitute the proposed ETA Design Track and support a new Graduate Certificate in Design. Pedagogical approaches will include problem-based, studio-based, and experiential learning. The project will test the ability of ETA curriculum integration, as well as experiential learning in industry or government laboratories, to enhance creativity and innovation among participating graduate students.  Quantitative data will be collected using the Reisman Diagnostic Creativity Assessment and contextualized using student and faculty interview results.   In addition, program outcomes will be tracked.  Expected program outcomes for the ETA Design Track include: increased integrative learning, innovative thinking, patents, high-quality publications, and start-ups by ETA graduates. 

The NSF Research Traineeship (NRT) Program is designed to encourage the development and implementation of bold, new, potentially transformative models for STEM graduate education training. The Innovations in Graduate Education Track is dedicated solely to piloting, testing, and evaluating novel, innovative, and potentially transformative approaches to graduate education.
Outcome Report:
1. Curriculum:
A. New Course Development (3 Courses)
I. ME 58901: Optimal Design of Mechatronic Systems: Robots and Interactive Structures. Catalog Description: This course introduces the fundamentals of transformation of knowledge from art/design to engineering/technology applications. Different variant forms of free form design, in relation to various structural topologies common in engineering and technology applications and related optimization techniques are discussed. This course utilizes the epistemology of studio practice implicit in the artistic process in order to acquire embodied knowledge. Reasoning innovative process can be taught through the crafting of mechanical structures while experiencing bodily interactions with the nature of materials and tools. Thus, this course introduces a range of design principles and critical studio practice methodologies while working with a range of variable materials and aims to help students grow in their creative thinking. It integrates mechatronic modeling / simulation, optimal design, and hands-on fabrication of robotic systems (sensors, actuators, electric circuits, and embedded controllers) and interactive structures in a makerspace environment.
II. ME 57301: Air Pollution and Emission Control. Catalog Description: This course is designed to promote creativity through immersive experience. It integrates the real-world problem solving experience into the course curriculum through guest lectures from experts working in the industry. Students study the air pollution sources and fundamental mechanisms of their impacting the environment and human health, and how automotive emission can be measured and controlled. In particular, measurement of particulate emission deposited in a diesel particulate filter is studied. Topics in emission control technologies, including sensors, control mechanisms, remedial systems are taught and combined into the course projects.  
III. ME 59700 (Selected Topics): Design of Complex and Origami Structures. Catalog Description: This course introduces principles in art and engineering analysis and optimization with focus on design of complex, irregular (organic), free-form, and origami structures. This course provides a sound grasp of structural analysis and design optimization methods, the origami arts, and fundamental creative strategies used in the design thinking process.
 B. Graduate Certificate program in Engineering Design Innovation:
Today's engineers are constantly faced with the challenge of solving complex engineering problems. This certificate program is designed to train the practicing engineers as well the degree seeking engineering graduate students on creative thinking and technical skills in complex system design while innovating new technologies.
This certificate program is designed to address industry's increased needs for engineers who can develop new and innovative technologies.  It will prepare today's engineers to be competitive in taking on the new challenges.
The purpose of this graduate-certificate program in mechanical engineering is to enable engineers to become more innovative in the design of engineering systems without formally pursuing a graduate degree.  The certificate provides a core set of courses on origami based design, optimal mechatronics system design, and environmental pollution control.  The projects assigned in these courses are based on new ideas which will be solved during the semester using studio based methodology.  Students completing this certificate will be able to contribute the knowledge gained to serve the respective companies more effectively.
Expected Outcomes:
To gain skills to innovatively solve complex engineering problems via studio based practices.
To apply creative design methodologies to develop innovative engineering products.
 C. MS in Mechanical Engineering in Design Track:
 This particular track in MS in Mechanical Engineering was establish during the grant period to further inculcate the design innovation thinking and train the graduate students and undergraduate seniors in developing skills in designing innovative systems in order to address current technological challenges in the industry. Students specializing in this track must take at least two of the three courses developed under this grant.

Title: NRT-IGE: Information Infrastructure for Society:  Integrating Data Science and Social Science in Graduate Education  and Workforce Development
Abstract:
This National Science Foundation Research Traineeship (NRT) award in the Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) Track to the University of Maryland will pilot an innovative, cross-disciplinary curriculum that integrates Data Science with Social Science. The project will advance the scientific understanding of the dynamics of human behavior by integrating the toolkits and analytical frameworks developed by social scientists with the new types of data, models and tools developed in the fields of computer science and statistics.  The curriculum provides an innovative approach to training students in the creative and scientific use of the growing number of available data.   It covers all phases of a research project, addressing social issues including problem formulation, data collection, manipulation, processing, and analysis. The project pilots an innovative modular training program that is tailored to fill specific needs of both traditional and nontraditional graduate students, and provides direct pathways both to future employers and to advancement with current employers.

The project advances the understanding of how best to train students and working professionals in the STEM fields, particularly social science.  The project tests a pedagogical approach that has been successful in other areas, namely, modular "nano" classes that are focused on experiential learning based on specific social problems and feature peer-to-peer learning between persons in the social sciences and computer science. Because the projects and problems to be worked on within the nano classes are designed together with federal, state, and local agencies, students will have the opportunity test and showcase their knowledge to current and future employers. The effectiveness of the program is evaluated by analyzing the reactions of the participants to the material provided, learning outcomes in terms of improved qualifications, use of learned material in their respective jobs, effects upon job performance, and estimates of rate of return. The data curation, management, interrogation and integration tools are built into a data facility system, within which collaboration is fostered, and which can be replicated and used by other curriculum adopters.  A series of small randomized experiments will allow the empirical test of learning modules and improve them based on the results.  The overall result of the project can be adapted by institutions in the US, and a program of outreach activities with the institution's international partners will allow an even broader transfer.

The NSF Research Traineeship (NRT) Program is designed to encourage the development and implementation of bold, new potentially transformative models for STEM graduate education training. The Innovations in Graduate Education Track is dedicated solely to piloting, testing, and evaluating novel, innovative, and potentially transformative approaches to graduate education.
Outcome Report:
From education to health to criminal justice, government regulation and policy decisions have important effects on social and individual experiences. New data science tools applied to data created by government agencies have the potential to enhance these meaningful decisions. To overcome institutional barriers limiting the realization of this potential, the project created an innovate graduate education program that included both graduate students and government employees.
The program—which trains students and government employees on how to perform applied data analysis with confidential individual-level data generated through administrative processes, and extensive project-focused work—provides both online and onsite training components. Training takes place in a secure environment. The aim is to help agencies tackle important policy problems by using modern computational and data analysis methods and tools, while drawing on the academic insights from graduate students. The program accelerates the technical and analytical development of the participants and demonstrates the potential value of working with individual-level data across agency and jurisdictional lines. The initial success is being expanded through the creation of a larger community of academic institutions, government agencies, and foundations that can work together to increase the information infrastructure for society.
The program had three primary components:
Technical (Computational and Data) Infrastructure with access to confidential agency microdata in a secure computing environment;
Training Curriculum including lectures, hands-on sessions, and code notebooks using data and problems from multiple jurisdictions across policy areas;
Collaborative Projects based on the needs of government agencies to seed new products.
Participants in the training program worked in a secure cloud-based environment and were introduced to new ways of collecting data and analyzing it using new computational and data analysis methods and tools. The overarching approach included training in how to keep fundamental statistical concepts like population frames, sampling, and valid inference while include modern computational data analysis tools, such as machine learning. Participants were also trained in the use of new types of data, including administrative data (records generated from the administration of government programs), data captured from websites or through application programming interfaces (APIs), and data with large spatial components, network structures, or text. The program is built on a foundation of social science research principles integrated with current analytic and computational skills, while being rooted in the study of real-world social and economic problem.
The materials are widely available.  The training materials are freely available in a textbook, which is now in its 2nd edition and available for anyone to read online. The syllabus and associated online videos are also available for broader use and adoption.   All the code is posted on github and can be reused by the broader data science community.
Since its inception, over 650 individuals have participated and been trained in data science basics. Many of those participants subsequently trained others in how to think and use data for evidence-based policy making and how to increase societal data infrastructure. Most notably, the program has helped inform the design of the federal data learning agenda.
The approach and associated material has been adopted and used in classes throughout the country in different disciplines: public policy, sociology, education, criminal justice, statistics, and economics. It has also created new federal and state capacity to tackle critical policy problems, ranging from improving understanding for human services providers about how to increase economic self-sufficiency for welfare recipients, to informing workforce boards about the characteristics of unemployment claimants to speed reemployment policy,  from using data to better target child nutrition policy, to building multistate dashboards that show state decision-makers about the links between educational investments and workforce outcomes. Finally, because the approach will be adopted by Historically Black Colleges and Universities and Hispanic Serving Institutions, the effects on building capacity for faculty training underrepresented minorities will continue for years to come.

Title: NRT-INFEWS: Paths to Sustainable Food-Energy-Water Systems in Resource-Limited Communities
Program(s): NSF Research Traineeship (NRT), Project & Program Evaluation
Abstract:
The complex interconnectivity of society's food, energy and water resources, as well as their inextricable link to socioeconomic factors, present both grand challenges and opportunities that demand new paradigms in problem solving and cooperation across non-traditional disciplines. Nowhere will this challenge be greater than in resource-constrained communities, not only in the developing world but also in the often-overlooked populations of rural America and poor urban centers, where solutions to food/energy/water challenges will need to be tailored to specific communities. This National Science Foundation Research Traineeship (NRT) award to the University of Iowa will produce a new generation of water sustainability professionals specifically trained to promote sustainable development of food, energy and water resources in these underserved communities, not only as researchers and professors, but also as entrepreneurs, consultants, and civic, professional and global engineers. This project anticipates training fifty (50) MS and PhD students via new graduate degree and certificate programs in Sustainable Water Development, including twenty (20) funded trainees, by leveraging university expertise in all facets of water sustainability including engineering, economics, policy, law, public health, geography, ecology and informatics.

This research aims to re-envision STEM graduate education in fields related to water sustainability at the nexus of food and energy resources. We propose a new training paradigm in which educational and research activities at all degree levels (MS and PhD) are focused on experiences that connect trainees directly to the most vulnerable communities in need, thereby satisfying students' stated desires to engage in work that addresses social injustices arising from disparities in resource security. Courses, research projects, community service, and professional training experiences will all be tailored to the trainees' desired career paths. To launch this model, we will create a new graduate degree program at the University of Iowa focused on the development of sustainable water resources in resource-limited communities (e.g., rural and poor communities). The Sustainable Water Development degree will be housed in the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, while building upon strengths across the campus in the area of water sustainability and emphasizing the critical roles of both water quality and quantity as well as food and energy production. Major research efforts will address high priority research needs for such communities, including: forecasting, mitigating and adapting to climate variability; innovative solutions for minimizing waste streams and promoting resource recovery; new water treatment infrastructure suitable in scale and associated energy demand for small communities; and management of biogeochemical cycles and agro-ecosystem structure to promote environmental quality. In addition, we will develop a graduate certificate program in Sustainable Water Development available to the entire graduate STEM population at the university, thereby adding valuable specialization to existing degree programs in water-relevant STEM fields (e.g., chemistry, biology, physics and mathematics).

The NSF Research Traineeship (NRT) Program is designed to encourage the development and implementation of bold, new potentially transformative models for STEM graduate education training. The Traineeship Track is dedicated to effective training of STEM graduate students in high priority interdisciplinary research areas, through the comprehensive traineeship model that is innovative, evidence-based, and aligned with changing workforce and research needs.
Outcome Report:
This NRT award established the Sustainable Water Development (SWD) Graduate Program within the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering (CEE) at the University of Iowa (UI). Over the duration of the award, NRT support contributed to the training of over 50 PhD and MS trainees. Major outcomes include:
A more flexible model for elective coursework that enabled graduate students to pursue content related to their preferred professional preparation (or SWD “Pathway”) while fulfilling their PhD and MS course requirements. For example, students with expressed interest in the professoriate were able to obtain a Certificate in College Teaching through the UI College of Education, and the coursework required for this Certificate was applied to requirements for their PhD in CEE.
Evidence of a positive influence of internships on STEM graduate training, both in terms ofs trainee professional development and job placement after degree completion. A signature element of the SWD program was the Pathway Training Experience (PTE). These were internship-like experiences required for NRT trainees. Example PTEs included placements with consulting firms, private industry, state and federal agencies, branches of federal government, communities and local governments, and research institutes and centers. Assessment activities revealed these experiences to be a formative part of trainee development. The experiences also were critical for professional networking and career exploration, with multiple students using their PTE to acquire full time positions in careers beyond academia.
High impact research products related to water resource sustainability at the intersection of food and energy systems. Trainee research focused on topics including equitable access to safe drinking water; low-carbon technologies for water purification and resource recovery; watershed management practices to promote community resiliency; surface water quality monitoring to assess human health risks; and the environmental fate and ecosystem impacts of chemicals used in food production. In these areas, trainees authored numerous peer-reviewed papers and gave frequent presentations at local and national meetings.
A revamped, modern curricula in Civil and Environmental Engineering that better prepares trainees to address emergent societal issues of relevance to our disciplinary community, while also better preparing them to engage stakeholders beyond our discipline.  The SWD program involved the creation of five new courses, which have now been institutionalized as the core curriculum for the broader Water & the Environment Graduate Program within CEE at UI. These courses allowed several new and emerging areas of study to be integrated into the core of graduate student training in CEE at UI. These topics include data science, computer programming, and informatics; science-policy and regulatory economics; systems thinking and integration of food, energy, and water systems; community engagement; and technical communication.
A strong culture of excellence in science communication with CEE at UI as a result of the SWD NRT program. All CEE students are now required to take a technical communication course. All thesis (MS and PhD) trainees are also required to take two semesters of a "Coaching Seminar", where they prepare different forms of presentations ]e.g., posters, figures, three-minute theses (3MT), standard research talks] and receive structured feedback from dedicated faculty instructors. Assessment activities revealed that students valued this training focus on communication skills development, which they believed would be helpful in professional development and career placement.
A STEM graduate program intentionally designed to broaden participation through implementation of evidence-based best practices. The SWD program was built with practices and features specifically identified in the literature by under-represented racial minority (URM) trainees as desirable in a graduate program (e.g., see Campbell et al., CBE-Life Sciences Education, 2014). Accordingly, we were able to recruit our first two (and largest) cohorts with over 70% female and over 30% URM trainees (out of over 30 total trainees). These numbers far exceed the norms within CEE and the College of Engineering at UI. With these successes, however, we also experienced challenges in ensuring an equitable and inclusive environment for our trainees, both at UI and in the surrounding community of Iowa City. This, in turn, negatively impacted the experience of URM trainees in our program and affected our ability to retain the diversity in our cohorts. Ultimately, it has been difficult for the NRT leadership team to drive institutional change in a meaningful way that fully supports and empowers URM trainees once on campus at UI.
A new interdisciplinary graduate program centered on the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). A top priority of the NRT leadership team was to create opportunities for the best aspects of the SWD program (based on assessment activities) to be sustained beyond the lifetime of the NSF award. To this end, we created and established the interdisciplinary Sustainable Development MS degree program offered through the Graduate College at UI. By housing this degree program in the UI Graduate College, all content is available to all members of the UI campus.

Title: NRT-UtB: Neurophotonics
Program(s): IGERT FULL PROPOSALS, NSF Research Traineeship (NRT)
Abstract:
This National Science Foundation Research Traineeship (NRT) award to Boston University will train scientists and engineers in the emerging interdisciplinary field of neurophotonics - the use of light-based tools to study brain function at the cellular scale. Understanding how neural activities and circuits drive human computation, behavior, and psychology is motivated by a critical societal need to address brain diseases that involve disruptions or deterioration of neural circuitry - including Alzheimer's, traumatic brain injury, Parkinson's, cerebral palsy and multiple sclerosis. Recent scientific discoveries and powerful new tools in brain research have inspired broad student interest in career paths focused on understanding brain structure and function, as well as new industrial and academic career opportunities. Neurophotonics is among the most rapidly evolving research frontiers in brain science because it allows researchers to monitor and influence neuron activity and neural circuits at their most fundamental level. A prominent neurophotonic technique is optogenetics, through which communication signals from neurons are precisely monitored, activated, or inhibited using light. This project will support training for eighty (80) PhD students, including twenty (20) funded trainees, across the disciplines of neuroscience, biomedical engineering and photonics.

Trainees will become versed in the biology of neural function and the development of optical instruments, photo-excitable materials, and imaging techniques to sense and affect neural circuits. NRT trainees will graduate having attended a hands-on neurophotonics technology boot camp, participated in multiple laboratory research rotations, completed a four-course core curriculum, conducted challenging doctoral research in a neurophotonics laboratory, and written a neurophotonics-themed dissertation co-mentored by NRT faculty. The traineeship project will emphasize immersive experiential learning activities and peer-to-peer learning, two educational approaches that have been shown to reinforce learning while simultaneously improving outcomes for STEM trainees, especially underrepresented minorities. Interwoven with educational activities will be a professional preparation program that supports trainee career goals, develops communication skills, and builds professional networks. Trainee learning objectives will focus on identifying important research problems in neurophotonics, applying light-based methods to measure and control neural circuits, working on team-oriented projects, and communicating effectively.

The NSF Research Traineeship (NRT) Program is designed to encourage the development and implementation of bold, new potentially transformative models for STEM graduate education training. The Traineeship Track is dedicated to effective training of STEM graduate students in high priority interdisciplinary research areas, through the comprehensive traineeship model that is innovative, evidence-based, and aligned with changing workforce and research needs.
Outcome Report:
Intellectual Merit – Our vision was to train diverse cohorts of scientists and engineers in the deeply interdisciplinary field of neurophotonics research. Trainees became versed in the biology of neural function and the engineering of photonics tools, materials, and techniques that can be used to sense and affect neural circuits. Our primary goal was to create an innovative educational program within a thriving interdisciplinary research environment, using photonics as an enabler for understanding and influencing cell­ scale brain function. Drawing on evidence from current literature we emphasized experiential learning opportunities where students learn by doing. NRT project goals were to: Recruit 20 doctoral research Fellows to participate in the program; Immerse fellows and an additional 80 trainees who were not supported on fellowships in a profoundly experiential learning environment, beginning with a one-week interdisciplinary summer Boot Camp and including experiences at topical summer schools and short course programs; educate trainee cohorts using high impact practices that improve learning outcomes, anchored by a four-course core curriculum and team-based research in neurophotonics; and construct strong, sustainable, multi­tiered professional networks for each trainee while expanding their interdisciplinary perspectives, their communication skills, and their career options. 
Broader Impacts –Ninety-three trainees were accepted into the training program including 21 fellowship recipients. Of the fellowship recipients, 33% were minorities, and 50% were female, exceeding targets for both demographics in the original proposal. Trainees organized and led five annual symposia on the topic of neurophotonics. They also participated in multifaceted professional development programs, including workshops on technical communication, research ethics, responsible conduct of research, and skills training for neurophotonics imaging techniques, machine learning, and optogenetics. The program has been sustained at BU even after completion of the NSF sponsorship through direct fellowship and trainee program support provided by the BU Photonics Center. An additional broader impact was the cumulative positive effect that this program had on translating scholarly innovations in neurophotonics into products the benefit society in the fields of life science and engineering. 
Research Products – Eight NRT fellows have graduated with PhDs, each having attended a hands-on technology boot camp, participated in multiple laboratory research rotations, completed a four-course core curriculum, conducted challenging doctoral research, and written a neurophotonics themed dissertation co­-mentored by NRT faculty. Fifty-five publications resulted from this NSF award.

Title: MIT Institute for Data, Systems, and Society Inaugural Workshop: Sociotechnical Systems, Cambridge, MA September 22-23, 2016
Program(s): PFI-Partnrships for Innovation, NSF Research Traineeship (NRT), EFRI Research Projects
Abstract:
This award supports a workshop marking the inaugural year of MIT's Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS) that aims to advance education and research at the intersection of engineering systems with statistics, information and decision systems with social and behavioral sciences.  Our lives are shaped by complex, interconnected systems that generate increasingly vast amounts of data -a proliferation that is redefining various domains of engineering. IDSS is at the forefront of this development and this workshop will showcase the recent advances in studying such systems and pave the way for the future. This award will support and fund the sessions focused on smart services, smart cities, smart grid, and graduate education. Bringing together researchers from all five MIT schools as well as distinguished speakers from across the nation, including engineers in various disciplines, together with statisticians and social and behavioral scientists, the workshop will show how rigorous analytical methods can be used to better model, understand, and improve society's most complex systems. The research presented in the workshop takes a holistic, data-driven approach to solving critical societal problems across a range of application domains. Within the broad scope of this research, this NSF-funded workshop will help showcase research across several key areas: smart services and operations in energy systems (the smart grid), urbanization and smart cities, and generally smart services. The research highlighted in the workshop paves the way for new interdisciplinary research in all of these areas. 

The workshop will showcase the state of the art of research in these domains through a series of panel discussions led by top thinkers in their fields. These discussions will foster dialogue about new directions for research and create opportunities for collaboration, while strengthening IDSS?s multidisciplinary research community. The 2-day workshop will be open to the public with free registration and will involve researchers from government, industry, and academia, as well as graduate students in the relevant areas. The Launch Event will also feature a student session that explores IDSS's new programs in Social and Engineering Systems and also in Statistics, and what impact these new programs might have on the future of interdisciplinary, data-driven research for solving society's biggest challenges. There will also be a student Q&A session in which the students get to ask questions and exchange ideas with the distinguished panelists.

As part of its research efforts, IDSS is not only advancing new technologies and new smart services in energy, health, transportation and urban science,, but it is also looking at the powerful implications of these innovations for individuals, larger systems, and society as a whole. There will be a report issued that will present the major findings of the event.

Title: Collaborative Research:  Standard:  Comparison of Communications across Campus Cultures  (4C Project): Toward Evidence-based Customization of Learning Experiences for CCE STEM
Abstract:
Ethical behavior of STEM professionals is essential for the progress of science, advancement of the national health, and prosperity and welfare. Therefore STEM trainees must receive the appropriate education to mature into responsible professionals that display an awareness and understanding of ethical challenges within STEM. Does "one size fits all" STEM ethics training result in a well-trained STEM workforce?
The goal of this collaborative project is to define, through data, STEM ethics learning communities and then develop a strategy for matching communities with resources effective for them. Through this study, hundreds of STEM trainees from four distinct higher learning institutions will each provide individual demographic and academic information, survey data, and writing samples. The data sets generated will be analyzed to determine which common qualities define ethical STEM learning communities. Evidence-based identification of learning communities will then provide the basis for strategically matching them with a subset of the many resources and experiences already developed for ethical STEM education. This study will be conducted simultaneously at campuses with different constituencies and cultures: (1) Saint Mary's College, an all-women's college; (2) the University of Notre Dame, a Catholic research university; (3) Xavier University, a Historically Black College or University (HBCU); and (4) the University of Virginia, a public research university. 

The methods employed will include administration and analysis of five validated scales (for learning style, personality, moral concern, moral action, and environmental orientation) and automated text analysis of student writings in three different formats (electronic journal entry, online discussion forum, and Twitter). To develop and test principles of differentiated instruction emerging from this research, investigators from each institution will design and offer pilot learning experiences combining a single established resource or approach for ethics education with one defined learning community. The resulting case reports and underlying principles are expected to be articulated in the Strategic Engagement of Learning Communities for Ethical STEM Handbook and distributed across STEM research networks, the science and engineering ethics community, informal science and education networks, and K-12 science education networks.
Outcome Report:
Because science and engineering affects everyone in society, science and engineering students should gain experience addressing the moral and ethical aspects of the work that they do. There are many open questions about how to best approach ethics learning for STEM (science, technology, engineering, and math) students. Techniques that are effective for learning about the objective and technical aspects of these fields are not compatible with some important aspects of ethics learning, as questions regarding moral issues are more nuanced and subjective.  Our project is concerned with ethics education about broad and complex matters that arise where science and technology interact with society at large.  We hypothesized that STEM ethics learning is personal, in that it is important to understand individual perspectives (where someone is coming from) to meet students where they are and promote holistic learning and development. 
When we started our project, little was known about some of the similarities and differences among STEM learners that are likely to be relevant for ethics learning.  We postulated that factors such as personality, personal and societal level moral values, and attitudes towards the natural environment might play an important role in how students respond to ethics education. To investigate this, we conducted a multi-component survey that included questions from the Big Five Personality Index (BFI), the New Environmental Paradigm (NEP), the Moral Foundations Questionnaire (MFQ), the Values in Action (VIA), and the ASSIST Learning Style assessment.  
  We collected data from 659 STEM students at four different US universities: The University of Notre Dame, University of Virginia, Saint Mary's College, and Xavier University of Louisiana over four years.  The survey captured data about each student's major/program of study, gender, race/ethnicity, religious affiliation and practice, prior formal ethics learning, and more.  The most important finding from our survey research about STEM learners is that there is far more diversity within any group defined by a commonality (such as major/program of study, gender, race/ethnicity, or religion) than between different groups.  This is important because it shows that educators should not make assumptions about a starting point for ethics learning based on a student's major/program of study, their gender, or other group-identifier. 
  Our project also addressed an additional gap in the field of STEM ethics learning.  While the educational value of reflective writing in response to assigned prompts has been recognized by other fields, such as medical education, the responses of science and engineering students have not been well studied.  By coordinating assignments with different educators at the previously mentioned universities, our research addressed the way individuals responded to the same open-ended questions, at the same time, in online discussion with one another.  This approach connected learners from different majors at different universities and allowed for the exploration of STEM ethics in societal context through real-life examples.  For example, online discussion facilitated thoughtful consideration and interaction about the soaring price of Epi-Pens as the phenomenon was in the news.  To learn all we could from what the students wrote, a team of researchers used a systematic approach to record data about specific ideas and themes expressed.  One of the most important things we found is that students recognize that the experience of online reflective writing in discussion with others led to learning about STEM ethics, and in some cases, led to a fundamental shift in students' understanding of what ethics means in the context of science and engineering practice.  This project provided the proof-of-concept by using prompts for reflective writing that was facilitated in an online discussion with peers. This approach will be sustained by the Online Ethics Center for Engineering and Science.  Our findings about ethics learning through reflective writing in online discussion will be reported to scholars in the STEM ethics education field through a full-length research manuscript that is accepted, pending revisions in the Journal of Science and Engineering Ethics.
  Our project has directly involved undergraduate and graduate students from the four different universities involved, including four undergraduate University of Virginia students, two Indiana University students, two Saint Mary's College students, and one Xavier University student, advancing their training as researchers, professionals, and practitioners prepared to lead future exploration of ethics in the context of STEM.

Title: CyberCorps Scholarship for Service at the University of Massachusetts Amherst
Program(s): NSF Research Traineeship (NRT), CYBERCORPS: SCHLAR FOR SER
Abstract:
This proposal will inaugurate a CyberCorpsÂ® Scholarship for Service (SFS) program at the University of Massachusetts (UMass) at Amherst, the Commonwealth?s flagship institution of higher education. This program will support and expand several of the University?s advanced programs that educate and train cybersecurity researchers and professionals. It will support four interdisciplinary cohorts of seven scholars across four nationally-recognized colleges and departments at UMass: computer science, electrical and computer systems engineering, mathematics and statistics, and business. The proposed program has several key objectives. It will create the CyberCorpsÂ® community that ensures their success through strong peer-mentoring, faculty advising, and academic and professional support. The program intends a 100% placement in government cybersecurity positions, leveraging the UMass faculty?s many relationships with various federal and state labs and offices. UMass?s academic programs in cybersecurity have and will continue to provide high-quality education and research opportunities, with instruction from and collaboration with leading scholars in the field. Its academic programs will address the multifaceted nature of cybersecurity by continuing to expand and integrating interdisciplinary material. 

The program will prepare students for successful careers in cybersecurity, through a combination of strong curricula, ample professional development, extensive advising, interdisciplinary enrichment, and access to recruiting opportunities. In addition, the program will continue and expand UMass?s existing mechanisms to recruit and retain women and underrepresented minorities into our undergraduate and graduate programs. This program will directly impact the cybersecurity workforce by training 28 cybersecurity professionals. Further, this program directly encourages interdisciplinary work between faculty. More generally, the developments under this program, including curriculum, professional development, broad interdisciplinary collaboration, and recruiting focused on women and underrepresented minorities will provide a broad and sustained base to attract more students into UMass?s cybersecurity programs into the foreseeable future.
Outcome Report:
The CyberCorps Scholarship for Service at the University of Massachusetts Amherst supported the education and professional development of 34 students across four nationally-recognized UMass colleges and departments: Computer Science, Electrical and Computer Engineering, Mathematics and Statistics, and Management at both the undergraduate and graduate level. We created for SFS students an academic community that ensured their success through strong peer-mentoring, faculty advising, and academic and professional support. We prepared them for successful careers in cybersecurity through a combination of strong curricula, ample professional development, extensive advising, interdisciplinary enrichment, and access to recruiting opportunities.

23 students went on to fulfill their service obligations in qualifying positions; nine are still in the service phase and in qualifying positions; and one is currently seeking a qualifying position. Three additional students began under this award, and will be continued under a subsequent SFS renewal grant. Ten of our students were women, and three were transfers from local community colleges, aligning with our diversity and broader impact goals.

Students fulfilled their service obligations at a broad list of agencies, including National Security Agency (NSA), Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), U.S. Department of Justice, U.S. Air Force, U.S. Naval Research Laboratory (NRL), Naval Surface Warfare Center, National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA), Los Alamos National Lab (LNL), Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), the University of Massachusetts Amherst, MIT Lincoln Lab, and MITRE.

Student completed internships at a similarly broad list of agencies, including National Security Agency (NSA), Department of Homeland Security (DHS), U.S. Air Force Research Lab ACE program and Civilian Services, U.S. Naval Research Laboratory (NRL), Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Trade Commission, Space and Naval Warfare Systems Command, Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA), Institute for Defense Analysis, the Massachusetts Office of the Attorney General (Digital Evidence Lab), the Rome NY Air Force base ACE program, the Hanscom Air Force base, remote NSF-sponsored internships, and MITRE.

We also engaged in projects with significant synergistic value to SFS. In partnership with the Massachusetts Office of the Attorney General, we have created a year-round on-campus internship program for their Digital Evidence Lab. Several SFS students have interned in this lab, including during summer 2022. We started a new regional workshop "New England Hardware Security Day" which was held for the first time, virtually, in 2021, and in both subsequent years, most recently at Northeastern University in 2023. We planned and executed a summer 2022 event for high-school students at UMass -- held jointly with another NSF awardee -- to learn about computer science. The program was successful and will be run again in summer 2023.

Overall, the main goals of this grant project were met, including our broader goals of strengthening the cybersecurity program at UMass, and diversity and inclusion goals among our applicants.

Abstract:
This proposal will inaugurate a CyberCorpsÂ®: Scholarship for Service (SFS) program at the Tennessee Technological University. The hybrid program, ensuring students? participation in research and outreach activities alongside education in cybersecurity, will offer both accelerated and traditional graduate studies paths to students from Tennessee as well as students from women and underrepresented minority populations across the nation. The proposed CyberCorpsÂ® is a university-wide effort leveraging resources and expertise from the Computer Science Department, Cybersecurity Education Research and Outreach Center, College of Engineering, Student Success Center, Office of Admissions, College of Graduate Studies, Library, Office of Research, and Career Services. This CyberCorpsÂ® program will be the first one in the state of Tennessee and it will have the opportunity to serve the Appalachian area in Tennessee.

The project will provide strategies and techniques that have the potential to be effective in addressing challenges associated with SFS program management. The project will take recommendations from experts based on demonstrated evidence to develop and exercise a suite of best practices for effective management of SFS program. The project will draw upon teaching, research and outreach experiences of the investigators, and the assessment experience of the evaluation specialist.

The project provides broader impact by delivering a SFS program that will lead to broader participation and better preparation of the information assurance and cybersecurity workforce. Students underrepresented in cybersecurity are a major focus of this project. As such, an expected broader impact of the project is to contribute to the ability of the United States higher education enterprise to produce a diverse group of cybersecurity professionals. As part of its broader impact, this project will contribute to the statewide effort to meet a shortage of skilled workers by having the CyberCorps scholarship opportunity accessible to first-generation/low-income community college students impacted by the TN Promise initiative. Since TTU is situated within and serves Central Appalachia, this project will have the opportunity to serve the Appalachian area in TN, which is one of the poorest regions in the country. The region also has a lower education attainment level than the country as an average.
Outcome Report:
In 2016, Tennessee Tech University (TNTech) received a $3.95 million SFS award entitled: "Tennessee CyberCorps: A Hybrid Program in Cybersecurity". This award aimed to launch a hybrid SFS program in TNTech that supports students' participation in cybersecurity education, research, and outreach activities. Through this award, TNTech has been an SFS institution since 2016, hence, becoming the first of its kind in Tennessee. Currently, TNTech is the largest and one of two such programs in Tennessee. The following project outcomes are reported over the period 2016 - 2022.
Workforce Development of Cybersecurity Professionals:
The original target of this award was to introduce 26 workforce-ready professionals in cybersecurity. However, during the award period (2016 - 2022), this award has served a total of 38 students that have been trained in cybersecurity. Thus, the TNTech SFS program has exceeded its target by serving 146% of the proposed students. The TNTech SFS program has graduated 28 students and the remaining 10 students are being supported through a renewal of the SFS award. Of those who completed their degrees (28), 24 (86%) received an M.S. degree, 2 (7%) received a B.S. degree, 1 (3.5%) received an A.S. degree, and 1 (3.5%) received a Ph.D. degree. Since the majority of the SFS graduates (86%) hold an M.S. degree, they are qualified for the upper 20% of the cybersecurity market opportunities. All (100%) of the graduated TNTech SFS students have been successfully placed in jobs. The TNTech SFS Program does NOT have any defaulters. All TNTech SFS alums are currently working on federal and state agencies such as NSA, DHS, FBI, and national labs such as Oakridge National Lab, Los Alamos National Lab, and many more.  
Formal and Informal Education in Cybersecurity: 
All TNTech SFS students (100%) participated in formal and informal cybersecurity-related training. Formal education involves coursework in network security, cryptography, secure software development, cyber-physical system security, AI-assisted cybersecurity, cloud security, application security, etc. In addition, students participated in informal learning through cyber interest groups for defense, offense, and capture the flag (CTF). Also, all the TNTech SFS students participated in informal learning through cybersecurity competitions such as the National Cyber League, picoCTF, CyberForce, and HiveStorm. It is worth mentioning that TNTech SFS students won the third place in the Global Collegiate Penetration Testing Competition finals in 2022. Moreover, the majority of the TNTech SFS students had participated in cybersecurity conferences. Also, all of TNTech SFS students have successfully been placed in internships.
Research Experience in Cybersecurity: 
All of the TNTech SFS students participated in research through their coursework, summer internships, graduate projects, and/or faculty-sponsored projects. The research topics include cyber-physical security of critical infrastructures, smart farming, malware analysis, secure data containers, etc. As an outcome of their research work, the TNTech SFS students published more than 20 research papers in peer-reviewed conferences, journals, and book chapters.  
Outreach Activities in Cybersecurity: 
All of TNTech SFS students participated in paying it forward. The students have participated in various Computer Science on-campus student communities that include CyberEagles, ACM, ACM-W, and WiCyS Student Chapter. Several TNTech SFS students had served as mentors in the Cyber Interest groups. The TNTech SFS students have also generously volunteered in numerous off-campus events such as the GenCyber Summer Camps and Community College Outreach.
Contributions to the SFS Community 
(a) SFS Bootcamp and NS3 Seminar Series: 
As part of this award, TNTech developed training programs for new SFS students both at our university and around the country. The initial training programs were called Bootcamps and were held on the TNTech campus. In 2020, the Bootcamp went virtual due to COVID. In 2021, the program shifted to an online seminar series (NS3). Among the goals of the SFS Bootcamp was for the new students to understand the responsibilities of being an SFS scholar and learn about being a successful SFS scholar. Since it was launched in Aug. 2016, the SFS Bootcamp and the NS3 Seminar Series have served more than 500 SFS students from all around the country. The collected feedback from the participating students showed that these events helped them in networking, learning about the SFS program expectations, federal agencies, job opportunities, technical and soft skills, and internship opportunities.
(b) SFS Program Related Materials:
For the SFS cohort program, we developed a customized SFS Student Agreement for TNTech that serves as an additional contract between our students and school in addition to the general SFS OPM contract. We also developed Promissory Notes for students addressing anyone defaulting to the program. We have shared these materials upon request with various new SFS schools. 
Summary
Overall, this SFS award has met its goal in creating a hybrid SFS program in TNTech that supports students' participation in cybersecurity education, research, and outreach activities. In addition, the TNTech SFS program has contributed positively to the SFS community.

Title: NRT-DESE: Risk and uncertainty quantification in marine science
Abstract:
NRT-DESE: Risk and Uncertainty Quantification in Marine Science

The ocean is the last great frontier on Earth, a major driver of climate and productivity, and a critical resource for humans and wildlife. Managing ocean resources requires scientists and managers to work seamlessly to understand the top-down effects of human actions and the bottom-up effects of climate-change on the ocean system. This National Science Foundation Research Traineeship (NRT) project at Oregon State University (OSU) will prepare a new generation of natural resource scientists and managers who will combine mathematics, statistics, and computer science with environmental and social sciences to study, protect, and manage ocean systems. This traineeship program anticipates preparing sixty-one (61) MS and PhD students, including thirty (30) funded trainees, to work in transdisciplinary research groups on user-inspired problems using large and ever-expanding data resources.  With powerful analytical tools, they will be best equipped to track and study the top-down effects of human actions and the bottom-up effects of climate change on the ocean system. Besides fulfilling current educational gaps in marine science and management, this OSU NRT program promotes: 1) a transformative and scalable new marine science and policy graduate minor that teaches students to quantify and communicate risk and uncertainty of data-based model forecasts and policy scenarios; 2) the discovery of mechanisms that control the response of marine systems to climate change and human pressures; 3) the development of evidence-based practices for recruiting, training, and retaining diverse graduate students and for placing them into a range of successful careers in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM).  

Through a combination of technical coursework, communication workshops, national and international internships, stakeholder engagement, peer mentoring, and involvement in transdisciplinary research projects, OSU NRT trainees will learn about the science of big data, risk and uncertainty quantification and communication and sustainability. They will learn tools and techniques to assist communities in managing resources through change and to recover quickly in the event of a disaster. In line with the learning objectives, the training and research will link new developments in mathematical and statistical quantification of risk and uncertainty, complex and large datasets on marine systems emerging from novel sensors, and outreach and engagement of stakeholders who affect, and are affected by, ocean systems.  In addition, students with diverse expertise, developed through internships, will leverage each other's strong disciplinary knowledge and skills as they collaborate to address complex stakeholder-identified climate and policy problems. These collaborations will have the ultimate goal of devising management solutions in the face of change and uncertainty. 	

The NSF Research Traineeship (NRT) Program is designed to encourage the development and implementation of bold, new, potentially transformative, and scalable models for STEM graduate education training.  The Traineeship Track is dedicated to effective training of STEM graduate students in high priority interdisciplinary research areas, through the comprehensive traineeship model that is innovative, evidence-based, and aligned with changing workforce and research needs.

This work is supported, in part, by the Alliances for Graduate Education and the Professoriate (AGEP) program.  AGEP is committed to the national goal of increasing the numbers of underrepresented minorities (URMs), entering and completing STEM graduate education and postdoctoral training to levels representative of the available pool. The AGEP program supports the development, implementation, study, and dissemination of innovative models and standards of graduate education and postdoctoral training that are designed to improve URM participation, preparation, and success.
Outcome Report:
Intellectual merit
The project successfully addressed all four Goals. 
Goal 1: Educate and train scientists, engineers, and resource managers to work in transdisciplinary teams that create tools and techniques for DESE applied to marine systems.
Outcomes 1: External evaluation indicated that students who completed the training and advising faculty were more prepared to work in interdisciplinary groups inside and outside of academia. Students rated internship opportunities, and getting involved in transdisciplinary research topics and teams, as the most valuable parts of the Program. Students produced societally relevant and actionable outcomes such as apps, tsunami models, and tools to predict the ocean conditions for fishermen and other stakeholders.
Goal 2: Promote a transformative and scalable new transdisciplinary marine science and policy education program that teaches students to quantify and communicate risk and uncertainty and to engage with stakeholders.
Outcomes 2: There are three tangible outcomes. The first is the Oregon State University graduate minor in Risk and Uncertainty Quantification in Marine Sciences was established in 2016. This interdisciplinary minor provided graduate students with knowledge and skills to quantify and communicate risk and uncertainty derived from the analyses of large data in earth system science. Students extend their ability to perceive and solve problems in a transdisciplinary context related to statistical inference, uncertainty quantification, risk analyses, earth system science, and social systems. 
In addition to the Minor, we submitted a proposal to the OSU graduate school for a Graduate Certificate in Transdisciplinary Research for Marine Social-Ecological-Technological Systems (SETS). The proposed certificate meets employer and student demand for training in systems thinking, communication, collaboration, and research to address societal challenges. It includes: 1. Skill building in transdisciplinary approaches; 2. Experience with collaborative team science; and 3. Application of these skills to problems in marine systems, such as conservation, food/water/energy security, and climate change adaptation. The proposed certificate complements existing interdisciplinary programs at OSU, and could expand in the future, beyond marine systems and in person training, to broader topics and online modality.
Lastly, as a result of the NRT Summit Transformative Connections (Goal 4), seven academic institutions produced a Declaration of Cooperation expressing institutional commitments to transdisciplinary research and education.
  Goal 3: Provide students with a transdisciplinary collaborative research experience and education to prepare them in related careers in academia, the private sector, government, and industry.
Outcomes 3: Trainees were engaged in several professional training activities, including: working toward a transdisciplinary report and interdisciplinary thesis chapter, participating in the annual IFC (Intensive Field Course) prior to fall term, and taking the required professional training for the minor. Through these activities students worked in research groups, attended lectures by academics and government entities, participated in panel discussions with stakeholders, traveled to internship sites, engaged with practitioners and stakeholders, communicated and published their research, and devoted at least one chapter of their dissertations addressing on their NRT group?s project.  
Goal 4: Host a nationwide summit for all NRTs with a coastal/marine theme with the participation of graduate students, PIs/Co-PIs, faculty, and higher up administrators, to provide a synergistic platform for accelerating transdisciplinarity and discussions on successful university sustainability of programs.
Outcomes 4: We hosted a Nationwide Summit for programs that have a marine and/or coastal focus. The Summit was successful and provided several opportunities for networking for graduate students and communication avenues for entities such as students and higher end administrators. As an outcome from the summit we produced a Declaration of Cooperation, as a commitment to advance transdisciplinary and convergent marine/coastal research through National Science Foundation Research Traineeship (NRT) Programs at Academic Institutions. The declaration was signed by the administrative leadership of the six participating academic institutions, and is uploaded to our NSF NRT final report.
Broader Impacts
Since the inception of the grant (2015; 4 annual student cohorts) we have had 44 graduate students and faculty participate in the Risk and Uncertainty Quantification in Marine Science NRT Program at Oregon State University (OSU). Students took classes, traveled to conference and internship sites, and worked in transdisciplinary teams to address interdisciplinary,  compelling, and timely research problems ranging from microplastics to tsunamis and other large scale challenges such as climate change and food and energy security.
External evaluations indicated that the program was successful in:
Establishing a network of faculty and students, and creating new synergies among interdisciplinary marine-focused programs.
Sharing examples of successful forward-looking transdisciplinary research/education programs linking coupled natural-human dimensions, data science, and analysis.
Allowing students and faculty to participate in a comfortable and safe space to talk about challenges and opportunities in transdisciplinary education.
Fostering professional training in communication, engagement and collaboration
Providing career opportunities
Understanding and articulating what we are doing in transdisciplinary marine sciences to inform NSF, professionals, and academic administrators.

Title: NRT-IGE: Nanomedicine Academy of Minority Serving Institutions
Program(s): NSF Research Traineeship (NRT), ECR-EDU Core Research
Abstract:
NRT-IGE: Nanomedicine Academy of Minority Serving Institutions

Nanomedicine is an emerging paradigm that seeks to develop engineered nanometer size particles to solve key problems in modern medicine, such as early diagnosis of disease and targeted delivery of therapeutics. This field is exciting to students and there is worldwide demand for training in this area. This National Science Foundation Research Traineeship (NRT) award in the Innovations in Graduate Education (IGE) track to Northeastern University will translate cutting-edge advances in nanomedicine research into an education model to pilot and test a scalable, interactive network that empowers low-resource institutions to build capacity in nanomedicine training and develop degree programs in this emerging field.  This project will create a reciprocal knowledge-sharing relationship among a large national pool of students across five institutions. The successful implementation of this new model of higher education is expected to broaden the participation of minorities in the nanomedicine workforce thus reducing disparities in the health workforce, establish new degree programs, and serve as a blueprint for the creation of similar education programs in other disciplines. 

The goal of the project is to create a scalable network for knowledge delivery and scientific collaboration that is designed to enable student learning from expert instructors as well as from peers unrestricted by geographical location. The partners include five research universities with a tradition of providing higher education to underrepresented communities ? Northeastern University, University of Puerto Rico Mayaguez, Tuskegee University, Morgan State University, and Florida International University.  The project will offer synchronous content through live, web-based videoconferencing protocols, allowing students to interact with instructors and peers at other universities in real-time. A parallel enterprise-level online learning environment will be created to enable team-based discussions and assignments. Courses to be offered include Introduction to Nanomedicine, Nanomedicine Research Techniques, Nano/Biomedical Commercialization, and a Nanomedicine Seminar Series.  Faculty facilitators at each institution will coordinate the physical and online classroom environments, contribute to cross-institutional assignments, and provide supplementary instruction. Students will receive degree credit at their home institution through the establishment of course-equivalency at each partner institution. The implementation of these learning tools, together with the assessment of student learning, student demographics, and career development, is expected to generate sufficient new knowledge to enable expansion of this new and unique higher education model to a nationwide program.

The NSF Research Traineeship (NRT) Program is designed to encourage the development and implementation of bold, new, potentially transformative, and scalable models for STEM graduate education training.  The Innovations in Graduate Education Track is dedicated solely to piloting, testing, and evaluating novel, innovative, and potentially transformative approaches to graduate education.

This work is supported, in part, by the EHR Core Research (ECR) program.  The ECR program emphasizes fundamental STEM education research that generates foundational knowledge in the field.  Investments are made in critical areas that are essential, broad and enduring:  STEM learning and STEM learning environments, broadening participation in STEM, and STEM workforce development.
Outcome Report:
Advances in the assembly and manipulation of nanoscale structures has led to a widespread application of nanotechnology in medicine, including over 50 FDA-approved nanoparticle drugs. This interdisciplinary field, known as nanomedicine, is made possible by collaboration, knowledge sharing, and creation of a research culture across a range of disciplines including physics, chemistry, biology, materials science, health science, and engineering. Recognizing that few universities outside large metropolitan areas have the resources and expertise to offer nanomedicine training, faculty at Northeastern University, Morgan State University, Tuskegee University, Florida International University, and University of Puerto Rico Mayaguez sought to find new ways to remove barriers to nanomedicine accessibility in low resource settings. The Nanomedicine Academy of Minority-Serving Institutions was created in 2015 with the goal of increasing the diversity of the nanomedicine workforce by piloting new strategies for student learning and collaboration across multiple institutions.
The Nanomedicine Academy of Minority-Serving Institutions established a one-of-a-kind graduate education program that provides enhanced access to specialized knowledge, training in essential nanomedicine tools and techniques, and opportunities for interactivity among geographically remote students. This was accomplished through the creation of a ?national nanomedicine classroom? where students from all 5 institutions collaborate together to learn new knowledge and skills while earning degree credit at their home institution. This education model was made possible through the development of a custom scalable, interactive online network that supports synchronous multi-institutional web-based lectures and symposia, asynchronous multi-institutional team activities, and synchronous face-to-face activities in local classrooms led by local faculty.
Using this online network for teaching and learning, the Academy developed and implemented five multi-institutional courses including: Introduction to Nanomedicine, Nanomedicine Research Techniques, Nano/Biomedical Commercialization, and Nanomedicine Seminar 1 & 2. Each course was designed to be unique in its design and implementation, such that students could engage with course materials, local and remote faculty, and their peers in a variety of different ways grounded in evidence-based principles of learning. Collectively, these courses offered students the opportunity to: 1) learn, practice, and reflect on enabling innovations in nanomedicine, 2) teach peers about research and career opportunities using a flipped classroom setting, 3) conduct experiments and analyze data in a virtual laboratory setting, 4) create a virtual startup company under the mentorship of biotech industry experts, and 5) hear first-hand accounts of nanomedicine research and innovation from guest experts across the nation. The courses were integrated into 24 M.S. and Ph.D. degree programs across the 5 institutions in order to attract and retain graduate students from a range of STEM disciplines. Additionally, a stackable Graduate Certificate in Nanomedicine was created at Northeastern University in 2017. All courses were rolled out in a hybrid format (2015-2018), and then piloted in parallel hybrid and online sections in the final year (2018-9).
Since 2015, the Academy courses have been attended by 322 M.S. and Ph.D. students from 18 different STEM disciplines, including 110 underrepresented minority (URM) students. 139 students completed 2 or more Academy courses and 33 Northeastern students enrolled in the 5-course Nanomedicine Certificate (22 complete to-date). Over two-thirds of URM students completed 3 or more nanomedicine courses, attesting to the unique value these courses add to degree programs in low resource settings. Even when Hurricane Maria necessitated a complete restart of the 2017-18 academic year in Puerto Rico, all 20 participants from UPRM opted to complete their nanomedicine studies that year. In surveys, students from all 5 institutions unanimously reported that the Academy courses offered new learning opportunities not previously available at their home institution. For 90% of students, this was their first time participating in interdisciplinary courses, and as such, they were particularly appreciative of the opportunity to engage with a large variety of students, resources, and faculty. Over 91% of all Academy participants reported that they were concurrently involved in nanomedicine or nanotechnology research while attending Academy courses and thus stood directly benefit from their coursework. Over half of these students reported directly applying concepts learned in class to their thesis, dissertation, co-op, or work-related research projects.
In summary, the Nanomedicine Academy of Minority-Serving Institutions is an entirely new model of education that empowers universities to provide a graduate coursework in a field that is resource-intensive and rapidly changing. Through careful design and implementation, it is possible to broaden student and faculty access to specialized knowledge, facilities, instrumentation, and expertise in a way that promotes interdisciplinary learning in an authentic collaborative setting.
