Title: IGERT:  Global Traineeship in Sustainable Electronics
Program(s): IGERT Materials Research, IGERT FULL PROPOSALS, NSF Research Traineeship (NRT), IGERT Chemistry
Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Traineeship (IGERT) award establishes a new integrative model for graduate research and education to enable meaningful and measurable improvements in the global sustainability of electronic products. Through a partnership between Purdue University and Tuskegee University the Sustainable Electronics-IGERT will be carried out in close collaboration with the global electronics industry and academic partners. 

Intellectual Merit: The IGERT will focus on establishing the scientific foundation for a new model of consumption for electronics that avoids the traditional design-manufacture-use-dispose approach: faculty and student expertise from business, social sciences, and materials, product, and process engineering will come together to re-envision the electronics consumption paradigm, while maintaining a focus on simultaneously benefiting people, planet, and profit. Research themes addressed by this IGERT are 1) polymers from nature for fabricating electronics; 2) product design and manufacturing approaches with a reduced environmental footprint; and 3) system, supply chain, corporate and consumer behaviors, and the role of regulatory frameworks. Trainees will develop depth in their disciplines as well as breadth in the context of sustainable electronics, enabling them to become innovators and change leaders in society.

Broader Impacts: This IGERT project will develop new cross-disciplinary graduate courses to form a core sustainable electronics curriculum, establish an interactive, international, team-based community to break-down barriers to solving problems that limit sustainability, and ensure that each trainee has an integrative international experience with industry or academic partners.

IGERT is an NSF-wide program intended to meet the challenges of educating U.S. Ph.D. scientists and engineers with the interdisciplinary background, deep knowledge in a chosen discipline, and the technical, professional, and personal skills needed for the career demands of the future. The program is intended to establish new models for graduate education and training in a fertile environment for collaborative research that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries, and to engage students in understanding the processes by which research is translated to innovations for societal benefit.
Outcome Report:
The NSF Purdue-Tuskegee IGERT: Global Traineeships for Sustainable Electronics provided the framework to create an innovative, interdisciplinary program to turn students into effective leaders in improving the global sustainability of electronics.  Sustainability has multiple dimensions: economic, environmental, and societal. Scientific breakthroughs are necessary but not sufficient to improve electronics sustainability: it requires understanding and working with supply chain partners, recognizing the importance of societies and cultures in adopting new technologies, integrating new technologies into the existing manufacturing and economic infrastructure and working with others to make long-term changes in products and organizations. The IGERT program - education, research, and training was designed by the Purdue-Tuskegee 14 faculty member team (11-Purdue, 3-Tuskegee) to educate and empower the trainees to become innovators in this domain through authentic experiences in working with sustainability leaders from industry, government, and NGOs. Key partners in the program were iNEMI, a global electronics industry consortium, the Indian Institute of Management - Udaipur, Seagate, the Green Electronics Council, Nokia, and Dell.  Trainees learned to be valuable members in team-based, cross-disciplinary, cross-cultural partnerships that dominate electronic product development and manufacturing. Through the IGERT, the graduate students - 28 NSF-supported trainees and 8 non-funded associates -demonstrated their ability to work and act globally by incorporating principles of partnership (among national and international academic institutions, government regulators, and industry experts), teamwork (among students, faculty and partners), and interdisciplinary breadth. The three 2-year cohorts included trainees and associates from Anthropology, Chemistry, Engineering (Materials, Civil, Mechanical, Industrial, Environmental & Ecological), Forestry & Natural Resources, Management, & Political Science.  The Purdue-Tuskegee team served as role models for the students in terms of creating a community focused both on making electronics sustainable and on guiding the trainees' education. training, and research to become innovators in STEM as well as in the global electronics eco-system.  
A key feature of the NSF Purdue-Tuskegee IGERT in Sustainable Electronics was the International Research Experience in India, a two-week long, intensive research visit designed and hosted by Prof. Janat Shah and Dr. Mohit Srivastava of the Indian Institute of Management - Udaipur in collaboration with Prof. Ananth Iyer, co-PI from Purdue. They developed a highly integrated plan for the IGERT team to learn about India and its people in the context of social justice, mining, global electronics manufacturing and supply chains, water supply, waste management and energy, and Indian culture and philosophy. What made this two-week research experience so valuable was the nine months of integrated education and training that the IGERT faculty used to prepare the trainees in each cohort for the experience. The IGERT education and training program was designed so it both deepened the trainees? understanding of the issues and made them capable of learning at a more sophisticated level during the trip. 
One major outcome of the Research Experience in India was in internationalization: trainees gained global awareness and perspective through engagement with those we visited. Another was in having the opportunity to be leaders. The trainees interacted with a wide range of people at the organizations we visited ? from CEOs and engineers to workers on the assembly line and in the NGOs. The trainees saw that leaders in these organizations welcomed us, took the trainees seriously, and engaged them in substantive discussions of issues related to sustainability, manufacturing, and culture.  All of the trainees described this experience as "life changing" with continuing impact on the ways the students viewed the world. This transformation started with themselves and continued in deepening their understanding what future roles they may have in creating the conditions where sustainable electronics can flourish.  The close collaboration between Purdue and Tuskegee trainees, associates, and faculty provided a unique education and research opportunity for the whole team, which is continuing.

Title: IGERT: Adaptation to Abrupt Climate Change (A2C2)
Program(s): IGERT FULL PROPOSALS, INSPIRE, EPSCoR Co-Funding
Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Traineeship (IGERT) award facilitates the interdisciplinary training of Ph.D. natural and social scientists in adaptation to abrupt climate change, one of the greatest challenges to the sustainability of human society and ecosystem services in the 21st century. 

Intellectual Merit: This program meets the challenge of abrupt climate change by training students to conduct collaborative, interdisciplinary research across the natural and social sciences, and to develop innovative policy and management solutions from their research that fosters resilience and adaptation in response to abrupt climate change. Research themes focus on three major challenges that society faces with abrupt climate change: threats to global security, reductions in ecosystem services, and adaptation in social systems. Novel training elements of this program include a collaborative interdisciplinary research project, and a policy and management internship with organizations that span international, federal and state agencies, as well as the private sector. 

Broader Impacts: The risks of abrupt climate change are globally pervasive and include increased numbers of environmental refugees and political conflicts over resources. Determining how to anticipate, avoid, and manage abrupt climate change was recently identified as one of the five grand challenges to global sustainability. This IGERT award trains the next generation of scientists to meet these environmental and social challenges. To promote future recruitment of a diverse science workforce, all IGERT trainees will conduct outreach activities with K-12 students from underrepresented groups. The program also fosters a strong international perspective through research collaborations as well as internship experiences abroad.

IGERT is an NSF-wide program intended to meet the challenges of educating U.S. Ph.D. scientists and engineers with the interdisciplinary background, deep knowledge in a chosen discipline, and the technical, professional, and personal skills needed for the career demands of the future. The program is intended to establish new models for graduate education and training in a fertile environment for collaborative research that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries, and to engage students in understanding the processes by which research is translated to innovations for societal benefit.
Outcome Report:
The Adaptation to Abrupt Climate Change (A2C2) IGERT program at the University of Maine was designed to foster enhanced understanding of the dynamics of coupled natural and human systems in response to abrupt/rapid climate change, with program research being organized around the following core questions:
 a)  How does abrupt climate change (ACC) alter the dynamics of coupled natural and human (CNH) systems?
 b)  How do we inform policy and management to improve environmental security by enhancing resilience and adaptation of CNH systems experiencing ACC?
Over the course of our program, our trainees and faculty collaborated on numerous research projects focused on a variety of different types of ACC in many locations around the world. Our research addressed rapid climate change currently occurring in the Arctic, in alpine and coastal regions of Peru, Chile, and Argentina, and right in our own backyard in the lakes and coastal marine ecosystems of Maine.
By integrating social/ethnographic study with novel biophysical monitoring/experimentation, modeling, and analysis, our research groups advanced the frontiers of knowledge by creating an integrated interdisciplinary framework that has already helped to identify and fill knowledge gaps in a variety of coupled natural-human systems facing the threat of abrupt climate change. Through active and ongoing dissemination of the results of this interdisciplinary research by way of peer-reviewed academic publications, educational brochures, web sites, and numerous presentations at various meetings and public forums, our trainees and participating faculty strengthened their commitment to innovative scientific management of natural resources, thereby providing the general public with a clear example of the benefits of publicly-funded scientific research and increasing their understanding of and appreciation for the scientific enterprise in general.
Our students also had numerous opportunities to conduct research and internships abroad to enhance their global perspective and expand the geographic scope of their research and its application to populations that are vulnerable to abrupt climate change. Students investigated research questions addressing connections between contemporary ACC and ecological processes in the Arctic, continental ice sheet melting and iceberg dynamics, and implications of various non-Western ideologies for adaptation strategies - among others - which were best addressed through international work. In conducting this work, our students became keenly aware that the impacts of abrupt climate change cross borders and came to understand that professionals working in the realm of adaptation must become familiar with differences across cultures to achieve success. The international opportunities in this IGERT broadened our students' perspectives and provided them with tremendous opportunities that they almost certainly would not have enjoyed in more traditional graduate training programs.

Title: IGERT: Training Innovative Leaders in Biofabrication
Program(s): IUSE, IGERT FULL PROPOSALS, NSF Research Traineeship (NRT)
Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Traineeship (IGERT) award establishes a unique training program at WPI for Ph.D. students in the field of bioengineering, and specifically biofabrication. The program will train students in the entrepreneurial mindset, providing graduates with skills necessary to contribute to the innovation economy while also addressing important medical needs.

Intellectual Merit: The goal of this training program is to produce engineers who will be future innovators in academia and industry, leading to the translation and commercialization of bioengineering and biofabrication technologies. Today?s medical devices suffer from the drawback that their materials are foreign to the human body and prone to rejection. The growing field of biofabrication uses biological matter as the basic building blocks to assemble advanced biological tissues for treatments and screenings. Trainees will participate in mentored lab research, formal coursework in their discipline, and international research collaborations. In addition, trainees will develop an entrepreneurial mindset through integrated entrepreneurship training modules, and an immersive innovation culture at WPI?s Life Science and Bioengineering Center, a mixed-use research/industrial facility. Finally, hands-on industry training will expose the IGERT trainees to the needs and use of consumers.

Broader Impacts: This program will help sustain America?s innovation economy by training Ph.D. students to be future leaders in biofabrication. True to WPI?s educational and training philosophy, ?Lehr und Kunst? (Theory and Practice), the proposed research aims are focused on practical approaches to developing commercially viable enabling technologies to fulfill critical unmet needs in biofabrication. International research experiences will be provided in collaboration with Politecnico di Milano in Italy and Tsinghua University in China. Outcomes of the IGERT experience are also anticipated to extend beyond the program and may be measured as new companies launched, jobs created, patents filed, and products reaching clinical trials.

IGERT is an NSF-wide program intended to meet the challenges of educating U.S. Ph.D. scientists and engineers with the interdisciplinary background, deep knowledge in a chosen discipline, and the technical, professional, and personal skills needed for the career demands of the future. The program is intended to establish new models for graduate education and training in a fertile environment for collaborative research that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries, and to engage students in understanding the processes by which research is translated to innovations for societal benefit.
Outcome Report:
The NSF IGERT Training Innovative Leaders in Biofabrication program successfully trained 19 PhD students, all of whom have defended their theses at WPI and will officially have graduated by December 2020. The program provided students with specific training to develop an innovator’s mindset, from the first days of their PhD education. Along with their disciplinary coursework, students were exposed to interdisciplinary training in innovation and entrepreneurship, with many of the trainees also earning a Graduate Certificate in Entrepreneurship, simultaneous to their PhD training. Trainees also engaged in industrial internships and global research experiences with partners in Italy, Ireland, China, Switzerland, and the UK. The professional development seminar and boot camp experiences that were created for the IGERT trainees were highly successful, and were later institutionalized across the entire WPI graduate school (for all Master’s and PhD students in all disciplines). These seminars focused on creating Individual Development Plans, professional communication skills, team building, networking, wellness, and other topics related to professional and career preparation. The research that the students engaged in was highly interdisciplinary, involving faculty from multiple departments and programs within science and engineering. During the five-year training period, our students were recognized with the following honors: 14 finalists in university-wide poster competition (out of 800 participants); 5 winners, 1 honorable mention in university-wide pitch competition; >61 conference presentations; >30 journal publications, 1 book, 1 book chapter, 6 patents or patent applications, 1 technology license, 2 National Academy of Inventors Members, 1 American Heart Association Fellowship, 1 NSF GRFP fellowship, 2 NSF GRFP honorable mentions, 1 VentureWell E-Team Stages 1-3 Grant, 1 NSF I-Corps Grant, 2 innovation awards (Kalenian and Hitchcock), 1 startup company, 7 industrial and 1 government internships, 12 international research experiences. All of the trainees are currently employed, with half in industrial positions and half in post-doctoral roles at this time.

Title: IGERT:  Systems Biology of Cells in Engineered Environments (SBE2)
Program(s): NSF Research Traineeship (NRT), IGERT FULL PROPOSALS, Cross-BIO Activities
Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Traineeship (IGERT) award facilitates the unique interdisciplinary training of Ph.D. scientists and engineers in the field of biotechnology by elucidating how cells interact with specifically designed environments based on a broad understanding of changes in the molecules within cells. Trained students will be ready to address a wide range of problems facing society, from agriculture and energy to human health and medicine. 

Intellectual Merit: This program addresses this challenge by focusing on two areas of importance in biotechnology: cells' behaviors based on growth in a variety of environments; and "systems biology" - the integrated analysis of numerous molecular changes, particularly those related to gene expression, that occur within cells when exposed to different environments. A key feature of this work is that the environments will be specifically engineered. For example, different materials will be used to support the growth of a particular type of cell. By studying the impact of these controlled environments on the expression of the cell?s genes, one can begin to design strategies to target specific environments for specific applications: growth of cells as tissue replacement for healing, and design of better ways to deliver medicines, among others. The cross-training effort synergizes diverse areas of expertise available at the University of Delaware. 

Broader Impacts: This program addresses a critical question related to biotechnology research: how do molecular changes within a cell relate to the environment in which the cell is exposed? There are many important application areas and our program will provide students with an opportunity to learn critical experimental and computational techniques to best prepare them for careers in the life sciences industry. An emphasis on innovation will provide students with an opportunity to engage in industry internships and public policy, intellectual property workshops, as well as research experiences at institutions around the world. We will work to develop programs that broaden minority participation at multiple levels.

IGERT is an NSF-wide program intended to meet the challenges of educating U.S. Ph.D. scientists and engineers with the interdisciplinary background, deep knowledge in a chosen discipline, and the technical, professional, and personal skills needed for the career demands of the future. The program is intended to establish new models for graduate education and training in a fertile environment for collaborative research that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries, and to engage students in understanding the processes by which research is translated to innovations for societal benefit.
Outcome Report:
The Systems Biology of Cells in Engineered Environments IGERT program at the University of Delaware brought together two synergistic, complementary, distinct groups of faculty known for their excellence in their respective areas, but not known for cross-disciplinary research findings. One area is systems biology and systems-related analyses where faculty were focused on technologies and approaches to understanding molecular-scale, typically genome-scale, changes in cells. The second area is the 'cells in engineered environments' area where faculty were focused on understanding how cells respond to various environments for a variety of applications such as tissue engineering and drug delivery. In this area, faculty were focused on understanding how (engineered) changes in the environment impact cell responses. By bringing these two groups together, the IGERT sought to align the research interests of those working on understanding how cells respond to external environments with those working to understand how cells respond at the molecular level inside the cell. Moreover, the program relied heavily on bioinformatics advancements and foundational expertise to provide an avenue for research discoveries and applications. The program had Broader Impacts not only on trainees and education generally, but also had significant Intellectual Merit as evidenced by more than 500 peer-reviewed publications authored by the IGERT faculty.
  This IGERT program provided direct (and indirect) support for many graduate students at the University of Delaware across a number of departments and programs. Each individual trainee benefited from their participation in the program through opportunities related to novel coursework providing important foundational knowledge and complementary skillsets, through rotational experiences to offer perspective on systems biology and cells in engineered environments approaches, through mentoring and a sense of community - particularly important to those students from underrepresented backgrounds, as well as through many individualized experiences unique to each student and their situation.
  The Systems Biology of Cells in Engineered Environments IGERT program at the University of Delaware provided the foundation for fundamental changes and updates to PhD educational programs at the University of Delaware, had a lasting impact on the education of dozens of graduate students, impacted non-science faculty who co-taught a class to trainees, impacted graduate recruitment to the University of Delaware, helped build a community of like-minded scholars from a variety of disciplines, and had noteworthy impacts on science outreach to the broader community.

Title: IGERT: From Data to Solutions:  A New PhD Program in Transformational Data & Information Sciences Research and Innovation
Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Traineeship (IGERT) provides Ph.D. students with the unique interdisciplinary training necessary to extract useful information from vast amounts of collected data. Consumer opinions, information on disease and its symptoms, and breaking information on social websites allow us to gather information on a scale previously unknown. However, such big data is useful only if we can extract information from it. Columbia and CUNY, in collaboration with international partners in Argentina and Brazil, propose the interdisciplinary training of students in making sense of big data. Researchers from Computer Science, Electrical Engineering, Psychology, and Statistics will partner with Biomedical Informatics, Business and Journalism, to educate the next generation of information scientists in solving real world problems. We will train students to extract information from multiple data types ? text, video, audio ? and familiarize them with a wide range of techniques for making sense of information from a world in which Youtube, Wikipedia, Facebook, and Twitter are supplanting newspapers, encyclopedias, television, and consumer surveys as everyday sources of information.  

Broader Impacts: A curriculum based upon the concept of studio learning will integrate techniques from Business, Journalism, and Biomedical Informatics. Aided by advisors from large corporations, major research labs, and small start-up companies, the program will encourage IGERT trainees to pursue patents, and to apply their research in society. A second goal will be attracting more diverse students to information sciences by emphasizing real world applications, a supportive environment, and diverse faculty role models. The mentoring and career development activities proposed will help to retain this diverse population and prepare them for their future careers. 

IGERT is an NSF-wide program intended to meet the challenges of educating U.S. Ph.D. scientists and engineers with the interdisciplinary background, deep knowledge in a chosen discipline, and the technical, professional, and personal skills needed for the career demands of the future. The program is intended to establish new models for graduate education and training in a fertile environment for collaborative research that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries, and to engage students in understanding the processes by which research is translated to innovations for societal benefit.
Outcome Report:
This IGERT program "From Data to Solutions" was created to provide STEM PhD students with interdisciplinary training in information science. It was a collaboration with faculty from Computer Science, Electrical Engineering, Psychology, Statistics, Biomedical Informatics, Business and Journalism to educate the next generation of information scientists focused on real world problems. It included a collaboration with CUNY faculty as well as faculty at the University of Buenos Aires and the Universidad Estadual de Campinas in Brazil. Students all took an IGERT seminar in which faculty from STEM and disciplines including History, English, Sociology, and International Affairs presented research questions they would like to collaborate with STEM students on; students then proposed solutions to these problems in term projects.  IGERT trainees were also taught technical writing oral presentation, and intellectural property/technology transfer courses and additionall had to take four studio courses from a set of courses related to data science.  Each student was support for two years on the IGERT.  A total of 31 students participated, 14 of whom were women, 3 Hispanic male, and 1 African American male.  Activities included brown-bag lunches with invited speakers, poster sessions, panels, and other social events to build community among the students and provide educational and networking opportunies.  Our IGERT seminar was so successful that it is now serving as the model for proposed PhD concentrations and PhD programs in Data Science.  Our website gives more details of the program:  http://www/cs/columbia.edu/igert/

Title: IGERT:  Solar Utilization Network (SUN)
Program(s): IGERT FULL PROPOSALS, NSF Research Traineeship (NRT)
Full Address: 660 S MILL AVENUE STE 204, TEMPE, AZ, ="852813670"
Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Traineeship (IGERT) award focuses on the energy transition from the current fossil-fuel-based economy to one where solar energy harvested by means of photovoltaics, solar-thermal, and photosynthesis-driven bioenergy approaches will become a keystone in global human energy use. Scalability, efficiency and economy of these three technical solar energy conversion approaches, along with societal components such as sustainability policy and responsible energy use, will all be necessary for success. This program supports the interdisciplinary training of diverse student cohorts in multiple solar energy conversion areas at different scales, integrated with a policy and social understanding, thus educating the next generation of citizen-scientists, innovative thinkers and enlightened policy makers who can guide society toward a sustainable energy future.  

Broader Impacts:  In order to further enhance inclusion of students from all backgrounds, the SUN IGERT project will leverage agreements with schools and programs with significant enrollment of underrepresented groups, particularly Hispanics and Native Americans, to lower barriers for underrepresented minorities. Effective mentoring and use-inspired, application-oriented, integrative research projects will enhance retention in the program. This program will also provide the groundwork for a novel Energy Ph.D. program. Successes from our program can be emulated and adapted at other institutions nationally and globally, thus catalyzing the training of a much larger group of students who can shepherd society to a new, sustainable energy future.

Outcome Report:
The IGERT-SUN program focused on educating the next generation of leaders who will need to seamlessly navigate a very transdisciplinary field in order to guide society toward a solar-based, sustainable energy future.  An important, lasting outcome of the program was the establishment of an interdisciplinary Sustainable Energy PhD program at Arizona State University (ASU) that is designed to train doctoral students to see beyond disciplinary boundaries and to learn to work at the interface of science, engineering and public policy.  Patterned after the interdisciplinary curriculum developed during the first four years of IGERT-SUN, the Doctor of Philosophy in Sustainable Energy program was officially launched in November 2016.  The new program is a hallmark of the intellectual merit of the IGERT-SUN program.  As indicated on the Sustainable Energy program's website, https://schoolofsustainability.asu.edu/degrees/doctor-philosophy-sustainable-energy/, students in the program "will conduct collaborative cross-disciplinary research integrating energy science with societal and policy insights."  Graduates of the new Sustainable Energy PhD program will be uniquely poised to take on leadership roles in industry, government and academic institutions to transition society from a fossil fuel-based economy toward a sustainable energy future.
An important aspect of interdisciplinary studies in the IGERT-SUN program was learning to design collaborative projects that addressed both cultural and disciplinary diversity.  Students were asked to develop such projects as part of the IGERT-SUN course work and were encouraged to advance their ideas via the Competitive Innovation Incentive Fund (CIIF) portion of the program.  In total the program sponsored six CIIF projects involving a total of 13 IGERT-SUN trainees and three independent collaborators.  The CIIF projects exemplify the broader impacts of the IGERT-SUN program, and three of these projects are briefly mentioned here.  First, in the WaterE project, IGERT-SUN trainees worked with the community of Mompos, Colombia to address water quality issues. They built a prototype solar-powered system to teach local students about water filtration and water quality, performed water testing and conducted surveys to evaluate energy access, water quality and perceptions on quality of life. 
In a second CIIF project trainees focused on helping to bring a sustainable waste management strategy to the rural community of Sittee River, Belize.  In collaboration with the local community, they built an anaerobic digester to turn waste to biogas and taught classes at the local school on the basics of the engineering process to engage students in the project.  Working with young women of color in Belize, the trainees, who were among the 25% of underrepresented minority students supported by the IGERT-SUN program, were inspired to start BioGals, an organization to empower women of color in the United States to conduct their research abroad, which in turn could inspire women of color abroad to pursue STEM fields. BioGals officially gained non-profit status on October 24, 2018 and reaches a larger audience through their website, https://www.biogals.com/, where interested students can find an application to join the team.
Finally, in another CIIF project IGERT-SUN students collaborated with Sustainable Energy PhD students to address the energy needs of a hurricane-ravaged community center in Puerto Rico.  The team worked closely with stakeholders in Puerto Rico to design a patent-pending retractable photovoltaic solar system that could be safely stowed in advance of a hurricane, allowing for a quick resumption of power following a storm.  The system was successfully installed in July 2019.  These three very diverse CIIF projects illustrate the power of collaboration across disciplines to impact real-world challenges. 
All IGERT-SUN trainees also had the opportunity to participate in one of two summer experiences: the Netherlands experience, which exposed trainees to two diverse solar energy research programs at Wageningen University and at the Technical University of Delft, and the Washington experience, which was focused on government and science policy development and communicating complex technical information to a broader community.  These experiences were designed to: 1) develop the students' ability to place research projects into a broader and more global perspective, and 2) develop the students' ability to effectively communicate the importance of their research.  Students gained both direct and indirect value from these experiences and an overwhelming majority of participating students provided positive feedback to program evaluators and rated it very useful or better.
In total the IGERT-SUN program supported 27 trainees across 11 STEM disciplines generating 51 journal articles in refereed publications, one non-refereed publication, seven book chapters, two patent applications, 26 conference publications and 140 conference presentations.  Of the 12 trainees who have completed their schooling, two hold academic faculty positions, two hold post-doctoral fellowships, one is a research associate at a national laboratory, one works in an analytical laboratory, five work in various energy/sustainability-related industries and one works as a policy analyst.

Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Traineeship (IGERT) award initiates a novel model for interdisciplinary graduate training in biophotonics across the biomedical sciences, physical sciences, and engineering. Biophotonics technologies provide powerful capabilities to probe and manipulate biological components and processes. Their utilization in the life sciences and medicine represents an estimated annual economic impact of $50 billion. This program aims to produce the next generation of biophotonics leaders to make transformative advances in the development and application of new tools for biological and medical discovery and maintain global U.S. leadership in biotechnology, pharmaceutical and medical device industries.
Intellectual Merit: This IGERT award creates a hands-on training program that integrates physics, chemistry, engineering, and life-science principles across spatial and temporal scales. The interaction of, and collaboration between, biomedical scientists, physical scientists and engineers throughout the graduate traineeship will drive advances in biophotonics technologies, computational methods, and molecular probes to solve important problems in bio-molecular, cellular, tissue, and whole organismal systems.
Broader Impacts: The BEST IGERT project will promote dissemination of an innovative education framework aimed towards a diverse cadre of scientists and engineers. Moreover, IGERT faculty and trainees will engage vigorously in a spectrum of outreach, dissemination, recruitment, retention, and career development activities that leverages the commitment of multiple units within UC-Irvine, industry in Southern California, and a nationwide network of faculty contacts, including those at minority serving institutions, to inform the public and broaden participation by students from underrepresented groups.

The BEST (Biophotonics across Energy, Space, and Time) IGERT program at the University of California, Irvine enabled us to provide over 60 student-years of support to 34 PhD students enrolled in eight different doctoral degree programs (Biomedical Engineering, Chemical & Biomolecular Engineering, Chemistry, Mathematics, Molecular Biology & Biochemistry, Pharmaceutical Science, Physics, and Physiology & Biophysics).

Graduate education in the sciences and engineering rarely offers the training and experiences necessary to fully prepare graduates to enter directly into non-academic research and leadership positions. We developed a new interdisciplinary PhD program in BioInnovation to challenge this paradigm by coupling research with entrepreneurship towards the career development goal of training graduates who can lead the creation of innovative and cost-effective solutions to complex biomedical problems at the interface of academia and industry. We used the NSF IGERT training program to cultivate and assess our trainee?s abilities to develop clinically relevant biomedical technologies and devices leading to marketable products. We evaluated our career development objective through a direct measurement of our students? post-graduate career success.
  Tulane?s new interdisciplinary PhD program in BioInnovation spans the Schools of Science and Engineering, Medicine, and Public Health and Tropical Medicine. Twenty-five IGERT-supported trainees completed our BioInnovation curriculum, and these students received direct mentorship by thirty-five faculty members within these schools. The BioInnovation curriculum includes courses in science and engineering, entrepreneurship, marketing, and intellectual property. Our program includes an FDA internship where trainees learn about the regulatory pathway and establish non-academic research collaborations. Business plans were developed with colleagues in Tulane?s schools of Business, Law and Medicine. Research projects centered on drug delivery with application in regenerative medicine, biosensors or therapeutic materials.
  Our project created new training approaches and experiences to more fully prepare PhD graduates to enter directly into non-academic research and leadership positions. To do so, this project created a tightly interwoven program that connects research and broad experiences to train individuals with ?T-shaped? skills. As such, our graduates have deep experience in an area of focus, and the breadth necessary to collaborate across disciplines with experts in other areas and to apply knowledge in areas of expertise other than their own. To do so, we connected three objectives: 1) Research, 2) Education, and 3) Community. Our Research objective provided the essential expertise in an area of focus, while Education and Community objectives provided the breadth that is essential to collaborate. Assessments by independent evaluators confirmed the efficacy of this approach and indicated that BioInnovation students positively affected the training of other graduate students in affiliated laboratories.

Our trainee?s research provided the scientific capital that was used successfully to apply for project support for research translation to the marketplace. Our IGERT trainees have been exceptionally active in this regard with our trainees receiving five $50,000 I-CORPS grants to support advanced investigation into customer discovery. Bioaesthetics: a company developed to commercialize its nipple-areola graft (NACgraft biologic matrix)? a regenerative nipple graft for breast cancer survivors.
Instapath: a company developing an integrated technology platform that automates the entire process of tissue histology and creates digital pathology images.
Our trainees have successfully competed for substantial funding to support these companies through NSF SBIR (Phase I and II) and private sources.

Tulane BioInnovation graduates have moved directly into careers at the interface of academia and industry in a) startup company development and leadership, b) scientific consulting, c) regulatory affairs, d) data science, e) science/engineering advocacy and communication, and f) advanced post-graduate training.

Historically underrepresented groups were recruited through established relationships with diversity programs at Tulane University and through direct ties to SACNAS. Our students have been very involved in outreach through mentorship in high school STEM groups, and leadership in SACNAS and the FDA Diversity, Inclusion & Belonging Council. Finally, the development of new technologies and devices has expanded economic development and reinforced the burgeoning biomedical industry of the New Orleans region.

Title: Networking and collaborative Research with European partners: participation in the Eurocores Scheme
Abstract:
This project will support the Networking costs of US-based researchers undertaking international collaborative research projects within the framework of the EUROpean COoperative RESearch (EUROCORES) scheme.  The EUROCORES Programme, developed and coordinated by the European Science Foundation, is a mechanism designed to support bottom-up, investigator-driven international research collaborations.   National funding agencies, located primarily in Europe, make a programmatic decision to provide funds to support a Joint Call on an investigator-proposed topical Theme.  Individual investigators in each of the participating countries can propose to be part of a multinational Collaborative Research Project (CRP) that responds to the call.  After an international Merit Review process, successful CRPs (and therefore the associated Individual Projects) are supported by the national funding agency in the country where the PI is employed.   NSF has already supported the research costs of over 20 individual US-based investigators/projects within the EUROCORES framework.  This award provides funding to network the US researchers with their counterparts overseas in a coordinated mechanism.  

The Broader Impacts of the activities supported through this award are significant, focusing on international research cooperation activities for US researchers that leverage the NSF investment.  Networking activities within each EUROCORES programme include annual scientific committee meetings, biannual Topical Science Workshops, and programme-wide Conferences to disseminate results and foster new collaborations.  For junior researchers, the project supports Summer Schools with European counterparts and travel grants that enable direct collaboration with European-based colleagues along with access to unique European research infrastructure.  The success of EUROCORES in attracting both top-level researchers and multiple national funding agencies to a common Call demonstrates the quality of the research, and the importance of the international coordination and cooperation, within these programmes.

Title: Integrating Ethics Education: Capacity-Building Workshops for Science and Engineering Faculty
Abstract:
This Ethics Education in Science and Engineering project will build capacity for faculty to educate graduate students about research ethics in the context of the research environment. This approach is grounded in and flows from extensive empirical evidence that standards of conduct depend as much or more on the work environment than on participation in isolated courses or online tutorials. 
The four project objectives include: 1. Consensus Conference to develop a framework to build a curriculum for Capacity-Building Workshops. 2. Curriculum Development for the Workshops.  3. Capacity-Building Workshops. 4. Outcome Assessments: Revise and finalize the Workshop curriculum based on feedback from faculty participants and their graduate student trainees. 

This project will pilot the proposed workshops in 8 public and 7 private graduate institutions, including 3 Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs).  To foster approaches responsive to the globalization of the research community, the proposed Expert Panel includes a member with extensive academic connections in China, and Chinese graduate students will be among those assisting with key aspects of curriculum development. 

Broader impacts will derive from the activities, outputs and outcomes of this project and will enhance graduate ethics education for STEM graduate students while promoting the development of a diverse community of researchers better prepared to model the highest standards of scientific conduct. Results of the project will be promptly and widely disseminated through workshops conducted by participating faculty, established research ethics websites as well as the new National Center for Professional and Research Ethics.

Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Traineeship (IGERT) award is built around two grand challenges in biology: 1) How do genomes interact with the environment to produce biological diversity? and 2) How are biological systems integrated from molecules to ecosystems? Our training model is aimed at preparing students so that they are empowered to learn how an organism?s traits emerge from, and are continually shaped by, a complex interplay of genetic information stored in DNA and environmental information that an organism experiences throughout its life. This training will equip students with the knowledge, tools and perspectives needed to address pressing scientific and societal problems, including: effects of climate change on agriculture and food security; responses of organisms and ecosystems to anthropogenic influences on landscapes; emergence of infectious diseases, and influences of genes on behavior.

This proposal uses a ?back-to-the-future? educational model that asserts that the best way to use genomics to address grand challenges in biology is to have a graduate program that blends state-of-the-art training in genomics with an integrated, taxon-oriented, perspective. Our guiding principle is that to be able to use powerful new genomic resources as effectively as possible, students need to have strong foundation in the basic biology of the organisms they are studying. Another cornerstone of this IGERT is the recruiting and mentoring of underrepresented minorities into a scientific discipline.  Because genomic topics often deal with provocative issues, students will also get training in scientific ethics and on how to communicate sensitive topics to the public.

Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Traineeship (IGERT) award will train a corps of doctoral students to become the leaders needed to develop innovative adaptive strategies to respond to unprecedented challenges as a result of climate change. Intellectual Merit: Changes in the hydrologic cycle are expected to decrease the supply of safe water, forcing vulnerable populations in poor countries to drink dirty water, leading to increased disease. As contaminants continue to flow into water bodies and hydrodynamic patterns adjust to climate change, the coastal fisheries upon which human populations depend for food will face increased problems of eutrophication and anoxia. Integrated strategies are needed for predicting and adapting to climate driven stressors on water resources and human health. Among these strategies are smart growth land use practices resulting in reduced greenhouse gas emissions or water infrastructure systems that conserve water and energy.

Broader Impacts: The trainees will be scientific leaders and will engage in mentoring diverse high school students. Practical problems will be addressed by students through a capstone course centering on real problems in three very different areas of the world: the Chesapeake Bay watershed in the temperate developed U.S., the tropical underdeveloped Amazon basin in Peru, and the arid underdeveloped Nile basin in Ethiopia. IGERT students, highly trained in advanced water treatment and management, will learn to adapt skills and knowledge to address problems in diverse cultural, political and economic settings.

IGERT: Water, Climate, and Health 1069213

The IGERT support was successful in encouraging PhD students to pursue collaborations with their peers and with IGERT faculty across departments and schools (Arts and Sciences, Public Health and Engineering) in the University. Hence students were exposed to different ways to investigate environmental problems, and they learned that solving many of today?s problems requires a multifaceted approach.  Among the most significant research accomplishments were those which showed how changing climate exacerbates water quality in under developed countries and the effect this has particularly on the development of young children.  Another study invented an inexpensive and easily implemented method for measuring temperature at a very local scale, particularly useful for urban areas where extreme heat events and air quality affect human health and mortality.  This study led to the founding of a startup company which will deploy the hardware developed by the IGERT students to get detailed heat measurements in urban areas both in the US and in the underdeveloped world, starting with Peru.  Another study showed how changes in rainfall resulting from climate change exacerbates problems for agriculture in the Sub Sahara and the potential effects on food production in marginal regions of the world.  Others explored innovative methods for water purification in parts of the world that differ economically and politically.  Others are using climate models to predict the effects of changing climate on human health and food production.
The need for interdisciplinary programs to address current and future questions regarding the environment and human health was clearly demonstrated in this project and was shown to be achievable at a University where the different disciplines necessary for addressing these questions exist in different schools on different campuses.   The Igert students became a closely knit group who worked together on problems that involved different disciplines ranging from water sanitation to climate modeling, and formed relationships that will continue beyond their years as graduate students. Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Traineeship (IGERT) award supports the development of a new multidisciplinary, multi-institutional graduate training program of education and research in Wind Energy Science, Engineering and Policy (WESEP), at Iowa State University, in collaboration with the University of Puerto Rico - MayagÃ¼ez.  The purpose of this program is to provide doctoral students with multidisciplinary training in the skills required for conducting research at the disciplinary interface between engineering, atmospheric science/meteorology, agriculture/economics, and journalism/communication. 

Intellectual Merit: The thematic basis is that mitigating global climate change requires energy system transformation to reduce greenhouse gases from the electric sector; wind energy must play a central role in this, which will occur only through interdisciplinary leadership in advancing pertinent science, engineering, technology and policy. The vision is to strengthen the nation?s wind energy resources by producing technical experts, effective communicators, and ethical decision-makers who lead the U.S. transformation to a high-wind energy portfolio. The research will increase wind energy growth rate, decreasing its cost, and extend its penetration limits. Our education program includes a 3-6 month industry internship, a 3-month international experience, and a 3-level curriculum to provide breadth, interdisciplinary research strength, and advanced training and depth in WESEP. Trainees and faculty will experience the full research cycle every semester via participation in our real-time research collaborative. We will ensure that 30% of our IGERT student population is from underrepresented groups. Broader Impacts: This project will have near- and long-term impact on increasing supply of cost-effective clean energy, fundamental engineering and science, and energy policy.

Outcome Report:
This project, an NSF-sponsored Integrative Graduate Education and Research Traineeship (IGERT) focused on wind energy, provided a large infusion of Ph.D-level engineering, science, and policy-related talent to the US as our nation increasingly relies on renewable energy production to supply our electrical needs. The intellectual merit of this work is contained in the development of a new Ph. D. degree program at Iowa State University (ISU) in Wind Energy Science, Engineering and Policy (WESEP), the 28 Ph.D. students who participated in this program, and the corresponding research production. This research production included 171 public presentations; 2 book chapters; 126 peer-reviewed publications 77 of which appeared in technical journals; and four large WESEP-organized events (1 conference, 2 symposia, and 1 workshop) on the ISU campus.
Highlights of this research included (1) design of a national high voltage transmission overlay to reduce the cost of reaching a 50% by-energy renewable penetration level; (2) development of a new aluminium/calcium composite material and deployment for high voltage direct current transmission conductors to reduce cost of building the kind of overlay identified in item #1;  (3) design of a hexcrete 140ft tall tower to increase energy production per turbine; (4) new ways of efficiently detecting damage on turbine blades via image processing methods and by deploying a new "sensing skin"; (5) development of a wireless sensor network for smart monitoring and managing of wind farms; (6) development of a new turbine blade design method using isogeometric structural analysis; (7) new numerical methods for solving the Navier-Stokes equations to characterize air flow throughout a wind farm; (8) deploying numerical weather prediction models to predict wind ramping events; (9) a compact permanent magnet wind turbine generator design using a Halbach cylinder; (10) development and validation of a method to predict aeroelastic loads/response of wind turbine blades through wind tunnel tests for damage and flutter predictions; (11) replication of the dynamics of offshore environments in a dry-boundary layer wind tunnels using motion simulators; (12) development of an optimization approach to perform integrated transmission and generation design under uncertainty; (13) design of a new dual-rotor wind turbine to  mitigate aerodynamic ineffciencies in the blade root region near the hub and losses due to aerodynamic interactions between turbines in a wind farm; (14) use of statistical data processing to predict wind turbine lifetimes and identify  related maintenance needs; and (15) design of owl-inspired airfoils for low noise turbine operation. 
In addition, the WESEP Ph. D. program established four new graduate courses in wind energy and a new Wind Energy Systems laboratory to support WESEP-related research and coursework. These courses not only provide WESEP-focused training, but they do so with an interdisciplinary approach that teaches students to think across traditional disciplinary boundaries. 
Broader impacts of this IGERT program include the impact of students taking the real-time research collaborative course WESEP 594 each and every semester of the program, resulting in over 200 meetings of this class throughout the project's duration. In this 1 hour per week course, students were exposed to state-of-art research topics and methods together with training in professional ethics, science and engineering communication to the media, environmental impacts, and policy development. In addition, 10 out of the 28 students spent 2-3 months studying overseas, widening their breadth of perspective both in terms of their research and in terms of their overall view of the US as an influence in the world. Over 25% of the 28 students were female or minority. Students made a concerted effort to engage with a number of communities, including local K-12 students and teachers through school visits. and ISU undergraduate programs throught the establishment of the Wind Energy Student Organization. Of particular interest, ISU supported an undergraduate group who participated in the  US Department of Energy Collegiate Wind Energy Competition in 2018 and 2019, winning the "Project Development Award" in 2019.

Title: IGERT:  Climate Change, Water, and Society (CCWAS)

Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Traineeship (IGERT) award will provide a new generation of scientists with the tools to address effects of climate change on water resources. Monitoring data in the Western U.S. show alarming trends in temperature, river flows and snowpack. General circulation models (GCMs) indicate these and other climate-driven trends will continue and accelerate. Currently, major scientific gaps and socioeconomic factors preclude reliable predictions of climate change impacts on water resources, agriculture, and natural ecosystems on a sub-continental scale (e.g., California, Chile). Climate change requires attention from an unprecedented range of scientific disciplines, including atmospheric science, computational science, ecology, economics, engineering, hydrology, political science, and soil science, among others. 

Intellectual Merit: The Climate Change, Water and Society (CCWAS) project will develop needed synergies through 1) a framework for cutting-edge research that focuses on key interfaces of climate/water/social sciences, and 2) an unprecedented, integrative, flexible education and training program. CCWAS fellows will pursue a special degree designation in "Climate Change, Water and Society," core and interface courses in hydroclimatology and decision making under uncertainty, cyber-enabled audio and video instruction for joint course offerings and sharing among campuses, and an innovative "world cafÃ©" style capstone course that annually defines state of the art and research needs in climate change, future water availability, and water resources management. Broader Impacts: Transformative qualities of the research will be broadened through collaboration and comparative studies with colleagues in Chile, which faces similar climate change and water challenges as California. An internship program will engage students with the government agencies responsible for mitigating and adapting to climate change effects. 

IGERT is an NSF-wide program intended to meet the challenges of educating U.S. Ph.D. scientists and engineers with the interdisciplinary background, deep knowledge in a chosen discipline, and the technical, professional, and personal skills needed for the career demands of the future. The program is intended to catalyze a cultural change in graduate education by establishing innovative new models for graduate education and training in a fertile environment for collaborative research that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries.
Outcome Report:
The Climate Change, Water, and Society (CCWAS) IGERT admitted trainees from 2012-2015, with 24 trainees funded for two years each and five associates who remained active in CCWAS activities throughout doctoral study. In addition to CCWAS funding, six trainees or associates received NSF Graduate Research Fellowships and numerous others received fellowships from other sources.
  Trainees constitute our most important product. All have been prepared to work across disciplines, to consider societal implications of their research, and to communicate their work clearly to the general public. As of October 2018, two trainees graduated with MS degrees and one withdrew without a degree. Thirteen trainees are on track to complete PhD degrees in normative time. The balance of the trainees and associates have completed PhDs, with three trainees appointed to faculty positions. In addition, five trainee alumni have postdoctoral fellowships, two work in the private sector, four have gained positions as agency scientists, and one is in the job market.
Dissertation topics included:
Using economic instruments to manage groundwater
Optimizing reservoir outflows with a goal of sustainable fisheries management 
Assessing the vulnerability of California groundwater resources under climate change
Examining river flood regimes and floodplain inundation patterns using 2D hydrodynamic modeling to understand spatial and temporal variability of flood characteristics
The effect of large-scale atmospheric phenomena on the trans-Atlantic slave trade
Examining the effects of regional climate change on snowpack and water availability, and developing variable resolution climate modeling, with applications to mountain snowpack
Large-scale water management in the context of past development and future climate change
Workshops
Each year, the CCWAS IGERT trainees planned and hosted a ?State of the Science: Climate, Water, and Policy? workshop modeled after the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. These conferences were aimed at providing policymakers with up-to-date scientific information and identifying the outstanding scientific and policy research questions that can be the topics of dissertation research by IGERT students.
Over the funding period, we held four workshops.
2013. The Future of Water in California: Integrating Climate, Water, and Policy
Water resources in California are essential for meeting human needs for drinking water, agriculture, ecosystems, and recreation. Climate change increases the difficulty of meeting these multiple and often conflicting needs. CCWAS IGERT students organized a two-day workshop that included physical and social scientists, water managers, and policymakers, with the goal of improving connections between scientific disciplines and the exchange between science, management, and policy.
The workshop included top academic scientists who summarized the state of climate science, hydrology, and human reactions to policymaking; and decision makers who identified key research questions to inform scientists what managers and policy-makers need.
2014. Climate Change and the Future of Groundwater in California 
As climate changes, California will face decreased snowpack, earlier peaks in runoff, unknown changes in groundwater recharge, and more extreme events, such as drought. Many uncertainties exist, however, about how these changes will influence groundwater resources and management.
First-year CCWAS trainees organized and hosted a workshop, "Climate Change and the Future of Groundwater in California," that brought together diverse stakeholders for a day of discussion and brainstorming. Participants included academics, water managers, staff from environmental organizations, policymakers, and representatives from the agricultural sector. 
2015. Water Scarcity in the West: Past, Present, Future 
Trainees in the CCWAS IGERT admitted in Fall 2014 planned and organized a conference, "Water Scarcity in the West: Past, Present, and Future." Human existence in the American West has always been challenged by water scarcity, with drought, climate change, inefficiencies in use, and increasing demand exacerbating the issues facing water users today. In the workshop, trainees sought to examine how scientific, political, and historical perspectives inform our understanding of water scarcity in the West. In addition, they examined the role of scientists, policymakers, and the public in adapting to water scarcity in a changing climate.
Speakers at the day-and-a-half long conference included California Secretary for Natural Resources John Laird and Patricia Mulroy, former general manager of the Southern Nevada Water Authority. 
2016. Weathering Change: The Impact of Climate and the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act on California?s Water 
The trainees in the final CCWAS cohort worked together to convene a conference on California's groundbreaking legislation that implement regulation of California groundwater. TheSustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA) will strongly influence water availability and allocation in California. At the time of the workshop, their joint consequences had received little attention. Successful adaptation to hydroclimate change will hinge on new approaches to integrated water resources management in concert with SGMA. The workshop sought to highlight some of these challenges, and to outline potential fruitful paths forward.
The event was kicked off with a keynote address by Kevin de Leon, the Speaker Pro Tempore of the California State Senate, and included presentations and panel discussions from academic and agency researchers, water managers, staff from non-governmental organizations, and farmers.

Title: IGERT: Interacting with the Brain: Mechanisms, Optimization, and Innovation
Full Address: 2221 UNIVERSITY AVE SE STE 100, MINNEAPOLIS, MN, ="554143074"
Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Traineeship (IGERT) award supports the development of a multi-disciplinary, integrative graduate education and training program in NeuroEngineering (NE) at the University of Minnesota at Twin Cities. Intellectual Merit: The purpose of this program is to train doctoral students to develop the skills to revolutionize technologies for interfacing with the brain and advance the fundamental understanding of neuroscience processes that arise when interfacing with and modulating the brain. 

Broader impacts include the development of a multi-disciplinary training program that blurs the boundary between neuroscientists and engineers, thus enabling a new generation of scientists to competently and confidently take on the grand challenges in the interdisciplinary field of NeuroEngineering. The NE program includes major research themes in decoding brain signals, modulating brain dynamics, and bi-directional brain interfacing. The program is a "degree-plus" model in which pre-doctoral students are admitted to one of the participating graduate programs (Biomedical Engineering, Electrical Engineering, Mechanical Engineering, and Neuroscience), and are trained through a series of hands-on, modular neuroengineering courses. All NE Fellows will immerse themselves in a lab outside their major in the summer of their first year, engage in multiple lab rotations, and participate in at least one clinical lab rotation, summer internship at a neurotechnology company, or summer international research experience. NE Fellows will have co-advisors beginning in their first year, one from the engineering sciences and one from the basic or clinical neurosciences. The training program incorporates several outreach efforts to recruit women and underrepresented minorities, provide outreach to K-12 and industry, and train NE Fellows to be effective communicators. 

IGERT is an NSF-wide program intended to meet the challenges of educating U.S. Ph.D. scientists and engineers with the interdisciplinary background, deep knowledge in a chosen discipline, and the technical, professional, and personal skills needed for the career demands of the future. The program is intended to catalyze a cultural change in graduate education by establishing innovative new models for graduate education and training in a fertile environment for collaborative research that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries.
Outcome Report:
Neural interface technologies, including systems that electrically pace brain activity to restore function or use brain activity to diagnose disease or control a computer, have tremendous potential to improve quality of life. The University of Minnesota Neural Engineering IGERT (NE-IGERT) program was motivated by the notion that future breakthroughs in this rapidly-growing area of research will be made by engineers who understand the fundamental issues and principles of neuroscience that occur during neural interventions, and by neuroscientists who are truly competent in engineering concepts and tools. 
Our IGERT program trained 34 doctoral students in four major interdisciplinary research themes: a) modulating brain signals with stimulation, b) decoding brain signals to control systems, c) assessing brain signals with functional imaging, and d) modeling functional brain networks. The program developed a “degree-plus” model in which trainees worked to achieve a neuroengineering minor in addition to taking coursework in their home department.  Each trainee selected faculty co-mentors (one from engineering and one from the brain sciences), which provided trainees with unique opportunities to engage in high-impact interdisciplinary research starting in their first year of the program.
Trainees also had the opportunity to gain professional experience in applying neuroengineering principles through semester-long internships at several companies that specialize in neuroimaging and neuromodulation products.  Additionally, trainess engaged in numerous outreach and leadership activities from educating 2nd-4th graders through a Brain Awareness Week program to hosting high school students from groups underrepressented in STEM at the University to serving as graduate mentors for summer REU students to helping organize an annual Minnesota Neuromodulation Symposium that provides a forum for world leaders in the emerging field of neuromodulation (academia, industry, and government).
The University of Minnesota Neural Engineering IGERT program generated a number of research products including development of non-invasive brain computer interfaces for human use, high-field MRI (10.5T) for human use, MRI-compatible microelectrodes for measuring neuronal spike activity during fMRI, recording methodologies that combine EEG with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), computational models that can predict the biophysical effects of electrical stimulation within the brain and mechanical stimulation of the skin, high-density electrode arrays for interfacing with the brain, and novel signal processing approaches for real-time analysis of neural signals for use in closed-loop brain stimulation applications.

Title: IGERT:  Integrative Graduate Training In Ocean Change
Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Traineeship (IGERT) award will train a new generation of scholars to use integrative, cross-disciplinary, and cross-scale approaches to investigate problems of ocean change. Intellectual Merit: Human activities are causing physical and biological changes in the ocean. Some of these changes threaten the persistence of contemporary marine ecosystems and the societies they support. The scale and likely consequences of ocean change are substantial, but ocean change is difficult to observe and invisible to many sectors of society. A key innovation is to frame research questions in a problem-driven, socially-defined context. Trainees will collaborate to explore ocean conditions, biological and ecological responses to changing ocean conditions, their impacts on human institutions and welfare, and opportunities to build resilience in this social-ecological system. The research performed by trainees will enhance our understanding of change in the ocean and its impacts on ecosystems and social institutions. 

Broader impacts of the program arise from the coupled-systems approach. Trainees will emerge prepared to address problems of ocean change from a coupled social-ecological perspective, communicate with diverse groups, establish credibility inside and outside academics, and fairly represent uncertainties inherent in the study of ocean change. In so doing, they will serve societal needs and help to transform the way society views the ocean and the changes induced by human activity. We will seek to broaden participation from underrepresented minorities, especially those from coastal tribes, Alaska natives, and Pacific Islanders, and in so doing, we will serve communities and cultures likely to be among the first affected by ocean change.

IGERT is an NSF-wide program intended to meet the challenges of educating U.S. Ph.D. scientists and engineers with the interdisciplinary background, deep knowledge in a chosen discipline, and the technical, professional, and personal skills needed for the career demands of the future. The program is intended to catalyze a cultural change in graduate education by establishing innovative new models for graduate education and training in a fertile environment for collaborative research that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries.
Outcome Report:
We trained 30 graduate students at the University of Washington in interdisciplinary thinking related to changing ocean conditions. We began from the premise that rapid change in ocean conditions—including changes in fisheries, food production, and sea level—will create ecological, socio-economic, and cultural challenges in coming decades. We sought to train students to address these challenges through research designed and performed in collaboration with peers. Trainees worked in small cohorts to advance research of their own design. Their research products have been published in peer-reviewed journals, presented as white-papers to state agencies, and adopted as new curricula in K-8 classrooms.
  The intellectual merits of the trainees’ work are best reflected in scholarly outputs that serve both science and society. These include consideration of 1) scale-dependence and limits to inference in ocean change research; 2) social vulnerability to climate-associated fisheries closures; 3) creation of a community knowledge network for Pacific Islanders exposed to climate variability; 4) local adaptation to sea level rise; 5) assessment of blue carbon potential in Puget Sound, WA; and 6) translating climate science for use at regional scales.
  The broader impacts of this project are reflected in internal and external benefits. Internally, trainees learned to work with peers from diverse disciplines across the university—for example, trainees from atmospheric science, quantitative science, oceanography, and public affairs jointly worked on a project concerning local government responses to sea level rise. In another example, trainees from chemical oceanography, biological oceanography, fisheries, biology, and atmospheric science created a local learning network in Pohnpei, Micronesia. This cross-disciplinary collaboration and peer-to-peer learning expanded the horizons of each trainee, increasing their employability and offering downstream benefits to an educated and productive workforce.
  External benefits accrued to the larger community. For four consecutive years, trainees hosted a public seminar series featuring eminent speakers from around the U.S. and abroad. On a weekly basis, speakers addressed themes as varied as ecological change in coral reef systems, changes in fisheries and food production, the roles of government and NGOs in response to rapid ocean change, and social and ethical responsibilities associated with the changing ocean. These seminars were attended by up to 250 students and faculty from across campus and from the community at large and served the interests of a broad range of participants.
  Other benefits accrued to specific stakeholders. Trainees worked with coastal tribes, Pacific islanders, shellfish growers, fisheries managers, state agency personnel, and K-8 students and teachers to co-produce knowledge relevant to each group. Among the outcomes of these collaborations are improved prospects for mussel aquaculture in Puget Sound, new guidance for marine resource managers, improved understanding of the socio-economic and cultural challenges associated with changing ocean conditions, and new K-8 curricula and associated skills among K-8 students.
