Title: IGERT: Educating and the Interface: Nanomaterial Environmental Impacts and Policy   (EI-NEIP)
Program(s): Nanoscale Interactions Program, IGERT FULL PROPOSALS, NANOMANUFACTURING, ENG NNI Special Studies, IGERT Materials Research, IGERT Astronomical Sciences
Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Training (IGERT) award creates a new interdisciplinary graduate training program whose focus is nanotechnology, its environmental effects, and policy at Carnegie Mellon and Howard University, in collaboration with the Center for Environmental Implications of Nanotechnology.  

This program will operate at the interface of science and environmental policy and will produce an environmentally- and policy-literate generation of nanoscience professionals with the skills needed to assess and manage environmental risks associated with nanomaterials. The program's goal is to foster the creation of knowledge and the exchange of ideas within an innovative and stimulating educational experience that will advance not only our knowledge of nanoparticles in the environment but also our understanding of how best to avoid their potential negative consequences. Broader impacts include the training of interdisciplinary Ph.D.-level scientists and engineers who, in addition to receiving rigorous scientific training, will have an understanding of the principles of good environmental stewardship, societal concerns as they relate to nanotechnology, and will be prepared to take leadership roles in dealing with environmental risk. Graduate students from multiple disciplines will participate in this two-year training program where they will learn the fundamentals of their core discipline and gain proficiency in the analysis of environmental issues pertaining to nanotechnology, decision science, and policy analysis, in new nanotechnology-themed courses. To promote interdisciplinary research students will be advised by at least two faculty members from different academic disciplines and will participate in laboratory exchanges with international partners.

IGERT is an NSF-wide program intended to meet the challenges of educating U.S. Ph.D. scientists and engineers with the interdisciplinary background, deep knowledge in a chosen discipline, and the technical, professional, and personal skills needed for the career demands of the future. The program is intended to catalyze a cultural change in graduate education by establishing innovative new models for graduate education and training in a fertile environment for collaborative research that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries.
Outcome Report:
The Nanotechnology Environmental Effects and Policy (NEEP) IGERT project provided education and research experiences for 22 trainees over seven years.  IGERT trainees, along with their advisors and co-advisors, produced 31 peer-reviewed publications during the project, and gave 50 poster and oral conference presentations. These projects were highly interdisciplinary and most of the published papers are collaborative efforts with multiple IGERT trainees and PIs contributing to those papers. Many of the papers would not have been possible without close collaboration between the Trainees and the access to international collaborations. The major accomplishments can be categorized in several areas including 1) fundamental polymer-nanoparticle interactions, 2) transformations of nanomaterials in the environment, 3) nano-bio interactions, and 4) modeling of nanomaterial fate in the environment.
The research of several IGERT trainees increased our understanding of the interactions and physico-chemical characteristics of polymer-grafted nanoparticle materials. This understanding was used to better control the interactions and assembly of nanoparticles also as functional building blocks of nanocomposite materials for application in active self-regulating membrane materials. IGERT trainees also conducted fundamental work elucidating the role of polymeric ligands on the interactions between bio-derived nanoparticle systems. This understanding of the strength of interaction of the NPs in polymeric matrices was important in one of the IGERT capstone projects, where IGERT trainees developed a tiered strategy to determine the potential for release of NPs from consumer products containing NPs in polymeric matrices.
Many of the IGERT trainees’ research was focused on understanding the transformations of NPs in environmental and biological matrices, and determining the impact of these transformations on their potential risks. A consistent theme resulting from our IGERT research was that the fate of engineered nanomaterials is determined in a large part by the environmental properties (e.g. redox state, amount of organic matter, etc.). In many cases, the impact of the various environmental properties is more important to consider than the specific nanomaterial properties (e.g. polymeric surface coatings). The understanding developed on this project will enable the nanotechnology research community to better prioritize research aimed at predicting the effects that nanomaterials may have on the environment, and can inform manufacturers of NPs about desirable and undesirable properties in the materials from the point of view of environmental health and safety. 
Many of our IGERT trainees were fortunate enough to work with an interdisciplinary group of ecologists, toxicologists, materials scientists, and chemists, to probe the fundamental physical and biological processes affecting the fate of NPs in freshwater systems.  This included laboratory experiments with bacteria and aquatic and terrestrial plants, as well as conducting experiments in one of a kind wetland freshwater mesocosms. Interdisciplinary research by IGERT trainees has greatly improved our understanding of how bacteria respond to the presence of NPs, including effects on quorum sensing (QS) and their metagenomics responses to exposures to NPs. The discoveries underlying the properties of NPs and how they change and interact with biological systems has led to new lines of research focused on developing new applications of NPs (e.g., in electrochemical energy storage).  
The development of models of environmental fate are a culmination of efforts between IGERT trainees.  This is because the model development requires a fundamental understanding of NP behaviors as well as the data needed to parameterize those models. Including geochemical transformations significantly improved the accuracy of the risk assessment model.
Overall, the highly interdisciplinary work of the IGERT trainees has led to novel understanding of the fate and behavior of NPs in natural and biological systems, important transformations, and elucidated NP-biological interactions.

Title: IGERT:  Training Program in Sustainable Energy Recovery from the Earth --  Educational Innovation at the Intersection of Geosciences and Engineering
Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Training (IGERT) award supports the development of a new Ph.D. interdisciplinary training program at Cornell University focused on sustainable energy recovery from the earth. Students in engineering and in geosciences will be provided with a common language in interdisciplinary science and design that will accelerate technological progress in the sustainable exploitation of Earth's energy resources with acceptable environmental consequences. 

There are complex intellectual challenges associated with the design of new subsurface technologies that extract energy from geothermal, conventional, and unconventional fossil resources, or safely sequester waste products like CO2. Trainees will participate in research that adds to fundamental understanding of transport processes for thermal energy, and of fluids and fractures in engineered rock systems. The initial interdisciplinary training will occur through a series of courses that introduce natural systems phenomena, energy conversion principles, economic, social and ethical considerations, and methods of industrial ecology (life cycle analysis), of systems design and simulation, and of risk analysis. Student teams will draw upon this coursework foundation for their analysis and design projects that deal with real world, field-based, cases. Trainees will develop skills to design energy options in consideration of environmental, economic, and social benefits and risks, and to communicate with those who must make informed decisions. In doing so, the nation gains a workforce able to utilize the Earth's energy resources in better balance with the natural environment. 

IGERT is an NSF-wide program intended to meet the challenges of educating U.S. Ph.D. scientists and engineers with the interdisciplinary background, deep knowledge in a chosen discipline, and the technical, professional, and personal skills needed for the career demands of the future. The program is intended to catalyze a cultural change in graduate education by establishing innovative new models for graduate education and training in a fertile environment for collaborative research that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries.
Outcome Report:
In 2017, Cornell University completed a National Science Foundation-supported interdisciplinary graduate-level Training Program in Sustainable Energy Recovery from the Earth – Educational Innovation at the Intersection of Geosciences and Engineering. The Cornell Earth-Energy program trained, in a new way, doctoral and master’s students for a range of energy technology applications. Students in engineering and in geosciences were provided with a common language and a set of fundamental problem solving skills in interdisciplinary subsurface science and design. As their careers progress, they are well positioned to accelerate technological progress in the sustainable exploitation of Earth’s energy resources with acceptable economic and environmental outcomes.
There are complex intellectual challenges associated with the design of new subsurface technologies that extract energy from geothermal, conventional, and unconventional fossil resources, that can store energy produced by intermittent power sources, or that can safely sequester waste products like co-produced oil field water and carbon dioxide. The Earth Energy IGERT Trainees completed individual and team original research projects in order to discover and develop new technologies with which to utilize subsurface energy resources and materials at commercially relevant scales in an environmentally sustainable manner.
The research accomplished by the Trainees has added to fundamental understanding phenomena associated with transport and reaction processes for thermal energy utilization as well as the consequences that accompany extraction and utilization. Some of the Trainees characterized the occurrence and behavior of fluids moving through fractures in natural and engineered rock systems. Investigation of supercritical fluid mixtures led to new insight important to developing large scale energy storage devices. Concurrent with the years of this project, awareness grew of the risk of inducing earthquakes through manipulation of subsurface fluids, and the Earth Energy Trainees contributed to documenting the connections between fluid injection and earthquake generation. Trainees demonstrated the heterogeneity of unconventional reservoirs for natural gas, and investigated the connections between fracture behavior and that heterogeneity. Trainees evaluated the extent to which rocks of New York, Pennsylvania, and West Virginia are well suited for the extraction of geothermal energy in amounts sufficient to provide district heating for networks of residential, municipal, and commercial buildings as well as for low temperature industrial process heating.
The initial interdisciplinary training occurred through a series of courses that introduced natural systems phenomena, energy conversion principles, transport and chemical reaction in subsurface environments along with economic, social and ethical considerations, and methods of energy life cycle analysis, of systems design and simulation, and of risk analysis. Students drew upon this coursework foundation for their analysis and design projects that dealt with real world, field-based, cases. Annual field study modules were implemented to real-world energy production sites to allow students to utilize their course-based learning in multidisciplinary problem solving, to observe the interface between energy production and environmental resources like fresh water systems, and to interact with both energy industry professionals and the communities who host and must regulate the industrial sites.
Earth Energy Trainees developed skills to design and evaluate energy options in consideration of environmental, economic, and social benefits and risks. They learned to communicate with the general public, with technology specialists who are not from their own specialty, and with those who must make informed decisions. In doing so, the nation has gained a workforce able to utilize the Earth’s energy resources in better balance with the natural environment.
Twenty-two NSF-supported Trainees and four other doctoral students whose programs were like those of the trainees but funded by other sources have completed, or remain on course to complete soon, their doctoral degrees. Four additional Trainees chose to complete a Master’s degree and then move into the work force immediately. Over the course of the IGERT, more than 15 undergraduates were involved with IGERT-related research. Key elements of the educational and research programs developed under this NSF-sponsored program have been institutionalized by Cornell and are now a part of the College of Engineering’s graduate education program.

Title: IGERT: Sustaining Ecosystem Services to Support Rapidly Urbanizing Areas
Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Traineeship (IGERT) award supports the development of an interdisciplinary graduate program in Ecosystem Services for Urbanizing Regions at Portland State University, in collaboration with Heritage University, and an array of city, state, and federal agencies, and community partners. Ecosystem services are the conditions and processes provided by natural ecosystems that sustain and fulfill human life. Rapid urbanization has contributed to widespread degradation of ecosystem services, thus creating a demand for scientists and managers who can address these issues. This program integrates scholarship from economics, environmental science, engineering, geosciences, urban studies and planning, business administration and social sciences to understand the complex roles that ecosystem services play in supporting rapidly growing urban areas of the Pacific Northwest and beyond. 

Trainees will engage in a three-year study sequence, in research, and in field placements to develop an in-depth, interdisciplinary knowledge of ecosystem service issues at multiple scales. A diverse faculty team will build a curriculum and research program that integrates ecological, social, and economic concepts and that explicates the role of values in planning and management. Through new problem-based curricula, research, and community partnerships, the program will create a new generation of scientists and managers proficient in the science and cutting-edge management approaches for sustaining vital ecosystem services for urbanizing regions. Trainees' dissertations will be required to include a co-authored chapter on an interdisciplinary topic, deepening student understanding of the relationships between the natural and social sciences, and providing training for collaborative projects. Trainees also will have an opportunity to complete PSU's Graduate Certificate in Sustainability while pursuing a doctorate. National recruitment for the program will target high-caliber students, with an emphasis on under-represented groups, through a partnership with Heritage University.

IGERT is an NSF-wide program intended to meet the challenges of educating U.S. Ph.D. scientists and engineers with the interdisciplinary background, deep knowledge in a chosen discipline, and the technical, professional, and personal skills needed for the career demands of the future. The program is intended to catalyze a cultural change in graduate education by establishing innovative new models for graduate education and training in a fertile environment for collaborative research that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries.
Outcome Report:
The Portland State University IGERT program took NSF’s goal of training doctoral students to engage real-world problems through interdisciplinary perspectives seriously. Our IGERT, the Ecosystem Services supporting Urbanizing Regions (ESUR-IGERT), began as a set of graduate classes taught by a multidisciplinary group of seven faculty members, from six departments across three schools and colleges at Portland State University. This unusual combination of faculty brought their different lenses to the problems of ecosystem services (ES) and its relevance in supporting urbanizing regions. One of the many positive results of this wide collaboration is that students were influenced, and challenged, by a broad range of perspectives.
In their IGERT-specific courses, in their IGERT-specific committees, and in their discipline-specific research, the students confronted multiple theoretical lenses and worldviews. The result is a group of students who see problems from an interdisciplinary view and demand that solutions deal with the reality of an interdisciplinary world. The program included a set of requirements designed to demand and encourage interdisciplinary perspectives, including unique courses and co-curricular activities. These requirements resulted in a diverse portfolio of research accomplishments and on-going work.
The most important outcomes of the ESUR-IGERT, however, are not the individual results of one or multiple scientific studies. Rather, the most important outcomes resulted from developing research streams that engaged multiple students and faculty mentors from different scientific disciplines, using a variety of scientific methodologies, to address complex (wicked) problems of social and environmental importance.
Students accepted into our IGERT came from disciplines as disparate as engineering, environmental studies, public administration, and anthropology. Students all participated in a yearlong course sequence centered on ecosystem services. Each course in the sequence had both social science and natural science instructors in the room simultaneously. This combination of faculty and students from a variety of disciplines, with various worldviews, resulted in pushing all the participants to challenge their prior conceptions and to consider the broader implications of seemingly straight-forward problems.
As just one example of the impact of broad disciplinarity, students began addressing problems of social justice by recognizing the inter-related issues of systematically disenfranchised human populations and environmental degradation. Instead of addressing these issues as discrete, our students worked across disciplines using multiple methodologies to address the overall problems more systemically. As a result of this research stream, our students engaged with and studied the impacts of 1) projected cleanup of polluted river sites in the presence of homeless populations deriving subsistence livings from the sites, 2) the farm-to-table agriculture movement and the employment conditions of back-of-the-house restaurant staff and farm workers, 3) subsistence farming and small markets in mountainous central Mexico, and 4) power differentials’ influence on environmental decisions around depleted fisheries in South Pacific nations. All of these studies resulted from broadened perspectives due to the interdisciplinary nature of our IGERT.
The ultimate beneficial outcome of the ESUR-IGERT program is a cadre of scientists who will always look at problems as multi-dimensional and seek solutions that employ knowledge from all sources. This is a cadre of scientists ready to address the wicked problems of our time.

Title: IGERT: Integrative Graduate Education and Research Traineeship in Magnetic and Nanostructured Materials
Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Training (IGERT) award supports the development of an interdisciplinary graduate training program centered on the design and study of novel materials with structure-derived functionalities. The program is a collaborative effort between Purdue University, Cornell University and Norfolk State University (NSU). Its goal is to train students to conduct research that will lead to faster, smaller and more efficient devices and technologies with numerous applications, including information storage, signal detection, and biomedical possibilities. 

Technical and professional training opportunities include annual laboratory training at Cornell and NSU, ongoing video-conferencing of modular courses, regular consideration of the ethical and social aspects of magnetic and nanostructured materials, and student-driven research initiatives. Trainees will also explore engineering education research in order to learn about the challenges of translating new knowledge into educational resources for schools and the general public. Students will benefit from structured mentoring and training for individual career development--education elements that have been identified as essential for the retention and success of underrepresented minorities in science and engineering. This partnership, of two research universities and a Historically Black University, will bring greater understanding of how the integration of complementary capabilities and opportunities can better prepare the next generation of scientists and engineers.

IGERT is an NSF-wide program intended to meet the challenges of educating U.S. Ph.D. scientists and engineers with the interdisciplinary background, deep knowledge in a chosen discipline, and the technical, professional, and personal skills needed for the career demands of the future. The program is intended to catalyze a cultural change in graduate education by establishing innovative new models for graduate education and training in a fertile environment for collaborative research that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries.
Outcome Report:
The IGERT on Magnetic and Nanostructured Materials (IGERT-MMM), 2010-2017, is one of only two IGERT programs led by a Historically Black College and University (HBCU). The collaboration between Norfolk State University (NSU) as a Masters’-L University (as defined by the Carnegie classification system) and Purdue University and Cornell University as RU-VH (Research Universities, Very High research activity) combined the various research capabilities at the different types of universities. In addition to learning and working with the differences in institutional capabilities, the diversity of universities exposed students and faculty alike to the variety of institutional cultures. By integrating the project researchers’ expertise and interests, IGERT-MNM faculty and students have made broad scientific contributions in the area of magnetic and nanostructured materials, publishing 73 peer-reviewed articles and making 58 technical presentations.
The goals of the IGERT-MNM collaboration were successfully achieved through the following:
1. Students were trained to conduct interdisciplinary research, preparing them to be independent researchers that harness the technical capabilities of the three affiliated universities. They were trained in interdisciplinary research related to novel materials, integrating chemistry, physics, materials science and engineering.
2. IGERT Trainees were introduced to pedagogical principles through Purdue’s engineering education research emphasis, which guided the program annual evaluation and redesign. All Trainees prepared educational products in their areas of research, and several participated in engineering education research and publication.
3. IGERT Trainees developed the ability to communicate their science effectively through proposals and other forms of technical writing, and
4. Students were trained in issues related to ethics, responsible conduct of research, and intellectual property in order to handle professional ethical situations related to research of novel technologies.
IGERT-MNM succeeded in creating and sustaining a highly diverse Trainee cohort: 27 Ph.D. and M.S. students at Norfolk State University, eight Ph.D. students at Cornell and three M.S. and Ph.D. students at Purdue. The students’ backgrounds and research areas include chemistry, engineering (optical, mechanical, electronic, education), materials science, and physics. The IGERT-MNM Trainees/Associates profile includes 45% female and 41% ethnic/racial STEM under-represented minorities, with 25% of international participants as Associate Trainees. Trainees regularly worked in multi-campus teams to support and develop the IGERT-MNM project, learning about different cultures in an interdisciplinary, inter-gender, inter-racial, multiethnic and international environment.
The project goals were achieved by the implementation of the IGERT-MNM Model as envisioned in the proposal, through the intimate integration of multi-dimensional assessment, constant redesign, student leadership and effective communication/collaboration. As an expression of the project’s intentional and ongoing self-evaluation, Trainees applied a longitudinal mixed methods approach to follow three IGERT-MNM student teams as they proposed and conducted interdisciplinary materials science research.  Results indicate that high-performing teams have shared perceptions of the importance of components involved with collaborative research, and have strong agreement between personal and group competencies. The work earned the American Society of Engineering Education Graduate Studies Division Best Paper Award during the Summer 2016 national conference.

Title: IGERT: Stem Cell BIomanufacturing
Abstract:
The transformation of stem cell biology discoveries into technologies for a range of applications has enormous promise to impact a broad spectrum of society; however, achieving this aim will only occur if individuals are trained with the necessary interdisciplinary expertise to facilitate growth of the field. This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Training (IGERT) award to the Georgia Institute of Technology provides such training for Ph.D. graduate students by creating a comprehensive educational program that brings together technological innovation, commercialization, and public policy aspects of stem cell research. The specific research projects conducted as part of this training focus on developing standardized and quantitative methods necessary for stem cell isolation, characterization, propagation, and differentiation. Scalable biomanufacturing practices will be developed to efficiently produce sufficient numbers of stem cells and derivatives in readily accessible formats in order to meet the need for novel therapeutic and diagnostic applications of stem cells. 

In addition to the research and educational activities to train Ph.D. students to be leaders in the field of stem cell biomanufacturing, one of the broader impacts of this program will be to provide students with a global scientific perspective based upon the established relationships with our international partners. Graduates will contribute to the burgeoning stem cell industry, catalyzing new biomedical and biotechnological opportunities for stem cells to impact society. A key broader impact and long-term objective of the program will be to foster the participation of members of underrepresented groups in stem cell engineering. 

IGERT is an NSF-wide program intended to meet the challenges of educating U.S. Ph.D. scientists and engineers with the interdisciplinary background, deep knowledge in a chosen discipline, and the technical, professional, and personal skills needed for the career demands of the future. The program is intended to catalyze a cultural change in graduate education by establishing innovative new models for graduate education and training in a fertile environment for collaborative research that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries.
Outcome Report:
This National Science Foundation-funded IGERT on Stem Cell Biomanufacturing has stimulated the establishment of an educational program for Ph.D. students at the Georgia Institute of Technology in the area of the manufacturing of cells. Such a program is necessary if basic stem cell research is to be translated into clinical treatments for patients. This IGERT provided a foundation for Georgia to secure an award from the National Institute for Standards and Technology to fund the development of a roadmap for cell manufacturing. This resulted in the creation of a joint academic and industry cell manufacturing consortium. Because of the leadership of Georgia Tech in this area, the Marcus Foundation made a gift of more than 16 million dollars to the institution in order to establish the Marcus Center for Therapeutic Cell Characterization and Manufacturing. These funds together with the cost-sharing from Georgia Tech are being used to establish new core facilities and in the recruitment of additional faculty. The Marcus Center also has submitted a proposal to the National Science Foundation for the establishment of an Engineering Research Center (ERC) in this area. In addition, in order to further the education of our IGERT Ph.D. students an international short course has been organized in partnership with institutions in the United Kingdom and Portugal. This was first held in 2013 in Portugal, and in 2016 Georgia Tech hosted this course in Hilton Head, South Carolina. It next will be held in 2018 back in Europe. Originally funded for five years, this IGERT was given what totaled two years in no-cost extensions. Over this total of seven years, the Ph.D. students supported by this IGERT were provided a unique education. These students also have been integral in the establishment at Georgia Tech of a major center in the U.S. in the area of cell manufacturing with an emphasis on stem cells.

Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Training (IGERT) award supports the development of a graduate training program in information security and privacy. Trainees will learn to translate the foundational principles of security and privacy into information technologies based on a deep understanding of social, economic, behavioral and public policy implications and requirements. The program will produce a cadre of technologists and scientists who can integrate technical, legal, financial, and psychological knowledge into practical solutions.

The program has at its core a new paradigm for building trustworthy systems, where technical security issues are seen only as one spoke in a wheel, along with equally important legal, social, psychological, policy, and economics issues. Trainees with this interdisciplinary background will join academia, industry, create new companies and drive public policy. A unique bridging program with local and national minority serving institutions and organizations will ensure that the program recruits and retains a diverse set of trainees.

Title: IGERT:   Geoinformatics for Environmental and Energy Modeling and Prediction (GEEMaP)
Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Training (IGERT) award to the University of Iowa supports an interdisciplinary graduate training program designed to train students to use advanced computational methods to address real-world problems in environmental science and energy production. 

This novel Ph.D. training program uses team-based research projects, internships, and international research experiences to produce a new generation of quantitative and computational scientists who are prepared for interdisciplinary collaboration with engineers, social and natural scientists, government policy-makers, and industrial leaders in the global arena of environment and energy production. Geoinformatics--the science of measuring, storing, managing, analyzing and visualizing data related to phenomena occurring on or near the earth's surface--plays a key unifying role in the curriculum. Applications include prevention, control, and mitigation of floods; remediation of air, soil, and water contamination; and increasing wind and hydroelectric energy production--challenges that directly impact human health, safety, and quality of life. The project will broaden the participation of students from populations underrepresented in the science, technology, engineering and mathematical fields (women, U.S. ethnic minorities, and low-income and rural students) through coordination with established and successful recruitment programs at the University of Iowa, offering these students a unique program of innovative science, policy, and technology-based rotations. Student and faculty research results will contribute new computational tools and methods as well as scientific insights that will support the formulation of new environmental policy at the local, regional, national, and global scales.

IGERT is an NSF-wide program intended to meet the challenges of educating U.S. Ph.D. scientists and engineers with the interdisciplinary background, deep knowledge in a chosen discipline, and the technical, professional, and personal skills needed for the career demands of the future. The program is intended to catalyze a cultural change in graduate education by establishing innovative new models for graduate education and training in a fertile environment for collaborative research that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries.
Outcome Report:
The University of Iowa was the home of the NSF Integrative Graduate Education and Research Traineeship (IGERT) program entitled Geoinformatics for Environmental and Energy Modeling and Prediction (GEEMaP). Trainees were doctoral students in the departments of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Geographical and Sustainability Sciences, Statistics, and Biostatistics.
 The educational and training component of the grant offered collaborative research and professional development opportunities that complemented the graduate education that trainees received in their individual departments. Trainees from all departments met together weekly for a seminar, which focused on a different topic each semester. Topics included ethics in environmental research, grant writing, scientific writing, communication of science to the general public, and career opportunities for Ph.D.s in environmental science. Trainees also engaged in internships to obtain real-world experience. Former trainees are now working in academia, government, and industry.
Collaborative research achievements of this program addressed multiple areas of importance to environmental scientists, farmers, local governments, and citizens. Research results have appeared in journal articles and conference presentations in the areas of Geography, Statistics, and Engineering. Examples of research questions addressed by trainees were:
1. How do land characteristics and farming practices affect soil erosion, water quality, and climate change?  "Carbon sequestration" refers to the fact that trees and plants extract carbon dioxide (CO2) from the air through photosynthesis and store it in roots and, as plants decay, in soils. Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas, and increases in its atmospheric levels contribute to global climate change. Trainees investigated which agricultural practices may improve the ability of the soil to retain carbon and thus may help to offset the effects of fossil fuel use and other human activities that increase atmospheric CO2. Soil erosion is an important problem in agricultural areas. Erosion degrades farmland and carries nutrients and sediment into nearby waterways where they impact fish and other aquatic life. Trainees developed models to estimate how much of the run-off in rivers came from different types of surrounding land, such as forest and farm fields. They also investigated how characteristics of the land surface and soil, as well as farming practices, affect erosion.
2. Where is the next Flint, Michigan? Trainees combined data from government and volunteer sources to study the chemical characteristics of river and stream water that feeds public drinking water supplies in several Midwestern states. They identified locations in which surface water has corrosive properties that could cause leaching of lead from pipes.
3. How would frac sand mining affect the environment, economy, and quality of life in Winneshiek County in northeast Iowa? A special type of sand, which is used by the oil and gas industry in the hydraulic fracturing ("fracking") method of extracting petroleum from deep rock formations, occurs beneath the land surface in Winneshiek county. GEEMaP trainees and faculty participated in an interdisciplinary project of the Iowa Initiative for Sustainable Communities to assist the Board of Supervisors in Winneshiek County to decide whether to permit frac sand mining and processing in their county and, if so, how to regulate it. The role of GEEMaP trainees was to develop a model to predict where in Winneshiek County mining companies would be most likely to wish to site sand mines and processing plants. The information from this predictive model was passed to a team in Urban and Regional Planning, who assessed the potential impact on roads, water resources, outdoor recreation, and other aspects of county life. Preliminary results were presented to the county supervisors and residents in a video conference, and final results were presented to the local citizenry in a town meeting.
The broader impacts of the project include expanding participation of underrepresented groups, research addressing societal needs, and efforts to increase public scientific literacy and engagement. Most GEEMaP trainees were from one or more groups underrepresented in scientific and mathematical fields, including women, U.S. minorities, and first-generation college students. Trainees gave presentations to AP classes in Human Geography at a Cedar Rapids, Iowa, high school. One trainee actively participated in a low-impact development planning team for the City of Cedar Rapids to consider street design for stormwater management as part of 2017-2018 road construction plans. Another trainee worked with the city of Dubuque in developing a flood resilience survey. The trainees hosted a public workshop introducing ways in which ordinary citizens can participate in research in environmental science.

Title: IGERT--Interdisciplinary Evolutionary Primatology: Conservation and Human Evolution join Behavior, Bones and Genes
Organization: Research Foundation Of The City University Of New York (Lehman)

Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Training (IGERT) award supports the further development of the New York Consortium in Evolutionary Primatology (NYCEP), a program that draws upon faculty and resources from five institutions in New York City: City University of New York, Columbia University, New York University, the American Museum of Natural History (AMNH), and the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS). The program spans the integrative and interdisciplinary field of "evolutionary primatology," which applies methods and theories from a broad range of the natural sciences to the study of the biology and evolution of humans and other primates. 

This renewal award allows NYCEP to amplify its training in conservation science and human evolution; implement a number of innovative curricular initiatives that ensure interdisciplinarity; restructure the training program to enable students to progress faster towards the Ph.D. and publish earlier; expand international research opportunities; develop new partnerships with programs in geological sciences at Rutgers, Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory of Columbia, and AMNH, genetics and human evolution at Max-Planck Institute/Leipzig and UniversitÃ¤t TÃ¼bingen, and field behavior and conservation in South Africa, Kenya, Ecuador and Peru; extend its relationships with the Richard Gilder Graduate School at AMNH and in conservation science with WCS; develop novel approaches to recruit underrepresented groups; and enhance the NYCEP community by involving graduate students more extensively in NYCEP-wide activities. This innovative training program produces graduate students who are professionally and technically qualified to lead scientific research, education and public outreach in an increasingly socio-politically complex, interdisciplinary and global arena.

IGERT is an NSF-wide program intended to meet the challenges of educating U.S. Ph.D. scientists and engineers with the interdisciplinary background, deep knowledge in a chosen discipline, and the technical, professional, and personal skills needed for the career demands of the future. The program is intended to catalyze a cultural change in graduate education by establishing innovative new models for graduate education and training in a fertile environment for collaborative research that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries.
Outcome Report:
NYCEP (the New York Consortium in Evolutionary Primatology) is a multi-institutional graduate research and training program including PhD students and faculty from the City University of New York, Columbia University, New York University and the Richard Gilder Graduate School at the American Museum of Natural History, as well as staff of the Wildlife Conservation Society. NYCEP has been supported by NSF since 1991, the most recent funding being from the IGERT program between July 1, 2010, and December 31, 2017. NYCEP represents a rare combination of public and private universities together with privately endowed (and publicly assisted) institutions dedicated to education and bringing science to the public. NYCEP research and training focus on primate (including human) evolution, social behavior, ecology, conservation biology, genomics, population genetics, comparative morphology, paleontology and systematics.
Sixty-four NSF-funded trainees and 23 unfunded associates (and over 60 associated faculty) participated in NYCEP activities during the 2010-2017 time span of the award. Twenty-nine trainees received the PhD (5 of these entered in fall 2010 or afterward), along with 9 associates. There are 35 current trainees and 14 associates in the program. 75% of the trainees are female, and 9% are members of under-represented minority groups. Of the 14 associates, 12 are female, 6 international and 2 minority. These students were served pedagogically through a redesign of our core course package; updating of our innovative "Professional Development" course; and teaching a range of new and continuing team-taught interdisciplinary courses and specialty elective courses.
All IGERT students participate in an international field-based project, usually directed by a NYCEP faculty member or partner, typically during the first (or sometimes second) summer of the trainee's graduate career. Since 2010, IGERT students have undertaken paleontological field research in Kenya, Madagascar, South Africa, Tanzania, Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Greece, Romania and Spain; and primate behavioral, ecological and genetic studies in Congo, Ethiopia, Kenya, Madagascar, Nigeria, South Africa, Tanzania, Uganda, and Zambia. Forty-five trainees worked in 25 countries (a total of 102 student-country visits) from 2010-2017.
NYCEP trainees have been outstanding in receipt of research grants from major providers and other awards. Eight have received NSF Graduate Research Fellowships (as well as three honorable mentions), while 18 (plus 7 associates) have been awarded NSF Doctoral Dissertation Improvement Grants (DDIGs). One trainee won the Judge's Choice award in the 2013 NSF IGERT Video and Poster competition. Six trainees received Dissertation Fieldwork grants from the Wenner Gren Foundation (the leading anthropology-wide funding source), while seven were awarded dissertation research grants from the Leakey Foundation (focusing on paleoanthropology and primate behavior/ecology). Four trainees received dissertation fellowships from the American Association of University Women, two won U.S. Student Fulbright Fellowships (to work in Madagascar and Zambia), one received a James F. Nacey Fellowship from the Nacey Maggioncalda Foundation, and one was awarded a Point Foundation Fellowship for LGBTQ Scholars. The American Association of Physical Anthropologists makes awards each year for the best student podium and poster presentations. NYCEP students received seven awards and four Honorable Mentions from 2014-2018.
Of the 29 trainees who received a NYCEP PhD since 2010, 11 hold tenure-track positions as Assistant Professor of Anthropology, Anatomy or Biology; two are in the American Museum of Natural History Education department, one in a senior, the other a junior position. Eight are postdocs and three are adjunct Assistant Professors; two hold appointments in writing programs, one is in industry and two others are seeking full-time jobs while teaching. NYCEP trainees, associates and faculty participated in 473 outreach activities and authored 1578 publications over the course of IGERT funding.

Title: IGERT: Distributed Renewable Energy: From Science and Technology to Entrepreneurship and Policy
Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Training (IGERT) award supports the development of a multidisciplinary graduate training program focused on distributed renewable energy sources available from the sun. Research will be focused in the areas of inexpensive and environmentally benign photovoltaic materials, efficient sunlight capture using nanotechnology and advanced optical design, hydrogen generation using artificial photosynthesis, and improved fuel cells using hydrogen-based fuels. Research will also explore the changes in economic and business models necessitated by distributed energy sources and what motivates the adoption of renewable energy to facilitate its adoption in the marketplace. The education and training plans include teaching and fieldwork at partner African universities, internships in U.S. or European institutions, and a new curriculum that includes entrepreneurship and social sciences, and makes students effective communicators. 

The program will produce scientific leaders and entrepreneurs trained in the field of renewable energy who are ready to initiate major advances leading to sustainable development and global prosperity, while protecting the environment. Significant activities include teaching and fieldwork in African universities and involvement of inner city high schools and the local community. The societal impact of the proposed effort will be used to foster the recruitment of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics students from under-represented groups.

IGERT is an NSF-wide program intended to meet the challenges of educating U.S. Ph.D. scientists and engineers with the interdisciplinary background, deep knowledge in a chosen discipline, and the technical, professional, and personal skills needed for the career demands of the future. The program is intended to catalyze a cultural change in graduate education by establishing innovative new models for graduate education and training in a fertile environment for collaborative research that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries.
Outcome Report:
A diverse set of PhD students were recruited for completion of an IGERT training program designed to broaden the PhD educational experience. The students came from a variety of science and engineering departments where they were carrying out basic research that could be applied to renewable energy. After the IGERT program, they completed their PhD work in their home department through the traditional faculty mentor relationship. During the two year long IGERT program, students were required to get outside of their home department for a variety of activities including coursework, internships, conferences, and outreach. A set of required courses were developed that cover the broader issues enabling implementation of renewable energy technology, such as effective technical communication, economics, entrepreneurship, and public policy. The courses impacted a large number of students outside the IGERT program and continue to be offered each year. The IGERT students were required to find a technical internship during the first year. Professional networking was encouraged to enable the students to find paid internships and to apply for independent funding to support travel to internships. In the second year of the IGERT program, teams of students were required to travel to Africa to teach and present research results. The students developed a self-contained set of classroom demonstrations to illustrate a variety of energy topics, including solar, chemical, batteries, and fuel cells, to grade school students. The students also developed a short course on the fabrication of solar panel from individual cells. The solar panels were constructed using locally sourced materials as much as possible. The solar panel workshop was targeted to high school and postsecondary students. Over the grant period, the IGERT fellows reached thousands of students through the classroom demonstrations and workshops. The breadth of PhD education offered through the IGERT program resulted in better training in technical communication to diverse audiences, working in teams, and non-technical issues that surround the adoption of renewable energy. The broader educational experience is reflected in the diverse achievements in professional development, entrepreneurship, and education for the students who have completed the program.

Title: IGERT: Returning the Radio to Chemistry: Integrating Radiochemistry into a Chemistry Ph.D. Program

Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Training (IGERT) program supports the development of an interdisciplinary, multi-institutional graduate training program in radiochemistry. Interdisciplinary fields such as molecular imaging, environmental remediation, nuclear energy, and national security rely increasingly on specialized radiochemical knowledge. But few chemistry graduate programs exist with the capabilities to train radiochemists and few students engage in radiochemical research. The goal of this program is to stimulate a resurgence of interest in radiochemistry among Ph.D. students, producing scientists who can fill this critical need.
 
Hunter College of CUNY, Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center, University of Missouri at Columbia, University of Nevada Las Vegas, and several other leading radiochemistry institutions (including national laboratories and industry) will together train future scientists across multiple scientific disciplines to innovate, understand and employ radiochemistry effectively. This model will include a venue for the development of effective communication skills to foster a better-informed public who are more accepting and knowledgeable about the use, benefits and safety of radiochemistry. By drawing upon the collaborative efforts of the partnering institutes as well as Hunter's experience in recruiting and training women and minorities, this IGERT aims to increase the number and diversity of Ph.D. scientists with strong radiochemistry backgrounds.

IGERT is an NSF-wide program intended to meet the challenges of educating U.S. Ph.D. scientists and engineers with the interdisciplinary background, deep knowledge in a chosen discipline, and the technical, professional, and personal skills needed for the career demands of the future. The program is intended to catalyze a cultural change in graduate education by establishing innovative new models for graduate education and training in a fertile environment for collaborative research that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries.
Outcome Report:
The Hunter NSF IGERT project “Returning the Radio to Chemistry: Integrating Radiochemistry into a PhD program” had a profound impact on the national radiochemistry community and a profound institutional impact on Hunter College and the City University of New York’s graduate programs in chemistry and biochemistry.  Radiochemistry is essentially chemistry using radioactive materials and bridges many disciplines.  
Our program firmly established collaborations and research opportunities between Hunter faculty and researchers at IGERT partner institutions (especially at Weill Cornell Medical College, Memorial Sloan Kettering) and the IGERT was the foundation for collaborations and research opportunities at several national laboratories (Brookhaven, Los Alamos, Argonne).  The research collaborations and opportunities provided to students (trainees) added value to the trainee educational experiences.  Students had the opportunity to conduct research in interdisciplinary research spanning many fields.  The partnership with research intensive institutions provided the opportunity for students to conduct scholarly research with an application or a clinical focus.  Faculty at Hunter also had the opportunity to employ their considerable talents in new projects that had clear application.
One of the hallmarks of the Hunter Radiochemistry IGERT is the co-mentorship model where all students had mentors at Hunter College and a partnering institution.  The co-mentorship model allowed students to work on high impact projects that had a scholarly component and also a clinical or applied component.  This model allowed students the opportunity to work in collaborators’ laboratories thus providing the trainees experience in different lab environments.   A key added value is the opportunity for training, critiques, and feedback from two co-mentors. The co-mentors and different institutions advanced the trainees’ education and career skills by access to advanced instrumentation and facilities that are not available in most university settings. The trainees and faculty embraced this model as an approach to produce scholarly, often fundamental research with clear applications, either clinical or related to isotope production, environmental remediation, nuclear fuel cycle and nuclear security.  One faculty states “We have now collaborations going beyond the actual the IGERT students and doing collaborations in different fields independent of the IGERT program, so it really fostered and started collaborations much more than- I would say it brings people together who would not usually have come together or sought out each other.” 
New courses were developed to add value to the trainees’ educational experience: Hunter College and the CUNY Graduate Center now offer Introduction to Radiochemistry as an elective in the undergraduate and first year graduate curricula. Courses were tailored for the students’ research needs. Courses were streamed from partnering institutions to Hunter.  
Research conducted by the trainees were of the highest impact due to the advanced facilities and application focus of partnering institutions.  As a result, trainees, Hunter faculty and partnering institution faculty were able to publish in extremely high impact and important journals. Trainees and faculty applied and received patents on their work. Research conducted was interdisciplinary and spanned many applications; these include medical imaging, therapy of cancer, neurogenerative disease, medical isotope production, studies of radioisotopes that are important to nuclear energy, nuclear waste remediation and environmental remediation.
Enhanced radiochemistry infrastructure at Hunter College: Hunter College administration was extremely supportive of the IGERT and understood the importance of Radiochemistry.  As a result, we added two new full-time faculty in Radiochemistry and provided them with competitive start-up packages and laboratory renovations.  Hunter also added a research associate (staff scientist) who facilitates research of Radiochemistry trainees and their collaborations at partnering institutions.  He also is the liaison to Environmental Health and Safety with respect to Radiochemistry.  Hunter is also providing classroom and laboratory space for the present Radiochemistry course and advanced courses.
Enhanced Radiochemistry opportunities at CUNY in general: The interest in Radiochemistry has spawned a radiochemistry program at Lehman College of CUNY.  Over the past five years, three professors with radiochemistry research and passion for radiochemistry education were hired.  These and Hunter professors provide a critical mass for radiochemistry research and education at CUNY.   Undergraduates and graduate students are quite interested in pursuing radiochemistry research following the model that the IGERT espoused.  We are extending and expanding our relationships with partnering institutions in the establishment of named fellowships for predoctoral students.
National scene:  The Hunter radiochemistry program has become nationally recognized for the caliber of students, the high impact projects, and the successes in winning competitive federal grants and publishing high impact papers of the young new professors both at Hunter and Lehman Colleges of CUNY.  We have graduated 12 students; these have gone on to academia, postdoctoral fellowships, industry, and entered the financial world.  As a result of these successes, the PI has been asked to take over the national directorship of the Department of Energy Nuclear Chemistry Summer Schools (NCSS) from 2019 to 2023.  The NCSS are the primary means to introduce Radiochemistry and Nuclear Chemistry to undergraduates.

Title: IGERT: Training, Research and Education in Engineering for Cultural Heritage Diagnostics
Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Training (IGERT) award supports the development of an interdisciplinary graduate training program in engineering for cultural heritage diagnostics. Forensic engineering, the investigation of failures and failure mechanisms, is uniquely suited yet rarely used to assess the damage to artifacts of cultural heritage, including ancient monuments, historic buildings and paintings, from the ravages of time, pollution, natural disasters and decay.

This IGERT, based at the University of California at San Diego, trains graduate students to develop diagnostic methodologies and analytical models that will be deployed and tested on a) Renaissance art works and historic structures in Florence, Italy, and b) archaeological sites and artifacts in Jordan and Israel. Trainees learn and develop new state-of-the-art methods for the long-term "health monitoring" of cultural artifacts, including non-destructive testing, cyberinfrastructure and engineering analysis. Using a team-based approach, trainees will create an integrated platform for diagnostic and predictive modeling, including multispectral imaging, simulation, data synthesis and visual analytics. Students are advised by three co-mentors, one from the student's primary discipline and two from other disciplines. Substantial field research abroad will prepare them for careers in international science and engineering, and the tools and methodologies developed for cultural heritage can be applied more broadly to the analysis of degraded or obsolete infrastructure, such as public buildings, roads and bridges, as well as almost any other engineered component or system. 

IGERT is an NSF-wide program intended to meet the challenges of educating U.S. Ph.D. scientists and engineers with the interdisciplinary background, deep knowledge in a chosen discipline, and the technical, professional, and personal skills needed for the career demands of the future. The program is intended to catalyze a cultural change in graduate education by establishing innovative new models for graduate education and training in a fertile environment for collaborative research that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries.
Outcome Report:
IGERT-TEECH enabled the creation of an agile and nimble engineering and science ecosystem, where students can immerse themselves in dynamic learning environments and cultivate new academic relationships, where they can broaden their worldview and acquire the professionalism necessary for responsible research, business, or advocacy in our increasingly global society. Cultural heritage challenges and problems often require different kinds of solutions from different fields of study. In the process of collaboratively addressing specific problems, students advance the state of the art as well as their own personal development. IGERT-TEECH serves to engage, enable, and empower students through experience-based learning, thereby creating resilient, resourceful, and responsive science and engineering professionals. Experienced-based learning, in which the research, education and training become a means by which life skills are acquired, has a lasting and indelible impact on students, who will reflect on their experience with a community of individuals who guided their growth from consumers to producers of knowledge. This ecosystem is primed for innovation and the development of tomorrow's talent pool and workforce. It trains engineers from across the academic career spectrum, from high-school students, undergraduate and graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, as well as research scientists and junior faculty at the beginning of their careers. It also provides an incubator for those seeking to transition to and succeed in the private sector. IGERT-TEECH seeks to break through barriers created by traditional research silos, linking collaborative and disruptive research across domains. Its silo buster mentality is aimed at creating a new methodology for collaborative research and training, joining human imagination, intuition and creativity (great minds) with big data to forge a new breed of engineers capable of tackling tomorrow's grand challenges in collaborative, interdisciplinary teams. The goal is to challenge traditional research models, theories and techniques by pushing trainees out of traditional silos through work at the interface of multiple domains, advised by mentors from multiple disciplines, to create a fresh and transformative new approach. All trainees will have triple-advisors representing multiple engineering and science domains. We have shown that this ambitious advising approach is both viable and highly transformative to overall trainee and team development, advancing and empowering the collaborative research and training approach. Each trainee will be assigned an international academic liaison, further increasing the impact of the planned international field research and education experience, grooming the student trainees' ability to communicate effectively and efficiently across domain boundaries and cultures alike. Incoming student trainees are paired with senior trainees, providing one-to-one mentorship, while enabling knowledge transfer and retention. Additionally, advisors will function as liaisons between students and our corporate and governmental partners and colleagues. IGERT-TECCH also became a catalyst, unifying campus interests and priorities, addressing both the academic and personal development of student trainees. It is in a unique position to offer students, across the broadest range of disciplines, the opportunity to contribute to the knowledge and preservation of material culture from across the span of human history. STEM- or STEAM-focused primary and secondary educational programs have demonstrated that such curricula translate into a competitive advantage for children of all backgrounds, and that they build character and self-esteem. Indeed, STEAM, and certainly engineering specifically, can serve as a pathway into every possible future career. This revolution in education, led by schools such as San Diego's High Tech High, is characterized in part by youth empowerment through close mentoring. Very often, however, inspired and motivated high school students go on to university only to be discouraged by less enlightened and sometimes impenetrable academic cultures. CHEI is designed to provide a seamless transition from STEAM-focused high school programs into the Jacobs School of Engineering at UC San Diego. Our open, student-centered collaboratory environment enables students to maintain their post-secondary STEAM momentum while giving them unfettered access to the resources and mentoring they need to thrive, on campus and off. With this ecosystem in place IGERT-TEECH (now continuing as CHEI) is poised to attract top domestic and international students, retain and nurture student trainees, create a sense of belonging, foster self-discovery and develop professional skills, and contribute to a larger community across and beyond the campus.
Among the program's lasting legacy are also a set courses, drawing highly interdisciplnary student cohorts, with focus on (a) 3D Printable Robotics aimed at delivering the right sensor to the right location at the right time, (b) Diagnostic Imaging aimed at recording the most representative data assets and (c) Forensic Engineering, studying cause and effect relationships captured by these big-data assets.

Title: IGERT:  Sustainable Grid Integration of Distributed and Renewable Resources
Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Training (IGERT) award supports a research and educational program at The University of Texas at Austin to address sustainable grid integration of distributed and renewable energy systems, a crucial priority for greenhouse gas reduction and energy independence. A key context for this project is The Pecan Street Project, a collaborative university-utility Austin-based effort to redesign and reformulate Austin's electric power system. The research goal is to revolutionize the way energy is produced, used, stored, and traded consistent with economic, environment, social, and security objectives. Results will be applicable to distributed power (smart grid) systems throughout the U.S. and will have a significant economic impact.

Trainees will be engaged in collaborative basic and applied research in data communications, cybersecurity, network management computation, distributed generation (solar, wind, fuel cells), power electronics and controls, energy storage (batteries, flywheels, compressed air, thermal storage, electric vehicles), building HVAC systems and energy efficient buildings, efficient appliances, and sensors for system performance, tracking, and optimization. IGERT trainees will develop course materials appropriate for high school math and science educators in support of UTeachEngineering, and will assist in the creation of content for a graduate-level course on the Grid Of The Future. Outreach to underrepresented groups in K-12 will be facilitated by UTeachEngineering and development of new educational materials for high school engineering courses.

IGERT is an NSF-wide program intended to meet the challenges of educating U.S. Ph.D. scientists and engineers with the interdisciplinary background, deep knowledge in a chosen discipline, and the technical, professional, and personal skills needed for the career demands of the future. The program is intended to catalyze a cultural change in graduate education by establishing innovative new models for graduate education and training in a fertile environment for collaborative research that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries.
Outcome Report:
The vision of a university collaborative inter-intra-departmental undertaking became a reality in spring of 2010 with the launch of IGERT: Sustainable Grid Integration of Distributed and Renewable Resources located at The University of Texas at Austin. A natural environment for scaffolding affiliations, networks, and research developed from the complex partnerships inspired by IGERT between UT and Pecan Street Inc. with participation from 20 faculty members from schools of Architecture, Engineering, Natural Sciences, Business, Law, and LBJ School emerged as the grant evolved. The exchange of students and research between TU Munchen and the Netherlands added international components that proved advantageous to all students involved.
The first year of IGERT met challenges that included inter-university participation coupled with graduate students who did not know each other or their colleagues’ research pressed into a collaborative setting. Year one resulted in a very lose coupling of the IGERT cohort. However, changes made in management of the IGERT weekly meetings, recommendations from the Advisory Committee, students working on a single project together under the direction of Dr. Thomas Edgar, and interspersing social activities transformed the IGERT program. The momentum generated from these changes resulted in an organic organization and group of researchers who established a reputation for their group – IGERT, and generated respect from other researchers in multiple research areas of sustainable resources and energy.
Following the next five years, IGERT became a brand that signified progressive inquiry in a variety of areas that led to important spheres of influence in public policy and research. Our IGERT alumni are now among experts in areas of sustainable grid integration and renewable resources’ research. The IGERT alumni are sought-after candidates for university professors, leaders in university forums and other research collaboratives associated with their research agendas to include topics on water and wind energy, Eagle Ford Shale drilling, electric vehicles and the smart grid. Some of the graduate students have continued their research as post-docs in areas that will extend their research findings beyond their dissertation topics and ultimately to patents as well as continue the spirit of the IGERT vision of supporting renewable energy for many years in the future. The IGERT legacy continues with the alternative course offerings and modified schedules at The University of Texas at Austin.
The IGERT participants heavily influenced the system of traditional semester course offerings. Prior to the IGERT program, alternative schedules of course offerings was limited. However, with the implementation of IGERT and the students’ exposure to a variety of closely connected research agendas, students insisted that they wanted more classes but in a condensed format. The weekly meetings exposed students to their peer’s research. Quickly, students made associations between their research and the other students with their research presentations. One student stated, “I am so interested in water and I know it will help my research but my class schedule is so tight, I can’t find a way to take a class.” The Advisory committee also recommended more class offerings in an alternative format. Thus, beginning in 2012, a three-day short-course “Introduction to Electric Power for Legal, Accounting, and Regulatory Professionals” and a one-day short-course “Locational Marginal Pricing” for non-technical professionals in the electricity industry was introduced followed by new courses that include: Technology Commercialization, Energy Development and Policy, Advanced Topics in Power Electronics,  Modern Control Theory, Clean.Smart.Energy, Water Technology and Policy, and Energy Technology and Policy. The short courses are very popular and continue to be in demand. A graduate portfolio program in Energy Studies (GPPES) has also been added at UT as a result of IGERT. The GPPES signifies an authentic response to mounting university-wide student interest in sustainable energy studies introduced by the IGERT program implemented in 2010 and supported by the UT Austin Energy Institute. The complexity of offering a multi-departmental program is counterbalanced by permitting students to design their own program to meet the coursework requirements of the GPPES by choosing from a wide range of courses offered by participating departments. Completion of the GPPES facilitates students’ interests in energy policy issues and enables students across the university to demonstrate to future employers through their final transcripts the students’ credentials in the field of energy. 
The IGERT program has produced a permanent and enduring legacy. As IGERT students graduate and enter professorships, research groups such as NREL, SANDIA, and Argonne National Labs, assume leadership roles as authors for Scientific American and editors for contemporary research journals, and respond to invitations to address national and international audiences on topics pertaining to sustainable and renewable resources, IGERT remains alive and well. Isaac Newton stated, “If I have seen further it is standing on the shoulders of Giants” [The Correspondence of Isaac Newton] and the IGERT alumni have become the giants for future researchers to stand on their shoulders.

Title: IGERT: Complex Scene Perception
Abstract:
This Integrative Graduate Education and Research Training (IGERT) award to the University of Pennsylvania supports the development of a new training paradigm for perception scientists and engineers, and is designed to provide them with a unique grasp of the computational and psychophysical underpinnings of the phenomena of perception. It will create a new role model of a well-rounded perceptual scientist with a firm grasp of both computational and experimental analytic skills. The existence of such a cadre of U.S. researchers will contribute to the country's global competitiveness in the growing machine perception and robotics industry.

Research and training activities are organized around five thematic areas related to complex scene perception: (1) Spatial perception and navigation; (2) Perception of material and terrain properties; (3) Neural responses to natural signals, saliency and attention; (4) Object Recognition in context and visual memory; and (5) Agile Perception. Interdisciplinary research will enable new insights into the astounding performance of human and animal perception as well as the design of new algorithms that will make robots perceive and act in complex scenes.

IGERT trainees will commit in advance of acceptance to a five-year graduate training program, comprising the following components: (1) Core disciplinary training; (2) one-year cross-disciplinary training in a chosen second discipline; (3) participation in two foundational and one integrational IGERT courses; (4) attendance of an interdisciplinary IGERT seminar; (5) co-advising throughout the 5 graduate years by an interdisciplinary faculty team ; and (6) completion of the Ph.D. dissertation.

IGERT is an NSF-wide program intended to meet the challenges of educating U.S. Ph.D. scientists and engineers with the interdisciplinary background, deep knowledge in a chosen discipline, and the technical, professional, and personal skills needed for the career demands of the future. The program is intended to catalyze a cultural change in graduate education by establishing innovative new models for graduate education and training in a fertile environment for collaborative research that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries.
Outcome Report:
The goal of this IGERT was to create a new training paradigm for perception scientists and engineers with a unique grasp of the computational and psychophysical underpinnings of the phenomena of perception. Complex scene perception involves the study of the brain and the design of algorithms for understanding visual scenes encountered in daily life. Twenty-four (24) trainees were educated cross disciplines with engineering classes attended by psychologists and neuroscientists and psychophysics classes attended by engineers. For six years, this interdisciplinary group was meeting weekly in a journal club learning how to cross boundaries in the study of perception both in research conduct and presentation. Thesis topics were concentrated around spatial perception and navigation, perception of materials, object recognition in context and visual memory, and neural responses to natural signals. An example is the study of spatial perception in animals during reorientation, a situation encountered in many robotics applications as well. When a navigator’s internal sense of direction is disrupted, she must rely on external cues to regain her bearings, a process termed spatial reorientation. Extensive research has demonstrated that the geometric shape of the environment exerts powerful control over reorientation behavior, but the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying this phenomenon are not well understood. Whereas some theories claim that geometry controls behavior through an allocentric mechanism potentially tied to the hippocampus, others postulate that disoriented navigators reach their goals by using an egocentric view-matching strategy. To resolve this debate,   hippocampal representations were characterized during reorientation. It was found that the alignment of the recovered hippocampal map was determined by the geometry of the chamber, but not by non-geometric cues, even when these cues could be used to disambiguate geometric ambiguities. Hippocampal activity was recorded as disoriented mice performed a classical goal-directed spatial memory task in a rectangular chamber, and again it was found that the recovered hippocampal map aligned solely to the chamber geometry. A strong correspondence between the hippocampal map alignment and the animal’s behavior made possible to predict the search location of the animal from neural responses on a trial-by-trial basis. Together, these results demonstrate that spatial reorientation involves the alignment of the hippocampal map to local geometry. In a robot navigation project, the estimation of motion direction of a robot was studied (figure). This is a difficult problem because of the nonconvex cost function of the perspective camera motion equation and because of the non-Gaussian noise in two-frame optic flow estimates. Nonetheless, a good estimate of motion under these conditions is important for robotic navigation, especially in the case of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles. Situations like monocular sensors on small platforms pose additional problems: computational resources are often very limited and estimates must be made in real time under unusual viewing conditions (e.g. with a vertically flipped camera, no visible ground plane, and a single pass through a scene). These contexts present many sources of noise. Real-time flow estimation produces unreliable data, and the associated noise is often pervasive and non-Gaussian, which makes estimation difficult and explicit outlier rejection problematic. Even in the noise-free case, the estimation of camera motion is plagued with many suboptimal interpretations (illusions) caused by the hilly structure of the cost function. Additionally, forward motion, which is very common in real-world navigation, is known to be particularly hard for monocular visual odometry. The novel contribution was the reformulation of the perspective camera motion equation using a lifted kernel for joint parameter and weight estimation.
